News.title: Migrant mega-dinghy carrying 140 people reaches UK from Normandy after ‘longest-ever Channel crossing’
News.content:
A MIGRANT boat carrying 140 people to the UK was launched from the furthest ever point in the Channel yesterday.

It comes just days after Prime Minister Andy Burnham hailed a crackdown on crossings.



The mega-dinghy was launched from the Jobourg region in Normandy, 180 miles west of Calais.

Despite launching six boats and two helicopters to monitor the boat, French cops allowed it to carry on, noting in a press release on Sunday morning: “The vessel is currently continuing its journey towards the United Kingdom.”



They said that despite the departure location being “unusual for the area”, they were still available to provide “rapid and robust assistance”.

The boat was then met by two RNLI lifeboats with the migrants taken ashore at Portsmouth before being transferred to the processing centre at Manston.

RNLI boats carrying migrants docked in Langstone Harbour near Portsmouth yesterday evening.

It comes after the PM met with his French counterpart Emmanuel Macron with the small boats issue a focal point of talks.

A new surge team of 45 officers has been deployed – but drew criticism as it emerged, they would have to seek permission in order to enter the water.

The crossings were the first in nine days after more than a week of no migrant dinghies, according to Home Office data.



It comes after masked protesters chanting “stop the boats” were able to bring chaos to the Port of Dover on Saturday.

Cars were stuck in huge queues after the balaclava-clad group blocked off roads from 7am.

Kevin Mills, who leads Dover District Council, criticised Kent Police for being “slow” to react to the far-right group, who were “exceptionally well organised”.

He said the force “appeared to be quite slow to keep the roads and the networks open, which is disappointing”.

“The protesters knew what they were doing, I’m not sure the police did know what was going to happen.



“But then I accept that the police resource is stretched.”

Kent Police said no arrests had been made and labelled the demonstration as “spontaneous”.

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds criticised the protest but declined to comment “on the security and policing side of it”.

He told Sky News: “I do think our police forces deal with a great deal across British towns and cities.

“And these days, people can use modern communications in ways that do make things happen quickly.



“I think on the whole, the police handle it very well. But look, peaceful protest, yes. Those kinds of scenes, absolutely not.”

Reform UK politician Robert Jenrick said he had “always hated people obstructing other people doing their daily life, whether it’s Just Stop Oil or whatever”.

He added: “And I don’t like people going around in balaclavas, which is obviously very intimidating. In fact, our party’s policy is to ban face coverings like that.

“But do I understand why people are extremely frustrated? Yes, absolutely. This needs to end. This farce of the small boats has been going on for far too long.

“And in fact you saw at our conference Nigel Farage and (National Rally president) Jordan Bardella, the likely next Prime Minister of France, signing an agreement which has the prospect of ending this once and for all.”



A Government spokesperson said on Saturday that it condemned the behaviour in Dover and the travel disruption it caused.

News.title: Huge volcanic eruption in Indonesia sends ash cloud 15km into sky closing 8 airports & leaving 170k passengers stranded
News.content:
AT LEAST 170,000 air passengers have been left stranded after after a furious Indonesian volcano blasted enormous plumes of ash 15km into the sky.

Eight airports have been forced to close as vast clouds of volcanic ash billowed across the atmosphere.



Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta International Airport was among those locked off, with officials warning that the ash could pose a serious danger to aircraft engines.

A staggering 1,558 flights have been delayed, with the affected airports expected to remain closed until midnight as authorities scramble to assess the fallout.





The eruption began late on Friday and has continued to rumble ominously.

Lava fountains and relentless seismic tremors have been reported following the dramatic blast.

Its booming eruptions have echoed across surrounding regions, with authorities warning of continued volcanic activity.

Two further eruptions struck in the early hours of Sunday, adding to fears among residents and travellers.



The health minister has urged people living in ash-hit areas to stay indoors and wear face masks.

Officials warn the fallout could cause respiratory problems as well as irritation to the eyes and skin.

The ash has already begun causing misery on the ground, with several schools cancelling activities after students and residents complained of sore, irritated eyes.

Some fisherman were also forced to abandon trips out to sea after reporting similar problems.



One resident, Aldi Candra Prayogi, told local newspaper Kompas that the ash had left his eyes feeling as though they were filled with “small grains of sand”.

He said he had been forced to use eye drops to ease the irritation, while the layer of volcanic dust was so thick that he had to sweep his front yard every five minutes.

There has been no tsunami warning linked to the latest eruptions, and officials have reported no casualties or ordered any evacuations.

But authorities have warned people to stay at least 3km from the volcano’s active crater, with the nearest settlement more than 16km away.



Anak Krakatau – meaning “Child of Krakatoa” – rose from the sea in the early 20th century inside the enormous underwater caldera left behind by the catastrophic eruption of Mount Krakatoa in 1883.

That eruption was one of the most powerful in recorded history, with explosions heard thousands of miles away and vast quantities of ash blasted into the atmosphere.

More recently, Anak Krakatau itself made headlines when a section of the volcano collapsed into the sea in December 2018, triggering a devastating tsunami that swept into coastal communities on Java and Sumatra.

At least 430 people were killed and thousands more were injured or displaced as huge waves slammed into the shoreline.

Researchers later found that some of the chunks of rock involved in the collapse were an astonishing 70 to 90 metres high.



The island was left at only around a quarter of its previous size.

The latest activity has been building since July, according to Indonesia’s Geological Agency, with Sunday’s eruptions described as the strongest during that period.

Lana Saria, head of the Geological Agency, said the repeated blasts suggested magma and volcanic gases were continuing to rise beneath the volcano.

But she warned there was no way of knowing whether the heightened activity would develop into something far larger.

Officials say the immediate dangers include thick ash, high concentrations of volcanic gases and chunks of scorching rock being hurled from the crater.



And with the volcano sitting in the Sunda Strait between two of Indonesia’s most heavily populated islands, authorities are continuing to monitor every movement beneath the restless peak.

Indonesia lies on the notorious Pacific “Ring of Fire” – a vast 25,000-mile horseshoe of volcanoes and earthquake zones encircling the Pacific.

Around 90 per cent of the world’s earthquakes occur along the belt, which is also home to roughly 75 per cent of the planet’s active volcanoes.

News.title: Germany’s far-Right AfD party set for big win in state election, exit polls show
News.content:
GERMANY’s far-right party is set to win a historic landslide in a key state election, exit polls show.

The Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is projected gain a whopping 44.5 per cent of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt.



The ultra conservative party soared past German Chancellor Frierich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) who are set to take just 18.5 per cent.

The AfD – who have faced probes and accusations by Berlin for right-wing extremism – need to reach 50 per cent to control the state parliament.



If they don’t manage the threshold, it could force several mainstream parties – who have balked at the idea of the AfD in power – to make a coalition with them.

The AfD wants closer ties with Vladimir Putin‘s Russia and a hardline approach to immigration.



The party’s co-leader Alice Weidel hailed it as a “historic” result which had given the AfD a clear mandate to govern.

The projected results mark a political earthquake in Germany – no far-right party has won control of a state in the nation since World War Two.



Should they gain full control of local authorities, they will have power over policing, education and culture.

Saxony-Anhalt, which has a population of 2.1 million, and its AfD officials have been called “far-right extremist” by German intelligence.

The party rejects this label.

Germany’s history with Nazism has fuelled fears of a rising far-right party, and prompted establishment groups to shy away from cooperation.

Some parties have outright refused to form coaltions with the AfD – a policy known as the “firewall”.



The CDU’s secretary general Franziska Hoppermann said her party “does not collaborate with extremists” in response to the exit poll.

She said: “Above all, not with right-wing extremists.”

Sunday’s result also marks another blow to Merz – with the German leader’s popularity seeing sharp declines since the beginning of his tenure.

The AfD has not only dominated the local election campaign – it is also sending political shock waves across the country.

It is now Germany’s most popular party and the latest victory will fuel belief among its millions of supporters.

News.title: Tributes to ‘beloved’ mum, 38, who died after car hit wall in UK city
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

CRASH TRAGEDY Tributes to ‘beloved’ mum, 38, who died after car hit wall in UK city

THE heartbroken family of a woman killed in a horrific car crash have paid a moving tribute to their “gorgeous” daughter, mum, sister and aunty.

Kelly Marie Lundie, 38, died after the red Nissan Juke she was travelling in left the road and smashed into a brick wall.



Emergency services rushed to the scene shortly after 11.30pm on Friday, September 4.

Kelly was tragically pronounced dead at the scene.



Her devastated family have now described her as “outgoing and full of life”, saying her presence could “light up a room”.

In a moving tribute, they said: “Kelly Marie Lundie was gorgeous, inside and out.



“She was outgoing and full of life.

“Her presence could light up a room, and her smile and personality will remain in the hearts of those who knew her.

“Above all, Kelly was a devoted and beloved mother to her son, Caleb.

“He was her world, and the love she had for him was immeasurable.



“She was also the best aunty to her nephews, who adored her and shared a very special bond with her.

“She brought so much fun, affection and happiness into their lives.

“Kelly was a cherished daughter, a much-loved sister, a wonderful aunty and a loyal friend.

“She meant something different and special to so many people, and her loss has left an enormous space in the lives of everyone who loved her.”

The family added: “There are no words that can truly express how deeply Kelly will be missed.”



Cops are continuing to investigate the circumstances surrounding the fatal smash.

They are asking anybody with information to get in touch, quoting reference 26000727021.

News.title: Teenager & two men charged with attempted murder after town centre shooting that left three injured
News.content:
SHOOTING CHARGE Teenager & two men charged with attempted murder after town centre shooting that left three injured

A TEENAGER and two men have been charged with attempted murder after a town centre shooting left three people injured.

Cops and emergency services swarmed the scene after the horror in Braintree, Essex, on Monday night.



Two teenagers sustained serious injuries to their face and upper body, while a third person was also injured.

Now, cops have charged Destiny Ema, 23, of Meadgate Avenue, Chelmsford, Kayden Brown, 18, of Noaks Avenue, Chelmsford, with attempted murder.



A 17-year-old from Braintree – who cannot be named for legal reasons – has also been charged with attempted murder.

Essex Police said that all three are due to appear at Chelmsford Magistrates’ Court on Monday.

Ema was also charged with numerous other offences connected to separate investigations, confirmed cops.

A 16-year-old boy previously arrested in connection with the incident has been released on police bail until 30 November.

Officers rushed to Market Place at around 10.10pm following reports of the firearms incident.

Cops later arrested three people and recovered a shotgun and ammunition.



The cordons which had been in place in the town centre have now all been lifted.

Chief Supt Kirby said previously: “I want to thank the community and local businesses for their support and understanding whilst the forensic part of the investigation was on-going.

“We do not underestimate the impact an incident like this can have, and will continue to be visible in the town centre so if you have any information or concerns please speak to one of our officers.”

News.title: I’m a sex-mad politician bonking constituents in secret hour-long city hall ORGIES – I want to create a swingers’ utopia
News.content:
POLITICIANS are often accused of naked ambition – but for this one, that’s no bad thing.

Julien Ferrat has made it his mission to bring sexual liberation to the masses – spectacularly blowing up the uptight image of the typical suited-and-booted politician in the process.



Sex-mad Julien, 35, is a leading politician in Manheim, Germany, and has dreams of transforming the city and the country – well-known for its love of bureaucracy and order – into a swingers‘ paradise.

Because despite their love of rules and process, Germans do have a few guilty pleasures.

The country widely embraces nudism – and has a very liberal view on sex.



Ferrat, a keen nudist and swinger himself, wants to take that lustful undercurrent very much into the mainstream – and isn’t shy about getting down and dirty in the process.

The leader of the liberal Die Mannheimer party told The Sun how he threw a wild swingers’ party inside his local town hall last Friday – after tricking officials into believing he had booked the room for a political meeting.

Seven people took up Ferrat’s invitation, agreeing to arrive at the town hall at a punctual 9pm – because apparently even a rendezvous of this sort must bow to the German devotion to timekeeping.

But the guest list could have been considerably more crowded.

Around 50 people initially approached Ferrat, prompting him to try to secure a city council permit to transform the civic hall into a veritable lair of lust.



The council, unsurprisingly, had other ideas – and his request was flatly denied.

But as the palatial clock turned 9pm, the gang crept into the meeting room and began their X-rated rendezvous.

Ferrat tells The Sun: “We were seven men and two women but two of the men watched so there were only seven active participants.



“The room was booked for three hours after I tricked the council and said it was for a political meet-up, therefore no one disturbed us.

“The actual orgy lasted about 60 minutes.”

Ferrat says the group, aged between 28 and 55, spent the rest of the evening knocking back booze, tucking into food and getting to know one another.

He describes the sex-fuelled bash as a success, calling it “a small but delightful swingers party.

“There was a great sense of closeness thanks to the preliminary meetings.



“It was the best event at the town hall I have ever attended.”

Asked why he came up with the idea, he explains: “It was designed to smash social taboos in Mannheim”, which is governed by the socially conservative Christian Democrats party.

He argues that “group sex with city council members would be the ultimate in closeness with the citizens”, claiming there are no laws that explicitly ban swinger parties at the city hall.



But his romp has sparked a furious backlash, with local politicians coldly warning him “there will be consequences,” local media reported

Ferrat says he could now face a fine of 1,000 euros or more over the stunt.

But the dad-of-three, dubbed “Germany’s craziest councillor”, said the outrageous orgy was the first step in his campaign to turn the city into a “nudist and swingers’ haven”.

From naked shoppers to designated bonking beaches, it’s a dream Julien can already imagine coming true.

Ferrat adds: “People who are nudists and swingers who are practising this lifestyle and coming to the town will be able to walk around naked to the supermarket, to the bank…



“We will also have designated locations where people can have sex like on beaches or swingers clubs.”

Asked about child safeguarding, Ferrat said: “It’s the decision of the parents if they want to bring their children here.”

He insists his cheeky vision could also deliver a financial boost to the city.



Julien explains: “I want to attract tourists and revenue, I think this is a great idea.

“If we have a lot of private investors, it won’t even cost the city a lot.”

A Mannheim city hall spokesman told local media: “Based on the rudimentary information available so far, there are considerable doubts about the admissibility and feasibility of the plans mentioned.”

The city hall denied Ferrat’s initial request, citing a lack of clear details and an explanation of how the planned event fitted his political mandate.

Officials stressed that their assessment would depend on a formal and comprehensive request being submitted.



Germany’s appetite for partner-swapping is far from niche, with an estimated 128,000 swingers and a thriving network of clubs and venues catering to the country’s non-monogamous crowd.

And Ferrat is proving more than willing to tap into Germany’s racier side, with sex and tourism becoming unlikely tools in his X-rated political pitch.

Last year, he floated an altogether unconventional proposal: an eight-day “fact-finding” jaunt to Cap d’Agde, the French seaside resort notorious as a mecca for swingers.

The idea was to take curious – and potentially sceptical – Germans to the resort to experience its permissive culture first-hand, with the ultimate ambition of transplanting some of its appeal to Mannheim.

For Mr Ferrat, however, this was not merely a matter of sexual liberalism.



He argues that transforming Mannheim into a German counterpart to Cap d’Agde could draw visitors, grow spending and give the city’s economy an unlikely new source of momentum.

He is hoping that stimulating the economy – and voters’ sexual desires – will be a vote-winner.

Who said politics needs to be boring?

News.title: Welcome to UK’s WORST street for road fines where 277 drivers get caught EVERY DAY…as council plans to go step further
News.content:
FINE HELL Welcome to UK’s WORST street for road fines where 277 drivers get caught EVERY DAY…as council plans to go step further

FURIOUS locals have spoken over their fury over a street that has wracked up the most driving fines in the UK.

Data shows more than 100,000 penalties were issued along Corporation Street in the city centre in Birmingham.



The data – which covers the 12 months to April – equates to an average of some 277 being caught every single day.

And it comes as last month the city announced they are also introduced 20mph zones, in a move slammed by critics as “anti-motorist”.





When The Sun visited the city in August, we found city where many are united by their hatred for one issue – the Clean Air Zone (CAZ).

Birmingham City Council said the high number of fines on Corporation Street is due to fact it connects to the very busy Aston Expressway.



And they defended the CAZ, saying it has slashed pollution the city and the numbers non-compliant drivers have dipped from 15.2% in June 2021 to 3.1% in June 2026.

The council’s rules force drivers to cough up fees for driving in their city – which is £8 a day for cars, taxis and vans, and £50 a day for larger vehicles.

Big brother-style cameras cover three square miles of Birmingham’s centre to monitor drivers – much as it does in cities such as London and Bristol.

But with 100,985 PCNs Corporation street – Brimingham earns the crown of having the most fined street in the UK, beating Irvine Street in Liverpool that has 74,708 and the capital’s Tottenham Court Road with 59,329.

The round the clock CAZ scheme launched in 2021 has pulled in more than £100million.



But the citizens of Britain’s second city are feeling more furious than flush.

Richard Hunt, 48, who runs a removal firm named MDL, is hit with the £8 charge for all city centre jobs.

He said: “If it was really a Clean Air Zone then they just wouldn’t allow these so-called polluting vehicles in at all.



“When they say, you can pollute all you like as long as you pay us £8, that shows how sincere they are.

“What annoys me is that I’m a regular payer but when it has slipped my mind, they don’t look at my record and send me a reminder. No, it’s a £120 fine, which you can pay for £60.

“My partner has an Eco diesel which she pays £30 tax because of how clean it is and yet she has to pay the Clean Air Zone charge.

“What are they doing with all the money…vacuuming the air?”

George Faizey, 22, a trainee lawyer, was also unimpressed by the scheme: “It is utter bull,” he said.



“Nothing to do with clean air makes sense to me because whatever we’re adding it is trifling compared to other places in the world.

“I don’t believe the scheme is about clean air. I think it’s more to do with an extra revenue stream.

“I don’t drive into Birmingham because I have a 2014 diesel and I have already been caught out in Oxford and London.”

Just to add to the madness, it turns out the City Council has fined itself a total of £470,000 because its own vehicles were non-compliant.

Allan Freeman, 59, an odd-job man, said: “Imagine not getting your own vehicles in order and then paying yourself. It’s ridiculous. I don’t drive and it even winds me up.



“I get the bus into the city centre from Nechells and when we get to the junction with the ring-road, nothing moves because all the traffic diverts onto the ring-road to avoid the Clean Air Zone.

“I’ve known a 20 minute bus ride take an hour with all the traffic idling and presumably polluting. Personally I see no reason for it. It’s like the smoking ban to me, a complete waste of time.”

Another non-driver unimpressed with the new scheme was Richard Gredden, 63, a support worker from Cannock.



“I haven’t noticed any difference in the air itself, but I have noticed the lack of shops and small shops in particular because not so many people come into the centre of town.

“I want a clean environment but you have to ask if this initiative is working and if they are considering the downsides of the damage being done to small businesses by people not coming in.”

“I’ve heard we are in danger of losing the Flea Market. Now you find tourists are here but not so much the Brummies.”

Those travelling into Birmingham by car face a potential double-whammy. Whilst many vehicles escape the CAZ charge there is no escaping the high cost of parking and the old one-two against drivers is having an effect.

Kashan Awan, 25, who works in hospitality in the city centre, said: “Everyone I know takes buses or trains into work because they can’t afford the parking charges or sometimes even find a space.



“I see a lot of people getting tickets because they think they can get away with it for a few minutes but they can’t. I can drive, I can afford a car but I don’t bring it into town.”

The central zone covered by the scheme includes some of Birmingham’s poorest and most populous places such as Ladywood and Highgate but living within it doesn’t change anything. If your vehicle is ‘non-compliant’ you have to pay.

Farouq Ahmad, 66, a recently retired lorry driver, said: “I live within the Clean Air Zone and I can tell you one thing – the air isn’t clean.

“Every week I have to clean my windows and my house from all the dust that comes in so something isn’t working.

“And it is ruining businesses. I have a friend who had a flower stall on the marke who had to pay £8-a-day for his van and with fewer customers it crippled him. To drive into town and park, you’re £15 down straight away.”



Down in Birmingham’s historic markets area, many stall holders are against the CAZ.

Here come the 20mph zones By Ethan Singh & Ross Slater BIRMINGHAM is set to become England’s first 20mph city under controversial plans to cut speed limits across almost all of its roads. The city’s council, led by a coalition of Liberal Democrats, Greens and independents, has pushed for every route except major A-roads to cap speeds despite critics blasting the plans as “anti-motorist”. Birmingham town hall leaders insisted the move would ensure private vehicles “no longer dominate street life”, while actively encouraging residents to walk or cycle instead. The controversial plan also promises to reallocate space on the tarmac to build a public transport network they believe is more fitting for a major city. But critics have branded the initiative an “anti-motorist policy” that will hamper travel and snarl up transit across the West Midlands. Richard Holden, the shadow transport secretary, said that left-wing councils had turned 20mph into the “national speed of bureaucracy”. Meanwhile, Reform UK’s Jex Parkin, the leader of Birmingham’s opposition, said of the latest proposal: “This is another anti-motorist policy from a council that seems determined to make getting around Birmingham harder. “People already have enough congestion, restrictions and disruption to deal with without another blanket measure being imposed on them.” The shift marks a stark turning point for a city once celebrated as Britain’s motoring capital due to its heritage of mass vehicle manufacturing and pioneering road engineering. Market stallholder Muz Khan, 58, said: “We’ve got more cars than ever in the city and if they are going to slow all the traffic down to 20mph, that’ll cause even more gridlock. “I agree with it around schools at pick up and drop off times but I don’t think even the buses and trams go that slowly. I can’t see it happening but there will be more reasons to fine people.” Parvinder Kaur, 69, said: “It’s always another thing making life hard for drivers. “I think 20, that’s a bit too low. It’s difficult to go at just 20 and I think this will hold up too many people.” The Department for Transport said in June that 20mph limits “should only be used where they are appropriate and supported by evidence”. Richard Hunt, 48, said: “Around the city centre itself, on the little streets, 20mph is not a problem but not every road in Birmingham. That’s taking it too far. People will have to drive around in second gear meaning more revs and causing more fumes.” Mary Day, 67, a retired care worker, added: “I think this is just a way for them to make more money out of drivers. They want to issue more fines. I wish I knew what they were doing with the money but they’re not fixing the potholes that is for sure.” A Birmingham City Council spokesman said: “Evidence from around the world on slower speed limits is very clear: it reduces collisions, saves lives and reduces injuries – so our message is simple: slower is safer. “Slower speeds are less intimidating towards those who walk or cycle, activities that we need to encourage more of if we are to reduce the number of harmful emissions and traffic levels in the city.” The spokesman added that the city’s 20mph rollout had so far been done on a “targeted basis in response to local road safety concerns or near to schools”.



Food stall holder Melanie, 50, said: “We had to buy a new lorry to make it compliant and the traffic is still chock-a-block in the city centre creating all manner of pollution so I don’t think it has worked.

“I feel sorry for night workers who start at 11pm and then go home the next day – they end up paying double. It does stop people wanting to come into town.”

Kiran Thandi’s mum Palvinder Kaur, 69, has been running a menswear stall in the market for 25 years.

Kiran, 42, said: “There was a long time when we had to drop Mum into work because her car was not compliant. She had to buy a new one in the end.



“It has certainly made some areas of town less busy. Parts of it are dead and businesses did not need that hit especially in 2021 coming out of Covid restrictions.

“Most of the bus stops are on the other side of town to the market so a lot of people need two buses to get here.”

Clothes stall vendor Jenny, 59, said: “I have been working here for 34 years and trade has gone right down.

“The Clean Air Zone does have a lot to do with it because people can’t afford the newer cars and they can’t afford the parking charges. It’s just them taxing the poor like they always do.

“You can say people can take public transport but if you are doing a big shop, you need your car and the trains are rammed. It is a terrible idea.”



Muz Khan, 58, who runs an accessory stall in the Flea Market, said: “I think it’s been a waste of time and money and where has all that money gone?

“You’d think Birmingham Council would be rich with all that.

“We have certainly noticed fewer customers and there has been no compensation for us, no reduction in rates or something to acknowledge the harm it has caused.”

Her daughter, Sienna-Rose, 17, who was helping out, added: “I don’t see how you can create a clean air zone when air moves around so the dirty air will blow in anyway from all the polluting cars circling the city centre.

“They want everyone to go electric but those things need big batteries and they are polluting too.”



In a statement, Birmingham City Council said: “The Council introduced the Clean Air Zone to tackle the primary source of the air pollutant nitrogen dioxide, which had been persistently above the legal limit.

“Since the introduction of the Clean Air Zone the percentage of non-compliant vehicles travelling through the city centre has reduced from 15.2% in June 2021 to 3.1% in June 2026, which means a significant number of people have changed their behaviours and the numbers of the highest polluting vehicles entering the Zone has decreased.

“Most importantly, the levels of nitrogen dioxide in the zone have fallen by, on average, 22.5% since 2019.

“The Clean Air Zone remains the Council’s most significant intervention to improve air quality. However, it forms part of a wider programme of measures designed to reduce air pollution and raise awareness of the impact poor air quality can have on public health.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“The volume of PCNs issued on a section of Corporation Street reflect the fact that this is a stretch of the A38 between Dartmouth Circus and Lancaster Circus, which connects directly to the A38(M) Aston Expressway, a motorway that extends into and through Birmingham city centre.

On average, more than 100,000 vehicles travel through the Clean Air Zone every day, which would equate to over 30m vehicles per year.



“It is important to note that the majority of vehicles travelling through the Zone use this particular stretch of road, which means that the number of PCNs issued over 12 months at this location represent less than 1% of the vehicles travelling through the Zone.”

News.title: Dozens of students trapped inside five-storey hostel after building collapsed with 4 found dead and 8 seriously injured
News.content:
AT LEAST four people have been killed and several more injured after a five-storey building collapsed, sparking an urgent rescue operation.

More than 50 people are feared to be trapped under the rubble of the student hostel which crashed down in Delhi, India.



Rescuers raced to the tragedy at around 1:30pm and tried to scramble through the collapsed walls to find survivors.

Around nine people have so far been pulled alive from the wreckage – with eight rushed to hospital.



A dozen fire engines have also been dispatched as bystanders desperately try to clear the debris for rescue teams to come through.

Eyewitnesses claim the horror unfolded after a neighbouring building crashed into the hostel which was accomodation for university students.

Rooms had been packed with young people because there were no classes on a Sunday.

It is unclear excatly how many people were inside the building when it came crashing down.

But one local resident told the Times of India that the hostel had around 15 rooms with two to three students per room.

Chief Minister of Delhi Rekha Gupta has visisted the site of the horror – and vowed that “no one will be spared”,” she says.” in the rescue efforts.



“Every possible effort is being made to safely rescue those trapped,” she added.

The building next to the hotel had been evacuated “as a precautionary measure”.

Construction work was being carried out on the basement of the “Hotel Haze” hostel – with builders among those buried under the rubble.



A local shopowner said: “They strengthened the upper building, but the pillars below were weak.”

Police have launched a probe and are searching for the owner of the building.

Prime Minister has also expressed his condolences for the “distressing” incident.

In a post on X, he said: “Condolences to those who lost their loved ones. Praying for the speedy recovery of the injured.”

But outraged commenteres wondered: “Who is responsible for this tragedy?”



The National Union of Students has demanded a thorough investigation into the devastating collapse.

News.title: Minister to meet Jaguar Land Rover boss as thousands of job cuts expected
News.content:
Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds will meet the bosses of Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) and the Unite union to discuss the impact of thousands of expected job cuts at the car maker.

JLR confirmed to the BBC it is opening a voluntary redundancy programme, a year on from a cyber attack which brought production to a halt for more than a month.

The company did not confirm the numbers but the Times reported as many as 4,000 jobs may be lost due to the impact of tariffs and a drop in sales.

Reynolds told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg the meeting early next week will focus on ways to "mitigate any job losses" but ruled out a bailout for the company.

Asked about the cuts, which are believed to impact mainly white collar workers, Reynolds said: "A company the size of JLR, which is a huge British success story, at various times in its business cycle, the number of, directly, people it employs will change.

"If this is about making sure over time that the workforce is right to make the business as competitive as possible, that's the conversation we need to have."

He said there would be no support "if it's to bail people out", but opened the door to a "long-term investment in the future" of the company.

The cuts come as Chancellor John Healey is preparing to deliver a speech in the Midlands on Monday promising to boost economic growth by changing how the government values investment in infrastructure such as transport and housing. JLR is based in Coventry, in the West Midlands.

The Liberal Democrats said the news would be "devastating" for JLR staff and called for Healey to use his speech to offer "support for those jobs at risk".

"This development lays bare that the government's growth mission is falling far short," the party's business spokesperson Sarah Olney said.

News.title: Jamaica to bring slavery reparations petition to King Charles
News.content:
The Jamaican government will hand a petition to King Charles over slavery reparations on Monday, the country's culture minister Olivia Grange has said.

It will ask the King, who serves as Jamaica's head of state, to refer three questions to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, the country's highest court, over the legality of the enslavement of Africans in Jamaica.

Grange said it could pave the way for a "long outstanding settlement for the hundreds of years of the most horrific abuse that our African ancestors endured".

She will also meet with British Museum officials to discuss the repatriation of artefacts taken during the colonial era.

The three questions which the Jamaican government is asking the King to refer to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council (JCPC) are: whether the enslavement of Africans in Jamaica was legal under English law, whether it broke international law, and whether Britain now has a legal duty to provide redress.

The petition, which is not a demand for payment, goes to the King who then refers it to the JCPC.

King Charles has no personal discretion in deciding whether to make a referral.

Grange said: "Once we get the answers, or once we get a response to those questions, then the next steps will be determined."

Buckingham Palace has been working closely with the Governor General of Jamaica to ensure the petition is correctly lodged.

A Palace spokesperson said: "His Majesty has on many occasions expressed his personal and wholehearted commitment to promoting greater understanding around the issue of slavery and finding ways to address historic wrongs for the benefit of communities today."

News.title: Iran warns of 'faster, heavier, more painful response' to US attacks
News.content:
Iranian state media also reported on Sunday that the country's Navy had attacked an American remote-controlled vessel that was trying to enter the Strait of Hormuz.

The US military has denied the claim.

"The report came from Iranian state media and it's a total lie," said Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for Centcom, according to the Associated Press.

US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has issued his own threats back at Iran, writing on social media on Saturday, "It's simple: if Iran shoots at US ships, we will destroy (and sink) their oil tankers."

A 60-day ceasefire between the US and Iran formally expired last month, and that period of relative calm was shattered when the US resumed attacks last Sunday.

Fighting has continued throughout the week, with the US launching multiple strikes on Iranian targets and Iran retaliating against US targets in the region, including in the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan.

US President Donald Trump said this week that the renewed fighting would not last "too long", echoing comments both he and his administration have frequently made since the now six-month-long war began in February.

Months of negotiations between the US and Iran have not amounted to lasting peace, and there's little sign of a further diplomatic settlement on the horizon.

The Strait of Hormuz, which is crucial to the world's oil and gas industry, has been effectively closed since the war began, and has become a major source of leverage for Iran.

Tehran has insisted it will not give up some measure of control over the waterway.

But Trump has declared that the strait is "open" and the US military has been helping ships navigate the southern route.

The conflict in the strait has led to an increase in gas prices globally, and ahead of the US midterm elections in November, Trump is facing pressure over how much the war is costing American consumers.

The average price for one gallon of diesel in the US hit $5.85 on Friday, compared to an average of $3.71 a year ago.

US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Sunday that an average of 9 million barrels of oil a day were passing through the strait, which could help ease pressure on energy prices.

Wright told CNN with oil also moving through pipelines in the region, "we're probably two-thirds or more of pre-conflict flows".

In an interview with ABC This Week on Sunday, Wright added that gas prices should start to come down for Americans as summer demand begins to wane after Labor Day.

News.title: Aviation faces hotter, stormier skies – and passengers might have to accept more disruption
News.content:
As the country sweltered through one of the many heatwaves of a baking summer in late June, towering thunderclouds were gathering over the south of England and across much of northern Europe. It was a Saturday, and with the holiday season getting under way, thousands of passengers were heading to London's Heathrow and Gatwick airports to catch flights abroad. It was always going to be a very busy day.

What followed, however, was chaos for travellers. As air traffic controllers struggled to route aircraft around the storms, airspace became heavily congested and many planes due to fly were simply forced to wait on the ground. In the end, some 900 flights to and from both airports were delayed, some by up to 11 hours. Dozens more were cancelled. At airports across Europe, passengers expecting to fly into London also faced long waits and uncertainty.

The weather in the UK may now have cooled, and passengers may soon forget their experiences. But some within the industry believe what happened in June should be seen as a warning.

The timing in this case was clearly unlucky. But there are concerns that such incidents are only going to become more common as the effects of climate change mount up around the world and weather systems are likely to become increasingly unstable, making disruption more likely and adding to costs for airlines, airports and travellers.

Tim Atkinson, an airline risk consultant and former pilot, says the very crowded skies over the UK and northern Europe mean the region is particularly exposed.

He thinks there is a real risk, for example, that all of London's airports could be affected by storms at the same time, potentially with major consequences in the air and on the ground.

"What we're seeing now is very rapid climate change," he says.

"We're going from the kind of weather activity which takes out an airport, and which the system kind of copes withâ¦ to a situation where, with very little predictability, it would be possible to lose all of the London airports from real-time operation quite swiftly and with little notice".

Such a scenario, he thinks, would make the disruption for passengers caused by the incident in June seem relatively minor â and could even put lives at risk. But how likely is it?

News.title: 140 migrants in single dinghy rescued in English Channel
News.content:
Around 140 migrants in a single dinghy have been rescued in the English Channel.

The people on the inflatable vessel, which launched from the Normandy coast overnight, requested help in UK waters and were picked up by two RNLI boats, the French coastguard said. They will now be taken to shore in the UK.

It comes days after Prime Minister Andy Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron met to discuss how to "scale up" efforts to reduce small boat crossings.

In August a single small boat carrying a record 230 people successfully crossed the Channel.

The dinghy launched in Bay of the Seine and was shadowed for around 10 hours by French rescue boats in case it got into difficulty. The French coastguard said it was not safe to attempt to stop the dinghy on water.

It reached UK waters at lunchtime and the people on board were met by lifeboats from Bembridge and Yarmouth.

French authorities said it was unusual for the migrant boat to depart from the area - 170 miles away from the usual launches around Calais making the crossing to the UK significantly longer.

Last year local officials told the BBC there has been an increase in people trying to depart from Normandy.

A Home Office spokesperson said on Sunday: "This government is bearing down on dangerous small boat crossings and restoring control at our border.

"Joint efforts have seen over 48,000 crossing attempts prevented and 1,100 boats and engines seized since the election."

They added: "But we must go further, which is why we have signed a payment-by-results deal with the French to put 40% more boots on the ground on French beaches."

In bilateral talks on Thursday, Burnham and Macron agreed they were making headway in reducing small boat crossings in the English Channel but now needed to go further.

While the number of boat crossings over summer months has dropped to its lowest since 2019, smugglers appear to have started loading more people onto fewer, larger vessels dubbed "mega dinghies".

It's thought the people smugglers organising the crossings have been forced to go to much greater lengths to avoid detection following more robust policing in the Calais area.

Between 1 January and 1 September 2026, a total of 16, 513 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France.

Downing Street says 45 extra police officers are being deployed to French beaches in a "surge team" to tackle larger dinghies with more people packed onto them.

News.title: Green Party deputy leader linked to property lets despite opposition to landlords
News.content:
The deputy leader of the Green Party, Mothin Ali, is linked to two buy-to-let properties, despite his party's opposition to private landlords.

Ali is the sole director of a company, which he set up and controls, that owns two rental properties in Leeds, bought in June 2022 and March 2025 - although he does not appear to profit from either of them.

The property purchases happened before the Greens adopted a policy committing to phasing out ownership of rental properties by private landlords in October 2025.

The Green Party told the BBC that, at the time Ali had set up the company, and since, he "has acted solely in the interests of vulnerable close family members for whom he has caring responsibilities".

Ali's connection to the rental properties via real estate company MA Holdings, which purchased them with buy-to-let mortgages, was first reported by the Times newspaper.

Records held by Companies House show that Ali is the sole director of MA Holdings, incorporated in December 2021, and he is listed in the records as the sole person with significant control, owning more than 75% of the shares.

The company's business includes "buying and selling of own real estate", "letting and operating of own or leased real estate" and "management of real estate on a fee or contract basis".

The BBC has spoken to the previous owner and resident of the second property, who confirmed that Ali's company had purchased the property and believed it was bought with the intention to be let out.

Asked why MA Holdings owns the rental properties, a Green Party spokesperson said: "We have provided deeply personal information to the BBC in confidence which shows that Councillor Ali has acted solely in the interests of vulnerable close family members for whom he has caring responsibilities.

"At Councillor Ali's request, we are not going to make this information public to protect his family."

The BBC is not publicising the personal information shared with it, at the request of the Greens, as it relates to private family matters.

In October last year, delegates to the Green Party's annual conference, passed a motion titled "Abolish landlords", external, headed "the private rental sector has failed, it is a vehicle for wealth extraction, funnelling money from renters to the landlord class".

The motion states: "The effective abolition of private landlordism and the private rented sector, coupled with the mass expansion of council housing, is the only way to end the housing crisis."

This is now official policy for the Green Party of England and Wales, with a plan to increase regulation and taxes on private rentals to make it difficult for landlords to make a profit, while boosting housebuilding by councils.

The policy would use existing Green policies such as imposing rent controls, ending buy-to-let mortgages and giving councils the right to buy a rental property when it is sold at a discounted price.

Asked whether Ali had sought to take any steps since the policy had been adopted to change anything with regard to the rental properties, a Green Party spokesperson told the BBC he fully supported the policy.

"The policy does not literally seek to abolish landlords, but rather to put in more regulations and taxes on private rentals through measures such as rent controls and expanded social housing," they said. "All of which Mothin Ali supports."

When the policy was introduced, Green Party MP Carla Denyer told the BBC "while the motion to conference had an eye-catching name, it does not actually 'abolish' landlords".

"It does, however, address the housing crisis, empowers tenants and improves their wellbeing," she added.

"It contains a range of policies which, over time, would reduce the proportion of the housing market that is privately rented, and increase the proportion of socially rented homes."

News.title: Fifa president Infantino will stand for re-election
News.content:
Fifa president Gianni Infantino will stand for re-election in March, says football's world governing body.

Infantino, who has filled the role since 2016, has been under pressure following his scrapped plan to sell stakes in Fifa competitions to private investment firms.

Infantino's lucrative plan sparked a global outcry, with European football's governing body Uefa threatening to boycott all Fifa competitions, including the World Cup.

"The Fifa president announced in April that he will stand for re-election in 2027," read a Fifa statement.

"Of course, nothing has changed. Mr Infantino will be standing for re-election."

Infantino refused to answer questions about his future when asked by reporters at the Women's Under-20 World Cup in Poland on Saturday.

It is the first time Fifa has said he will run for a new term since the plan was announced following the summer's World Cup.

Should the 56-year-old Swiss be re-elected, he will serve until 2031.

Fifa this week accused Uefa of a "smear campaign against it and its leadership", in a challenge to litigation over Infantino's plan.

Last week Uefa filed legal papers in the US requesting disclosure of evidence and documents from Fifa, warning it could lodge a criminal complaint in Switzerland.

News.title: Why more women carry the 'mental load' - and how couples can share it
News.content:
"My head's always full," says mum-of-three Stacie Matthias. "I go to sleep with a mental to-do list."

She's talking about the concept of the "mental load" - the burden of planning, organising, remembering and anticipating tasks that keep a household running.

These tasks include: remembering school trips, checking for updates in parents' WhatsApp groups, noticing which parts of the house need cleaning, monitoring how much sleep children get, scheduling doctors' appointments and buying school uniforms.

According to academics, this is work that in heterosexual couples disproportionately falls to women - particularly mothers - alongside the bulk of physical household labour.

All relationships and households are different, of course, but studies suggest clear patterns.

Children in the UK have just gone back to school from the summer holidays, and Stacie, 37, from Stockport, says her mind often feels especially busy in September.

"It's that feeling of always having something to remember, organise or worry about that makes this time of year particularly full-on," she says.

For Stacie this list of responsibilities leaves her mind feeling like a washing-up bowl that's being filled up throughout the day.

"If someone's not helping you remove those pots and pans, your water's overflowing by the end of the day," she says, "and you're at tipping point."

News.title: Police slow to respond to Dover protest, says council boss
News.content:
Police were slow to react to an "exceptionally well organised" protest that ground the Port of Dover to a halt for hours, a council boss has said.

Kevin Mills, who leads Dover District Council, told the BBC that demonstrators "caught several agencies on the hoof" when they arrived on Saturday.

Hundreds of masked men chanting "stop the boats" blocked roads, causing miles of tailbacks and preventing access to the port.

Kent Police is yet to comment, but cabinet minister Jonathan Reynolds said officers "did deal with it swiftly".

Mills said the force "appeared to be quite slow to keep the roads and the networks open, which is disappointing".

"The protesters knew what they were doing, I'm not sure the police did know what was going to happen," he told the BBC.

"But then I accept that the police resource is stretched."

The Labour councillor said "no-one actually knew" what was happening on Saturday morning and there "needs to be a wash-up over that".

"All in all it was a pretty traumatic day for a lot of people travelling, trying to get around their business," he said.

Kent Police said on Saturday that officers made no arrests and described it as a "spontaneous protest".

Mills added that the council later received complaints from villagers in Preston, where "protesters appear to have parked their vehicles before they came in".

Chris Vinson, leader of the council's Conservative group, previously said the men had "loaded into rental vans" and then travelled to the town.

News.title: Baby girl dies while camping with family in woods
News.content:
A three-month-old girl has died while camping in woodland with her family, police have confirmed.

Emergency services were called to land off Strawberry Lane, near Cheslyn Hay, Staffordshire, at 08:45 BST on Saturday, to a report of a child in cardiac arrest.

An air ambulance was sent to the scene but the child was pronounced dead by paramedics a short time later, Staffordshire Police said.

"While the investigation remains at an early stage, this is an isolated incident," Det Insp Katie Gregory said. "The death is being treated as unexplained at this time."

People living in the close-knit community, a village of around 7,000 people, have been left shocked by the child's death.

News.title: Nigel Farage tells BBC he 'wasn't listening' during foreign donor talks filmed undercover
News.content:
There's no question the allegations in the Channel 4 film have been embarrassing for Reform, and disrupted what they hoped would be a conference about their plans for office if they win the next General Election.

Everywhere around the huge, draughty exhibition hall in Birmingham are giant posters and placards saying, "Reform - the first 100 days".

They wanted to herald their deal with a serious contender to be the next French President, Jordan Bardella, to deal with small boats.

They were keen to highlight the promise to cut income tax if they win the election, scheduled to be in 2029.

They wanted to talk about their proposals for education, welfare, planning, and the rest.

Party members, delighted to have a reason to get together, have taken part in those sessions, applauded and cheered in the hall; gone wild for Farage on stage.

But for the rest of the country, most of the noise from the conference will have been the huge and awkward story about the toxic mix of politics and money.

What is harder to assess is the impact this mess will have on Farage's standing with the public, after a tricky summer and a recent poll slump.

At the top of the party there is a quiet admission that what has happened here is a genuine mistake.

One senior figure told me they could brush off other claims of murky funding, confident nothing had gone wrong - but they conceded these claims do matter, and that for a certain vital percentage of voters, it would "cause them to ask questions".

No one is pretending it's just what Farage tried to joke was a "little, local difficulty".

And there is a private acknowledgement that stories like this can be off putting to voters beyond Reform's no doubt very enthusiastic base.

Another party source told me they were "totally blindsided" by the revelations; stunned "there'd just been no diligence" and in disbelief at how Jukes and Orr, who both say they'd done nothing wrong, seem to have behaved.

A different member of the party's top team said, "hopefully, it's just growing pains". In other words, Reform's developed so fast that sometimes mistakes are made. But they told me: "The party has to step up â sometimes the people that got us here, aren't the people for the next stage".

Among Farage's fans at the conference, I found different views. One member was convinced the party is treated unfairly: "It's the blob, it's all against him," she said.

But another young Reform enthusiast rejected that, telling me: "It's all documented and there on camera â Nigel has to be more careful about what party members say."

But there is a sense of "here we go again". When I asked another member what they thought of the financial scandal, a weary answer, "Which one?"

This time last year in the same conference complex, Reform felt like they were simply sweeping all before them. Twelve months on, they are having to work harder, the scrutiny is more intense, and the pressure only growing.

Farage's claim that he "wasn't listening" to the conversation was telling â to get to power without more of these kinds of serious embarrassments, he may have to pay more attention to what is going on.

News.title: Swinney suggests Scots will not travel further for health care under reforms
News.content:
Scots should not have to travel further for health care under the government's plans to cut the number of health boards from 14 to two, John Swinney has suggested.

The BBC asked the first minister about the impact of such changes for people who are already travelling long distances - such as women living in the far north who have to travel 100 miles down the A9 to give birth in Inverness.

Swinney said it would "not be my intention" for people to travel further, with initial modelling showing the country divided into two east and west health boards.

He also said he could not put a "specific figure" on NHS job losses, but he had been "open about the fact that public sector employment will fall".

News.title: Three charged with attempted murder after shooting
News.content:
Two adults and a teenager have been charged with attempted murder after a shotgun was fired in a town centre.

Police were called to Market Place in Braintree, Essex, at about 22:10 BST on Monday following what officers described as a "targeted attack".

Two teenagers sustained serious injuries to their face and upper body, while a third person was also injured.

Destiny Ema, 23, of Meadgate Avenue, Chelmsford, Kayden Brown, 18, of Noaks Avenue, Chelmsford, and a 17-year-old from Braintree who cannot be named for legal reasons are due to appear at Chelmsford Magistrates' Court on Monday.

A 16-year-old boy previously arrested in connection with the incident has been released on police bail until 30 November.

Ema was also charged with numerous other offences connected to separate investigations including:

Attempted grievous bodily harm with intent

Possession of a firearm with intent to cause fear of violence

Possession of a firearm while committing an indictable offence

Possession of a firearm while prohibited for life

Harassment

Malicious communications

Possession of a shotgun with intent to cause fear of violence

News.title: Body-worn cameras given to school crossing wardens
News.content:
Lollipop men and women in Sheffield have been given body-worn cameras in an effort to combat abuse and aggressive behaviour from drivers.

Sheffield City Council said school crossing wardens at several unspecified locations across the city would be given the cameras, which will record interactions, as part of a new initiative.

The local authority said the measure would create a safer environment for families walking to school in the new academic year and provide reassurance to staff working alone.

Wardens have been subjected to "unacceptable behaviour" and dangerous driving by a "small" number of motorists, the council added.

Jefferson Nwokeoma, the authority's assistant director of city transport said: "These body-worn cameras will help protect our staff, provide valuable evidence when incidents occur and encourage motorists to follow the rules of the road.

"Ultimately, this is about making the journey to school safer for everyone."

Drivers who fail to stop for a school crossing warden can be fined up to Â£1,000 and have three penalty points added to their licence.

News.title: Police investigate Bielik fan clash at Portsmouth
News.content:
Police are investigating an incident between Cardiff defender Krystian Bielik and home supporters during Portsmouth's 2-0 Championship win on Saturday.

Bielik was involved in a physical altercation with a fan as he went to retrieve a ball from the crowd late in the second half.

Hampshire Police were notified of the incident during the match and launched an investigation immediately afterwards.

"We can confirm that we are investigating an incident in which a teenage boy was reportedly the victim of a common assault during the football match at Fratton Park. Our enquiries are ongoing," the police said.

Several Portsmouth supporters made gestures that indicated they believed the fan had been grabbed by the throat.

Cardiff head coach Brian Barry-Murphy claimed afterwards that Bielik "got slapped in the face", while clips circulating on social media appeared to show the Poland international grabbing a young fan around his upper body.

In the aftermath, another fan threw a ball at the head of Cardiff defender Perry Ng. Both supporters were ejected from the stadium.

After the game Portsmouth head coach John Mousinho apologised to Cardiff City's players.

Pompey added in a statement:, external "Portsmouth Football Club are aware of supporter concerns regarding the incident involving a young fan and an opposition player at yesterday's match at Fratton Park.

"As this remains a safeguarding matter and is currently under investigation by both the club and the police, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further on the circumstances at this time.

"However, we are aware that a number of claims and assertions are circulating on social media. We would urge caution against speculation while enquiries are ongoing.

"The welfare and safeguarding of young people are of paramount importance to Portsmouth Football Club. We will continue to liaise with the relevant parties as enquiries progress.

"No further comment will be made at this stage while investigations remain ongoing."

The Football Association is aware of the matter and will review the details in the referee's match report before deciding whether any action should be taken.

Cardiff City said: "We are satisfied with the way that match officials dealt with the situation during the game, having been in full view of it. Player protection will always be of paramount importance to us."

News.title: Royal Navy aircraft carrier departs for training
News.content:
HMS Queen Elizabeth has set sail with hundreds of sailors to take part in a pre-planned deployment around the UK and northern Europe.

The 65,000-tonne aircraft carrier, which was commissioned into service in 2017, left Portsmouth Naval Base at about 18:20 BST on Saturday.

Over the next three months, the Â£3.2bn warship and her crew of more than 800 sailors will take part in an intensive programme of training, the Royal Navy said.

The deployment marks the vessels first official sailing as Nato's command ship for the Allied Response Force - a designation it received in July this year.

As part of the operation, the carrier will rehearse how an Allied naval force would operate together in the event of a crisis, the Navy said.

This work, the Navy said, would aim to "enhance collective security, deterrence and readiness" among the UK and its allies.

News.title: Billions lost to Brexit could make NHS waiting lists disappear, top economist says
News.content:

Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. The billions that the UK has lost to Brexit could wipe out NHS waiting lists and create a world-class service if recouped, a leading economist has warned.

In an exclusive interview with The Independent, Nick Bloom, a professor at Stanford University, said up to 8 per cent of GDP was wiped off the UK economy by leaving Europe, through lost trade, increased red tape and delays in pushing the Brexit deal through.

That is close to the 9.7 per cent spent on health before the Covid pandemic, which he said could be used to bolster the overrun and struggling health service.

He said infamous claims made by the Leave campaign that Brexit could free up £350m a week to spend on the NHS, in a controversial slogan emblazoned across the side of a battle bus, were “exactly and perfectly wrong”.

Prof Bloom urged the UK government to forge closer ties to the bloc in a bid to limit the damage further and claw some of the losses back.

He said: “So we've lost six to 8 per cent [because of Brexit]. Imagine getting that back and spending all that money we lost on the NHS. Suddenly, you would go from the current NHS to one that would be amazing.

open image in gallery The Brexit bus was hugely controversial ( Getty )

“Budgets would go up by about two-thirds; probably, waiting lists would disappear. Hospitals would be refurbished, you'd have better-paid doctors, better-paid nurses, better equipment… So one way to look at it is all the money we’ve lost. If we hadn’t lost it, we could have spent it on the NHS. We’d have a world-class national health service.”

Prof Bloom, who was speaking to The Independent as part of its Europe: The Way Back campaign, which is calling for the UK to rebuild its relationship with Europe, is the co-author of research that shows Brexit caused the economy to shrink between 6 to 8 per cent – more than previously thought.

He said the figure “is an enormous amount”, adding: “It’s something like £3,000 a year, per typical British person, that we've lost.”

He said roughly half was lost because “Brexit itself was just bad news, because it makes it harder for British firms to trade with Europe, and Europe’s about half of our trade pre-Brexit”, while the other half was due to the “mess” of approving the final deal.

open image in gallery New prime minister Andy Burnham is facing a ‘juggling act’ ( Getty )

“So the vote happened in 2016, but it took several years of back and forwards, and multiple prime ministers, and votes, and re-votes, and haggles, negotiations. And so businesses over this period were left uncertain and paused on investment, paused on hiring, and finally we have Brexit done,” he said.

He said the government was doing the right thing by seeking closer ties to the EU but cautioned that one of the biggest threats to that was Reform leader Nigel Farage –for decades the main driver behind getting the UK out of the EU – who remains a “spectre” still impeding the UK’s economic recovery.

open image in gallery ( AFP/Getty )

“Andy Burnham’s doing a juggling act,” he said. “He’s got many balls in the air, but he’d like to get closer to the European Union. Why? Because it would improve the economy. Why? Because that would mean he doesn’t have to put up taxes or cut spending.

“But the big cost of it is this – Farage, and the Brexiteers waiting in the wings, ready to pounce on him. So he’s like every politician, trying to kind of do one thing, get closer, but say another thing, which is we are independent and have our sovereignty. And good luck to him squaring that circle.”

Former Tory health secretary Stephen Dorrell said the suggestion that Brexit would unlock more funds for the NHS was “fundamentally dishonest on a Trumpian scale” and said leaving the EU had “undermined the ability of the UK economy to create successful business and create wealth”.

Europe: The Way Back We’re campaigning to rebuild Britain’s future in Europe JOIN US HERE

He called on the “political class to face up to the fact that this has been a national disaster”, adding: “Until we address that issue head-on, we will continue to be impoverished by the events of 2016.”

Liberal Democrat health spokesperson Helen Morgan said that “patients in the NHS are paying the price with record waiting lists, crumbling hospitals, and overworked doctors and nurses... It’s time for the government to stop burying its head in the sand”.

Emma Knaggs, from pro-EU group European Movement UK, said leaving the EU had “hit us all in the pocket”.

She said: “While EU countries continue to trade with ease, UK businesses now waste tens of thousands of hours and millions of pounds meeting red-tape requirements that simply were not there before.

“That translates to billions of pounds of lost revenue that isn't available for vital services like the NHS. To deliver the government’s own agenda for growth, ease cost-of-living pressure for all of us and boost our public services, being part of the single market and ultimately the EU is the best way to achieve it. A decade on, the UK’s experiment with life outside the world’s biggest free market has failed with death by a thousand cuts. The time to be honest about that is long overdue.”

Naomi Smith, chief executive of Best for Britain, which campaigns for the UK’s restored EU membership, said Brexit had resulted in a “slow and painful death by 1,000 cuts for the UK economy, and the knock-on effect to our struggling public services, with experts like Nick Bloom now rightly highlighting the appalling damage to our healthcare”.

The Cabinet Office and Reform have been approached for comment.

Holly Ditchfield, who featured on Married At First Sight (MAFS) UK, has announced that her twin sons have died nine days after being born prematurely.

In a statement shared on Instagram, the reality TV personality and her partner Aaron Summers confirmed that the infants passed away within hours of one another.

"It has been the hardest, most heartbreaking, yet most magical 9 days of our lives," Ditchfield wrote alongside a series of photos.

"At 1pm on 03/09/2026, our darling Georgie peacefully passed away. Then, at 5am on 04/09/2026, his beautiful brother Marley followed him.

"My boys both took their final breaths in the arms of me and their daddy. There is no greater privilege, and no greater pain, than holding your children as they leave this world."

open image in gallery Ditchfield with her partner Aaron Summers ( Instagram )

The couple had previously revealed the boys were born prematurely at 23 weeks and five days, posting pictures of the twins in the neonatal intensive care unit.

She continued: "They gave us the most precious week of our lives. A week I would live over and over again, just to have those moments with them. To hold them. To look at them. To love them. To be their mummy and daddy.

"My boys are together again now, just as they should be, and I pray with all my heart that they are finally at peace."

"Nothing could ever prepare you for losing your children. Nothing prepares you for having to walk your babies to a mortuary. We have seen and faced more in these 9 days than I ever imagined possible, and my heart feels completely bruised."

Ditchfield, who featured on MAFS in 2024, added that she and Summers plan to take time away to process their loss.

"I would have given absolutely everything to have watched Georgie and Marley grow, to hear their voices, watch them take their first steps, and see the beautiful lives they deserved to have," she said.

"But for 9 precious days, they were here. They were ours. They were loved beyond measure. And they will forever be our beautiful boys."

In addition to her newborn twins, Ditchfield has two children, Daisy and Dec, from a prior relationship.
