World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Sheinbaum delivers her second-year report as trade tensions simmer
World.content:
Listen to this article

The week of Aug. 31, President Claudia Sheinbaum delivered her second annual government report, reflecting on the state of the nation as her second year in office draws to a close. She touted falling homicides and a stable economy, only to face a pointed rebuttal from opposition leaders who accused her administration of manipulating crime statistics and shielding officials tied to drug trafficking.

Mexico continues to grapple with security challenges on a variety of fronts, a fact underscored by a car bomb in Zacatecas Sunday night — the state’s third such attack in four days. But Mexico’s security forces remain active and on Monday claimed a high-profile target: Soldiers and marines killed Luis Enrique Barragán, alias “R5,” the accused leader of extortion against Michoacán’s avocado growers, in a shootout in Tocumbo.

Trade friction with Washington ran through much of the week. A dispute over cheese naming rights is complicating already-strained talks over the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA). Mexico continues to push back against the threat of U.S. tariffs, and Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard met U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on the sidelines of a G20 gathering Wednesday to press Mexico’s case against tariffs on steel, aluminum and cars.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Sheinbaum’s second-year report meets a sharp opposition response

President Sheinbaum delivered her second annual government report Tuesday, a 67-minute address touting a 51% reduction in homicides since taking office, record foreign direct investment and a stable economy. She said her administration’s relationship with Washington “has had its challenges” but reiterated that “sovereignty isn’t negotiated, handed over or shared.”

Opposition senators offered a starkly different account. PAN’s Ricardo Anaya disputed the government’s homicide figures, arguing that reclassified deaths obscure a rising toll, while PRI’s Alejandro Moreno accused the administration of an unspoken “pact” with organized crime, pointing to the unresolved U.S. extradition request for Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya. Sheinbaum has said her administration won’t shield anyone who has committed a crime.

The president also used Wednesday’s press conference to accuse the Trump administration of trying to “create divisions” within her cabinet ahead of November’s U.S. midterms, calling it part of a long-standing U.S. pattern of pressuring “independent governments.” Her approval rating stood at 68% heading into the report, among the highest of any Mexican president at this point in a term, according to polling firm El Financiero. Along with the high approval rating, the newest results of the MND Sheinbaum Index™ found an almost 10-point increase in the president’s performance.

Security: Zacatecas car bomb and a cartel leader’s death

Eleven people, including a policewoman, were injured Sunday night when a car bomb exploded outside a municipal police station in Ojocaliente — the third explosives attack in Zacatecas in four days. Authorities are investigating whether the blast was retaliation for the Saturday capture of an alleged Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) sicario. The explosion damaged 30 properties and 13 vehicles; classes were suspended and army troops deployed to the municipality.

The next day, Mexican Army and Navy forces killed Luis Enrique Barragán Chávez, known as “El Güicho” or “R5,” in a shootout in Tocumbo, Michoacán. Federal Security Minister Omar García Harfuch identified Barragán as the leader of the Cártel de Los Reyes and the main coordinator of extortion against avocado producers in the state; the U.S. had offered a $3 million reward for his arrest on drug and firearms charges.

At her Friday mañanera in Zacatecas, Sheinbaum’s Security Cabinet reported the state’s daily homicide rate fell 85% in August compared to September 2024, and that more than 3,800 people have been arrested there since she took office. Defense Minister Ricardo Trevilla Trejo, responding to a Fox News report on U.S. anti-drone operations at the border, said the drones are mainly used by migrant smugglers and declined to confirm Mexican military involvement in the U.S. takedowns.

Mexico-U.S. trade relations: Tariffs, cheese and an uncertain USMCA

Mexico-U.S. trade talks hit a snag over cheese this week, with U.S. officials pressuring Mexico to amend a May agreement with the European Union that grants regional-name protections to products like Parmigiano Reggiano and manchego. The U.S. government’s position is that these names are generic; the European Commission says the deal isn’t open to amendment, leaving Mexico caught between two trading partners.

Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard met U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on the sidelines of a G20 Innovation Ministerial in North Carolina on Wednesday, pressing the U.S. to lift tariffs on Mexican cars, steel and aluminum, which Mexico calls unjustified. Sheinbaum said Thursday her government is working to secure a better tariff agreement, noting that most Mexican exports still enter the U.S. duty-free under the USMCA.

The tariff dispute traces back to Washington’s decision not to renew USMCA in its current form for a further 16 years, leaving the pact’s future — and Mexico’s manufacturing-heavy states — in limbo pending ongoing bilateral talks.

Economy: The peso strengthens as growth forecasts improve

The peso hit a 28-month high against the dollar on Friday, trading at 16.863, reviving talk of a “super peso.” Analysts attribute the gains partly to peso strength and partly to the dollar’s weakness. A stronger peso cuts import costs and inflation but squeezes exporters’ margins and remittance values, with agricultural states like Michoacán most exposed.

Earlier in the week, Banxico raised its 2026 GDP growth forecast to 1.5%, up from 1.1%, citing stronger-than-expected second-quarter growth, while flagging USMCA uncertainty and geopolitical tensions as downside risks.

Mexico’s tourism sector added a bright note: The World Travel & Tourism Council ranked Mexico fourth globally in tourism-generated GDP, behind only the U.S., China and Germany, with Quintana Roo cited as the main driver.

Looking ahead

Trade talks with Washington remain unresolved on both cheese labeling and industrial tariffs, with no clear timeline for a new USMCA agreement as bilateral dialogue continues. Meanwhile, Hurricane Marie, a Category 2 storm off Baja California Sur, is expected to weaken to a Category 1 by Saturday as it moves out to sea, though Conagua warned that atmospheric instability could keep bringing rain to the country’s interior into next week. Zacatecas remains under heightened security following last week’s car bomb attack, with federal, state and municipal forces reinforcing operations in Ojocaliente.

Some good news to end the week

Mexico News Daily

World.title: The singing frog that came to symbolize midcentury Mexico
World.content:
While it may be a fine place to avoid New Orleans’ sweltering heat, Tulane University’s Doris Z. Stone Latin American Library serves a much larger purpose as a repository of Mexico travel and tourism ephemera, including magazines, hotel brochures and highway maps.

Together, the collection offers a unique look at how the United States’ southern neighbors were constructed as attractive vacation destinations throughout the midcentury.

Mexico especially loomed large in the imagination of U.S. tourists. It was a period when, as historian Mauricio Tenorio notes, Mexico was understood as a “Brown Atlantis” — where revolutionary thought fermented, and the Pan-American Highway promised access to exotic adventures. Everyone wanted to meet Frida Kahlo and visit Teotihuacán, all while dreaming up global politics anew.

Two brochures found in the Mexican ephemera collection tell how Mexico feted itself for an international community, including the crooning amphibian that would become the country’s unofficial mascot during the time.

The singing frogs of Taxco

First is a trifold brochure from arguably Mexico’s most famous nightclub during the second half of the 20th century — Cantarranas. However, the site didn’t always host the international glitterati.

Located in the silver-mining town of Taxco, roughly 2.5 hours outside of Mexico City, the estate was initially conceived in 1538 by Hernán Cortés, who ordered its construction so that he could extract the region’s precious materials.

Dubbed Hacienda Cantarranas, – literally “singing frogs” due to the loud chorus of frogs living in the nearby area – Cortés’ son Martín de Cortés oversaw its construction, which featured large stones along a hillside. Over the years, the infrastructure took its toll on the unstable land it was built on and was ultimately abandoned in favor of a new locale.

For the next four centuries, the site was nothing more than a derelict ghost of Mexico’s colonial past. That is, until one entrepreneur saw an opportunity.

Antonio “Tony” Reyes Ramírez, who would later become Taxco’s minister of tourism, officially opened Cantarranas in 1957. Eager to capitalize on its history, Reyes Ramírez kept the name and leaned on its playful imagery in his marketing materials.

Cantarranas quickly developed a global reputation as a lively hangout throughout the 1960s and 70s, and even featured prominently in a popular television show of the time.

The brochure for Catarranas promises tourists a night of “flamenco dancing by Estela Calderón,” “Carl Brice directly from Nassau, Bahamas,” “Primitive African Drums by the owner and Manager of Cantarranas Tony Reyes,” and “The Latin American Rhythms of the great pianist Juan García Esquivel.”

The nightclub also housed several distinct spaces, including the “Twilight Room,” the “Patio,” the “Flamenco Room” and the “Mulata Room.” Newspapers of the time reported that, inside Cantarranas, “the audience moves en masse from room to room as each show finishes.”

During that same decade, the brochure from Tulane notes that Cantarranas was chosen as the backdrop for an episode of the NBC series, “I Spy,” entitled “Return to Glory,” which aired Feb. 23, 1966.

In it, Alexander Scott – played by Bill Cosby – is tipped off by U.S. intelligence to visit Cantarranas, where he rendezvouses with the wife of a deposed president of an unnamed Latin American country. Famed Mexican actress Dolores del Río plays the part of the wife, as Cosby and costar Robert Culp try to negotiate the democratic leader’s return to his home nation.

Cantarranas’ popularity continued to grow throughout the early- to mid-1970s.

A newspaper article from 1974 lists several of the club’s attractions, including “Flying Indian Men,” a discotheque called “The Psychedelic Cave,” bullfighting lessons, a piñata party, and calypso songs by Carl Brice.

However, as a new decade dawned, Cantarranas was beginning to lose its luster.

An article from 1978 reported that “Cantarranas is a little rough around the edges.” Two years later, the club was described as “the kind of place that you wouldn’t miss if you missed it. But worth it if you’re utterly bored.”

Unable to sustain itself any longer, in 1983, the Mexican state of Guerrero acquired the property and converted it into a culinary school and arts center. In 1992, it changed hands once again, this time to the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México as a school for foreign nationals.

Despite its short life, Cantarranas heralded Mexico’s midcentury miracle as its nascent legacy was beginning to be forged.

The birth of Señor Frogs

Twelve years after Cantarranas opened, another Mexican restaurateur, Carlos Anderson, was cooking up a similar concept that would come to define the Mexican resort experience well into the 21st century – Señor Frog’s.

First opened in Mazatlan in 1969, Señor Frog’s capitalized on that same midcentury swagger, with waiters slinging tequila shots and cajoling spontaneous conga lines in a neon cave. It’s unclear why Señor Frog’s succeeded where Cantarranas ultimately failed, but it did.

It wasn’t just the nightclub scene, either. The Tulane collection includes another brochure with a singing frog on it — this one from Pemex or Petróleos Mexicanos, the company formed in 1938 by the Mexican government to sell the nation’s significant oil supply.

The brochure includes maps of Mexican highways and invites travelers to explore the best routes. There is no mention of Cantarranas, or Taxco, or even nightclubs. However, at this point the singing frog had become emblematic of Mexico’s exotic sights, electric nights and cultural spectacle.

From Hacienda Cantarranas to Tony Reyes’ “Singing Frogs” bar, through a national oil company and today’s Señor Frog’s franchises, the brochure in Tulane University’s Doris Z. Stone Latin American Library chronicles the birth of a national symbol, while documenting how tourists were meant to imagine the delights of midcentury Mexico – strange, inviting and culturally savvy, not unlike a crooning amphibian.

Kevin M. Anzzolin earned a PhD in Romance Languages and Literatures from the University of Chicago. He is the author of “Guardians of Discourse: Literature and Journalism in Porfirian Mexico,” published by the University of Nebraska Press (2024), which received an Honorable Mention from LASA-Mexico for Best Book in the Humanities in 2025. He currently teaches language and literature courses at Christopher Newport University (Virginia, USA). He also publishes in more public fora.

World.title: Is Mexican-made kombucha underrated?
World.content:
There are few drinks in history with an eccentrically bubbly origin story like kombucha.

The fermented probiotic can be traced back to China around 221 B.C. during the Qin Dynasty, when it was consumed as a “remedy for immortality” by those who considered the yeasty, naturally carbonated black tea a source of long-lasting health and vitality.

The long history of kombucha

In 414 B.C., the Smithsonian reports, the cloudy beverage was imported to Japan by a Korean doctor named Kombu, in order to treat Emperor Inkyo. To further complicate its history, Japan already had its own form of kombucha, made from kombu (brown seaweed) and cha (tea).

According to Forbes, kombucha began to spread during the global trade expansion of the 20th century, when the fermented Chinese tea variety migrated into Europe, with Russia and Germany having adopted it as “kambucha” and “kombuchaschwamm,” respectively.

In 1955, Italian piano prodigy Renato Carosone delivered a hit single, “Stu Fungo Cinese!” (translated as “The Chinese Fungus!”), which was rooted in a Chinese mushroom infusion similar to kombucha.

The drink gained mainstream popularity in China during the 1960s, ’70s and ’80s, with homebrews known as “Stomach Treasure” touted as digestive tonics.

Finally, in the 1990s, kombucha entered the North American market, largely thanks to major U.S. brands like GT’s Kombucha.

In the past decade, kombucha’s ubiquity — and value — has skyrocketed as one of the fastest-growing beverage markets on the continent. Now a mainstream supermarket item, North American kombucha sales generated revenue of US $2.1 billion in 2025, with revenues expected to top US $4 billion by 2033.

Of course, the United States accounts for much of the lion’s share. But a market study revealed that Mexico is predicted to have the continent’s largest compound annual growth rate for kombucha in the coming years.

So what has taken kombucha so long to work its magic in Mexico?

Mexico as a country of many beverages — except kombucha, until recently

In my personal recollection, the Eurasian style of kombucha was never plentiful in Mexico. As a child, I could get all sorts of aguas frescas, carbonated sodas and any flavored drinks imaginable. As I grew older, that evolved into other forms of consumption (micheladas, carajillos, etc.). But I have no memory of ever seeing kombucha on a restaurant menu, at a cafe or in mercados.

Here’s my theory: With all of the other beverages that are made in, and often native to, Mexico — including tepache, a naturally fermented pineapple drink — the craft of Asian and Western kombuchas couldn’t get a foothold. In a country where you can easily get tequila, mezcal, pulque, sugar cane aguardiente, rum, atole, arroz con leche and so much more on practically every corner in any pueblo (often made by someone in the neighborhood with generations of family knowledge, ancestral practices and native ingredients at their disposal), kombucha didn’t necessarily have much demand. I’ve watched señoras prepare natural tea remedies from flowers they’ve handpicked from their gardens. But getting offered kombucha inside someone’s home? Never.

It wasn’t until the mid-to-late 2010s that I started to notice kombucha — commercially and independently bottled — as a relatively more common option around Mexico.

Kombucha in Veracruz and other states in Mexico

Near my home in downtown Xalapa (a region known for its rich and deeply rooted coffee history), all of the new-school cafes now offer kombucha, with a noticeable amount of homebrewed and locally made brands available. While recently enjoying my neighborhood on foot, I popped into a few nearby cafes — touted for their espressos, flat whites and other caffeinated brews — and was excited to see artisanal kombucha on nearly every menu. I asked the owner of Marcelo whether she has noticed a rise in kombucha’s popularity and consumption; she confirmed that within the past five years (by her estimation) kombucha has exploded with trendiness across Mexico. She even started to experiment with brewing her own batches, but after failed attempts, opted to get her supply from LindaSol Fermentería, a micro-kombuchería located a few miles from her cafe in Xalapa.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by the pickle (@thepickleofbrighton)

My personal go-to is Agua Brava, made by the chef at Bravo Pizza, a small pizzeria that opened in Xalapa two years ago. Their kombucha flavors rotate weekly and are made in-house and bottled on-site. Among other favorites that I’ve found in Veracruz are Komboocha Puerto (from the port city of Veracruz), Dominga Kombucha (from Cholula, Puebla) and Naran Fermentos (from Xalapa). Mexico City, Guadalajara, San José del Cabo and other cities are no different, offering their own unique brands like Cali Kombucha in Baja California Sur. Data and testimonials suggest that kombucha first infiltrated Mexico’s market roughly a decade ago, when Mexican-owned brands like the aforementioned Cali Kombucha and Brew Lab from Oaxaca launched their brands around 2015 and 2016, respectively.

To highlight the Mexicanization of kombucha since then, “kombucherías” are now a thing in Mexico — as evidenced in the social media reel above, made by a British tourist tasting Oaxacan kombucha in Mazunte. Spoiler: It’s “banging.”

Kombucha a la mexicana: Basil jamaica, pineapple coconut, and more

Though you won’t casually walk past a kombuchería on every corner, you’re likely to encounter a local kombucha brewer in your neighborhood, who might directly sell unmarked jugs or labeled microbatches of their SCOBY-made (Symbiotic Culture Of Bacteria and Yeast) concoctions. You’ll also find it in most grocery markets with a cosmopolitan clientele, or in small businesses that are dedicated to holistic living and organic products.

Often, the flavors have a tropical Mexican vibe: maracuyá, tamarindo, coconut, mango. Some brands add additional ingredients like ancho chile peppers, jalapeño, honey or kiwi for an extra kick of spice, sweetness or tang. Puebla’s Domingo Kombucha has a killer guayaba option — subtly effervescent, fruity and mellow. Mexico City’s Umani offers canned options including orange turmeric, Mexican pepperleaf and fig. Bruja Sana from Yucatán emphasizes herbally minty options with green, earthy additions like romero and hierba buena.

Many of Mexico’s leading kombucha brands are independent, and offer or encourage other lifestyle supplements like yoga and Pilates classes, SCOBY workshops and more. It’s far from commercial profit and mass-made consumer-targeted sales; instead, kombucha offers a doorway into a wider range of health-centered practices and mindful consumption with regional flavor.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: Casas Bahia Is Named in the Sao Paulo Tax Credit Investigation
World.content:
BRAZIL · BUSINESS

Key Facts — What happened Sao Paulo prosecutors named the retailer as a beneficiary of an alleged tax credit scheme.

— Who is investigating The economic crimes unit of the Sao Paulo state prosecution service runs the case, known as Operation Parallel Tax Office.

— The catch The company is named as a beneficiary, not charged as a defendant, and says it has had no formal notification.

— Why it matters The retailer is already in court-supervised recovery, where creditor confidence decides whether a plan survives.

— What is alleged Investigators are examining manipulation of state value-added tax credits inside the tax administration.

— What comes next Prosecutors decide whether to charge anyone beyond the officials already under investigation.

Named as a beneficiary is not the same as charged. For a retailer already in court-supervised recovery, the distinction is the whole story.

Downtown Sao Paulo. The investigation centres on the state tax administration rather than on any single company. (Photo: “Avenue and the downtown skyline of Sao Paulo” by Wilfredor, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.)

Casas Bahia has been named in a Sao Paulo corruption investigation. State prosecutors cite the retailer as a beneficiary of an alleged tax credit scheme.

The case is run by the economic crimes unit of the state prosecution service. It has been publicly identified as Operation Parallel Tax Office.

The alleged scheme involves manipulation of state value-added tax credits. Those credits sit inside the Sao Paulo state finance secretariat.

The company is not a criminal defendant. It says it has not been officially notified of any investigation against it.

What Named as a Beneficiary Means

In Brazilian practice, prosecutors may identify a company that gained from a scheme without charging it. That is what has happened here.

The distinction is legal, not cosmetic. A defendant answers a charge, while a named beneficiary answers questions.

It can become a charge later. It can also stay exactly where it is.

Reporting the two as the same thing would overstate the record. So far Casas Bahia is in the second category.

A tax sealing notice on a shuttered stall on Rua 25 de Marco in Sao Paulo. Tax enforcement is a constant presence in the city’s commerce. (Photo: “Operação Setembro na 25 de Março (36336345304)” by Agência Brasil Fotografias, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.)

The Investigation Itself

The target of the case is the state tax administration. Investigators are looking at how credits were granted and reduced.

Value-added tax credits are worth real money to large retailers. A company with thin margins and high turnover lives on them.

That is why the case reaches beyond the officials involved. Any company that received an unusual credit becomes a line of enquiry.

The rail operator Rumo opened its own internal inquiry as the same case widened. It was named earlier in the process.

The company provides consumer electronics, home appliances, furniture, and other domestic items. It also engages in the manufacture, industrialization, and sale of wood-based furniture; ownership and management of equity interests; management of logistics operations; and provision of…

Why the Timing Is Difficult

The retailer is in court-supervised recovery, Brazil’s equivalent of Chapter 11. It filed in August owing about US$3.3 billion.

A court granted it a 180-day shield from creditors. The company has been selling stock at heavy discounts to raise cash.

Recovery plans depend on creditors believing the company will exist in two years. Investigations do not help that arithmetic.

None of this is a finding against the company. It is simply the worst possible moment to be named in anything.

How the Retailer Got Here

Brazil’s instalment retail model depends on cheap funding and steady jobs. Neither has held since 2023.

The chain is one of Brazil’s best-known household names. It sells furniture and appliances on instalment credit to lower-income buyers.

That model works when interest rates are low and employment is stable. Brazil’s benchmark rate has been high for three years.

The company has been shrinking stores and staff since 2023. A court ordered it to rehire workers in August after a dismissal round.

What the Company Says

The company says it has received no official notification. It has not been asked to respond to a charge.

It has not disputed that its name appears in the case file. Its position is that being mentioned is not being accused.

That is a narrow line to hold in public. It is also, on the current record, accurate.

What to Watch on the Guatemala Bodies Count

The first marker is whether prosecutors charge any company at all. So far the defendants are officials.

The second is the recovery plan vote. Creditors decide, and they read the same headlines.

The third is whether other retailers are named. A tax credit scheme rarely benefits only one buyer.

More: Brazil news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Casas Bahia charged in the Sao Paulo tax case?

No. Prosecutors have named the retailer as a beneficiary of an alleged tax credit scheme at the state tax office, but it is not a criminal defendant and says it has not been formally notified.

What is the investigation about?

The economic crimes unit of the Sao Paulo state prosecution service is examining alleged manipulation of state value-added tax credits inside the state finance secretariat, in a case known as Operation Parallel Tax Office.

Why does this matter for the company?

Casas Bahia filed for court-supervised recovery in August owing about US$3.3 billion. Recovery plans depend on creditor confidence, and an investigation makes that harder to hold.

Sources: Ministerio Publico de Sao Paulo, Estadao, Valor, Folha de S.Paulo, Mercado e Consumo, Rio Times.

World.title: Ambev Closes the Minas Brewery After Ninety Years in Uruguay
World.content:
URUGUAY · BUSINESS

Key Facts — What happened Fabricas Nacionales de Cerveza told the union it will close its brewery in Minas, in the department of Lavalleja.

— Who owns it The company belongs to Ambev, the Latin American arm of the world’s largest brewing group.

— Who it affects Fifty-nine workers were placed on Uruguay’s state unemployment insurance scheme.

— The catch The plant was closed once before and reopened with fewer staff, so the word closure has been used here already.

— Where output goes Production moves to the company’s Montevideo plant, with a stated investment of US$14 million there.

— What comes next There is no reversal and no confirmed closing date, and the government says talks continue.

The plant has been closed once before and reopened smaller. This time the company has already named where the beer goes instead.

Minas, in the department of Lavalleja. The brewery has been part of the town’s economy since 1936. (Photo: “Diagonal Oribe, Minas, Uruguay” by Rodrigo uy, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.)

Uruguay is losing the Minas brewery after ninety years. Fabricas Nacionales de Cerveza told the union it will close the plant.

The announcement was made at the Ministry of Labour on 18 August. Talks had run for about two months before it.

The plant sits in Minas, in the department of Lavalleja. It opened in 1936.

Fifty-nine workers were placed on Uruguay’s state unemployment insurance. The company says production moves to Montevideo.

Who Actually Owns It

Fabricas Nacionales de Cerveza is the Uruguayan operating company. It is controlled by Ambev.

Ambev is the Latin American arm of Anheuser-Busch InBev, the world’s largest brewing group. Ambev took control of the Uruguayan business in 2003.

The chain matters for how the decision reads. This was a regional consolidation, not a headquarters decision taken in Belgium.

Brewing tanks. Uruguayan production is being consolidated into the company’s Montevideo plant. (Photo: “Beer brewing tanks” by SteveStrummer, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.)

What the Plant Made

The site began under Compania Salus brewing the Serrana brand. That is why it is still often called the Serrana brewery.

The brand was renamed Patricia in 1956. Patricia remains one of Uruguay’s best-known beers.

So the plant’s history and its product carry different names. Both are correct, depending on which decade you mean.

Why the Company Says It Is Closing

Ambev cited a general review of its business. It also pointed to competition from imported canned beer.

High production costs were the third reason given. Uruguay is an expensive place to manufacture by regional standards.

The Montevideo plant is receiving US$14 million of investment. That is the destination for the volume Minas used to brew.

This Has Happened Before

The Minas plant was already shut once. It reopened with fewer workers after a dispute was settled at the labour ministry.

That history explains the local reaction. Several Uruguayan outlets described the company as closing the plant again.

It also explains why the union is not treating the announcement as final. The precedent runs the other way.

What the Minas Brewery Made

The Minas brewery bottled for the domestic market rather than for export. Uruguay drinks most of what it brews.

Its output was modest by regional standards. Ambev runs far larger sites in Brazil and Argentina.

That scale gap is the argument for consolidation. It is also why this plant was always the vulnerable one.

The Political Response

President Yamandu Orsi said the decision was actually taken in 2024 and then postponed. He said the government is in contact with the company.

The economy ministry and the Lavalleja local government are both involved. Orsi said the company is making offers to secure the best outcome for workers.

Adriana Pena, an opposition deputy for Lavalleja, criticised the government. She said it had not done enough to keep production outside the capital.

Why It Matters Beyond Minas

Uruguay has spent years trying to keep industry out of Montevideo. Regional plants anchor small-town employment in a country of three and a half million people.

Fifty-nine jobs is a small number nationally. In a town the size of Minas, it is a visible one.

The pattern is familiar across the region. Consolidation into a single efficient plant is cheaper for the company and expensive for the town.

What to Watch on the Guatemala Bodies Count

The first marker is a confirmed closing date for the Minas brewery. None has been published, and that is unusual three weeks after an announcement.

The second is what the company offers the 59 workers. Relocation packages to Montevideo would signal the decision is final.

The third is whether the government finds a buyer for the site. That is the only route that keeps brewing in Minas.

More: Uruguay news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is the Minas brewery closing?

Ambev’s Uruguayan company cited a general business review, competition from imported canned beer, and high production costs. Production moves to its Montevideo plant, which is receiving US$14 million of investment.

How many workers are affected?

Fifty-nine workers were placed on Uruguay’s state unemployment insurance scheme after the announcement on 18 August 2026.

Is the closure final?

There is no confirmed final closing date and no reversal. The plant was closed once before and reopened with fewer workers, which is why the union is still pressing.

Sources: El Observador, Infobae, Diario La Union, Radio Monte Carlo, Ambito, Rio Times.

World.title: Armed Gangs Strip Metal From Chile’s Copper Train Wagons
World.content:
CHILE · MINING

Key Facts — What happened Organised gangs are attacking copper trains crossing the desert in northern Chile and stealing metal in transit.

— How they do it Attackers jump from moving trucks onto wagons and throw copper slabs of about 80 kilograms to accomplices.

— The escalation Security analysts describe the groups as quasi-paramilitary, carrying firearms and wearing body armour.

— The catch The trains run through empty desert, so a response can be an hour away even when an alarm is raised.

— Who it affects Chile is the world’s largest copper producer, and rail is how the metal reaches the Pacific ports.

— What comes next Miners are weighing convoy escorts and route changes, both of which raise the cost of every tonne shipped.

The thieves do not stop the train. They jump onto it, push the metal off, and let the desert do the rest.

A freight train crossing the Atacama in northern Chile. The isolation that makes these lines cheap also makes them hard to protect. (Photo: “FCAB EMD GT22CU-3 San Pedro – Ascotan” by Kabelleger / David Gubler, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

Organised gangs in northern Chile are stealing metal from moving copper train wagons. Reuters reported the pattern on 2 September.

The attacks happen on isolated stretches of desert line. A copper train can run for an hour without passing anything.

The method is physical and direct. Attackers drive alongside, jump from a truck onto a wagon, and shove the metal off.

Each slab weighs roughly 80 kilograms. Accomplices collect them from the trackside once the train has passed.

How the Theft Works

Some crews use hook lines instead of climbing. They snag a stack of copper and drag it off a slow-moving wagon.

Both methods depend on speed. A train slowing for a grade is the easiest target on the route.

The stolen metal does not stay in Chile. It moves into scrap channels and leaves through informal export routes.

Copper in slab form is anonymous once cut. That is what makes it worth the risk.

The Chuquicamata copper mine. Metal from pits like this travels to the coast by rail across open desert. (Photo: “Chuquicamata copper mine – Chuquicamata-Kupfermine” by Alexander Gerst, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.)

Why Analysts Use the Word Paramilitary

Security analysts quoted by Reuters describe the groups as quasi-paramilitary. The term is about equipment and organisation, not politics.

The crews carry firearms and wear bulletproof vests. They work in coordinated teams with vehicles and lookouts.

That is a long way from opportunistic theft. It implies planning, financing and a buyer waiting at the other end.

It also changes the risk calculation for rail staff. A driver who stops is now facing armed men rather than scavengers.

Why the Desert Is the Problem

Northern Chile’s mining railways cross some of the emptiest land on earth. The Atacama has stretches with no settlement for a hundred kilometres.

That emptiness is why the lines are economic. It is also why policing them is close to impossible.

A response unit can be an hour away even when an alarm goes out immediately. By then the metal is gone and so are the trucks.

Why the Railways Exist at All

Chile moves most of its mined copper to port by rail. Roads across the Atacama are long, slow and hard on vehicles.

The lines run from the mining districts inland to the Pacific terminals. Antofagasta, Mejillones and Iquique take the bulk of it.

A single copper train can carry several hundred tonnes. Losing a few slabs per run is survivable, and losing a wagon is not.

What It Costs

Neither the mining companies nor the police have published a total value for the losses. That silence is itself a signal.

Insurers price cargo risk on route, not on national averages. A line with a theft history costs more to cover permanently.

The countermeasures are expensive too. Convoy escorts, drones and route changes all add cost to every tonne shipped.

Chile is the world’s largest copper producer. Anything that raises its logistics cost eventually reaches the copper price.

The Wider Pattern

Metal theft in Latin America has moved from opportunistic to organised over the past five years. Peru and Mexico have seen the same shift on their own freight routes.

The driver is price. Copper has traded at historically strong levels, and high prices pull in serious criminal capital.

Chile has also seen a broader change in its crime profile since 2020. Groups with regional reach now operate where local gangs once did.

What to Watch on the Guatemala Bodies Count

The first marker is whether the mining companies publish a loss figure. Silence usually means the number is embarrassing.

The second is whether escorts become standard. Once a route needs armed accompaniment, the cost does not come back down.

The third is arrests. Crews this well equipped are financed by someone, and no financier has yet been named.

More: Chile news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

How are gangs stealing copper from trains in Chile?

They drive alongside moving trains on isolated desert stretches, jump from trucks onto the wagons, and throw copper slabs of roughly 80 kilograms to accomplices waiting below. Some crews use hook lines to drag stacks off instead.

Why do analysts call them paramilitary?

Security analysts quoted by Reuters use the term because the crews carry firearms, wear body armour and work in coordinated teams with vehicles and lookouts. It describes their equipment and organisation, not any political aim.

How much has been stolen?

Neither the mining companies nor the police have published a total value for the losses.

Sources: Reuters, La Nacion, El Mercurio, La Tercera, Rio Times.

World.title: Guatemala Bodies in Bags: 65 Logged So Far This Year
World.content:
GUATEMALA · SECURITY

Key Facts — What happened Guatemala’s Public Ministry has registered 65 people found dead in bags, sacks or barrels this year.

— The period The figure comes from 54 separate complaints filed between 1 January and 2 September 2026.

— Where it concentrates Forty-nine of the 65 bodies were found in the department of Guatemala, around the capital.

— The catch Prosecutors have not said how many cases are linked, who ordered the killings or why bodies are wrapped.

— The wider spread The complaints came from ten of Guatemala’s twenty-two departments, so the practice is not confined to the capital.

— What comes next The category is a filing label rather than a case, so a single investigation may never be opened.

The number is official and the pattern is unmistakable. What the prosecutors will not say is whether the cases belong to one story or to sixty-five.

A street in Zone 1 of Guatemala City. Most of the bodies recorded this year were found in the surrounding department. (Photo: “Guatemala City, Guatemala (Zona 1)” by vaticanus, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.)

Guatemala’s Public Ministry has registered 65 Guatemala bodies found wrapped and abandoned this year. Prensa Libre reported the figure this weekend.

The count covers people found in bags, sacks or barrels. It also includes bodies wrapped in sheets or plastic.

The 65 deaths come from 54 separate complaints. They were filed between 1 January and 2 September 2026.

Forty-nine of the bodies were found in the department of Guatemala. That is the department containing the capital.

What the Number Is and Is Not

This is a filing category, not a case. The Public Ministry groups complaints by how a body was found.

That distinction matters more than it sounds. A category collects reports, while a case collects evidence.

Prosecutors have not said how many of the 54 complaints are connected. They have not named a group, a motive or a pattern of orders.

So the honest reading is narrow. Sixty-five people were found this way, and the state has not yet said why.

Guatemala City. The Public Ministry keeps the count as a filing category, not as a single investigation. (Photo: “MPGuatemala2015” by Nerdoguate, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

How the Count Is Kept

The Public Ministry records Guatemala bodies under a label describing how they were found. The label covers bags, sacks and barrels.

It does not record who the people were or how they died. Those details sit in the individual case files.

A researcher can therefore learn how many were found this way and almost nothing else. That is a limitation of the system, not of the reporting.

The Geography

The complaints came from ten departments. Guatemala has twenty-two.

The concentration around the capital is heavy, at roughly three quarters of the total. That tracks the distribution of organised crime activity generally.

The remaining sixteen bodies were spread across nine other departments. No second cluster stands out from the published figures.

Why Bodies Are Wrapped

Investigators in the region treat wrapping as communication. It is meant to be found, and to be understood by a particular audience.

The practice is associated with disputes between criminal groups. It appears across Central America and Mexico rather than in Guatemala alone.

It also complicates identification. Bodies moved and wrapped are harder to place at a scene.

None of that is a finding in these 65 cases. It is the professional context, and the Public Ministry has confirmed none of it here.

What Guatemala Publishes and What It Does Not

Guatemala publishes homicide totals monthly. It does not routinely publish clearance rates by category.

That gap is the reason a number like this circulates without an explanation attached. The count exists, the analysis does not.

Prensa Libre obtained the figure by asking. It was not part of a scheduled release.

The Wider Security Picture

Guatemala’s homicide rate fell through the 2010s and has been broadly stable since. Extortion, not killing, is the crime most businesses report.

The capital and the Pacific corridor carry most recorded violence. Both are transit routes rather than production areas.

Foreign residents rarely encounter this directly. The risk falls heavily on people involved in, or living beside, local disputes.

What to Watch on the Guatemala Bodies Count

The first marker is whether the Public Ministry links any of the 54 complaints. A joint investigation would change the story entirely.

The second is the monthly rate. Sixty-five in eight months is roughly eight a month, and a rise would be visible quickly.

The third is whether the category survives. Filing labels are sometimes retired once a pattern is either explained or disproved.

More: Central America news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many bodies has Guatemala recorded in bags this year?

The Public Ministry has registered 65 people found in bags, sacks, barrels or other wrappings, from 54 complaints filed between 1 January and 2 September 2026.

Where were they found?

Forty-nine of the 65 were found in the department of Guatemala, which contains the capital. The complaints came from ten of the country’s twenty-two departments.

Does Guatemala know who is responsible?

No. The Public Ministry has not said how many of the cases are connected, who ordered the killings, or why the bodies were wrapped and abandoned.

Sources: Prensa Libre, Ministerio Publico de Guatemala, Rio Times.

World.title: Peru Prison Emergency Covers Five Jails, One Left Unguarded
World.content:
PERU · SECURITY

Key Facts — What happened Peru placed five maximum-security prisons under a state of emergency for sixty days.

— The reason Officials say extortion rings are being run from inside the prisons using smuggled telephones.

— Where the soldiers go The measure covers the perimeters, with the armed forces supporting the national police outside the walls.

— The catch Infobae found no visible police or military presence at Castro Castro in Lima on the first day.

— Who it affects The five prisons are in Lima, Tacna, Pasco and La Libertad, four of Peru’s most affected regions.

— What comes next The decree runs sixty days and can be renewed, which is how previous emergencies became permanent.

The decree covers the walls, not the wings. On the first morning, one Lima prison on the list had nobody standing outside it.

A police station building in Lima. The emergency decree puts the national police in charge outside five prison perimeters. (Photo: “Comisaria Alfonso Ugarte” by Privado (imagen donada al publicador), via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

Peru has placed five maximum-security prisons under a state of emergency. The Peru prison emergency was announced on Friday and formalised by decree the next day.

Supreme Decree 128-2026 was published on Sunday, 6 September. It runs for sixty days.

The government of President Keiko Fujimori took office on 28 July. This is one of its first large security measures.

The stated target is organised crime run from inside the prisons. Officials say extortion rings direct operations by telephone from their cells.

Which Prisons Are Covered

Two of the five are in Lima. They are Miguel Castro Castro and Ancon I.

Challapalca sits in Tacna, high in the southern Andes. Cochamarca is in Pasco, and Trujillo Varones is in La Libertad.

The choice follows the map of extortion complaints. La Libertad and Lima produce the bulk of them.

Castro Castro was added after threats and explosives were found at its perimeter. Inmates there were also found to be in contact with criminal groups outside.

Peruvian national police officers on duty. The armed forces are to support them under the new decree rather than replace them. (Photo: “National Police of Peru officers” by Kline, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

What the Decree Actually Does

This is the detail foreign readers usually miss. The emergency covers the areas around the prisons, not the wings inside them.

The armed forces support the national police outside the walls. Running the prisons themselves remains the job of the penal authority.

A state of emergency in Peru suspends certain constitutional guarantees in the named area. It allows searches and detentions without a warrant.

It does not, by itself, remove a single telephone from a cell. That work happens inside, under different powers.

The Gap Infobae Found

On Sunday, Infobae went to look at Castro Castro. It reported no visible police or military guard at the perimeter.

The prison is in San Juan de Lurigancho, the most populous district in Lima. It is named in the decree.

That is not a legal exclusion. It is a deployment that had not arrived, on the day the decree was published.

The distinction matters for how the measure is judged. A decree without officers on the ground changes nothing at the gate.

Why Prisons Became the Front Line

Peru’s extortion problem has grown sharply over the past three years. Small businesses, transport operators and schools are the usual targets.

Investigators say a large share of the calls originate inside prisons. Mobile phones enter through visitors, staff and drones.

Blocking signals has been tried and has repeatedly failed. Equipment breaks, coverage leaks, and networks upgrade faster than the jammers.

Sending soldiers to the perimeter is the visible answer. It is also the fastest one to announce.

The Pattern to Watch

Peru has used states of emergency heavily in recent years. Districts of Lima have spent much of the past two years under one.

Sixty days is the standard term and renewal is routine. Several emergencies have run for more than a year through repeated extensions.

That is the risk with this one. An exceptional measure becomes the ordinary state of affairs, and the underlying problem is never addressed.

What to Watch

The first marker is whether soldiers appear at Castro Castro this week. A decree that is not staffed is a press release.

The second is whether extortion complaints fall in La Libertad. That is the number the government will be judged on.

The third is the first renewal in November. If it comes automatically, the emergency has become the policy.

More: Peru news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which prisons are under the Peru prison emergency?

Five maximum-security prisons: Miguel Castro Castro and Ancon I in Lima, Challapalca in Tacna, Cochamarca in Pasco, and Trujillo Varones in La Libertad. The decree runs for sixty days.

Does the emergency cover the inside of the prisons?

No. It covers the perimeters and surrounding areas, with the armed forces supporting the national police outside the walls. Running the prisons themselves stays with the penal authority.

What did Infobae report about Castro Castro?

It reported on 6 September 2026 that there was no visible police or military presence at the prison’s perimeter, despite Castro Castro being named in the decree.

Sources: Infobae, El Comercio, Radio Nacional, TV Peru, El Peruano, Rio Times.

World.title: Ibama Clears Three More Petrobras Wells in Foz do Amazonas
World.content:
BRAZIL · ENERGY

Key Facts — What happened Brazil’s environmental regulator authorised Petrobras to drill three more wells off the mouth of the Amazon.

— The block All four wells sit in block FZA-M-59, where the Morpho well already found oil this year.

— Why it matters The Equatorial Margin is the frontier Brazil hopes will replace declining output from older offshore fields.

— The catch Each well still needs its own technical clearance, so the authorisation is not a blanket permit to drill.

— Who objects Environmental groups say a spill near the Amazon delta could not be contained with current response capacity.

— What comes next The president is expected to mention the discovery in his Independence Day address on Monday.

The first well found oil. The next three decide whether that was a pocket or a province, and the answer arrives in the middle of an election year.

The mouth of the Amazon meeting the Atlantic. The drilling blocks sit offshore, north of the sediment plume. (Photo: “Amazon River mouth on the Atlantic” by Coordenação-Geral de Observação da Terra/INPE, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.)

Brazil’s environmental regulator has cleared Petrobras to drill three more wells in the Foz do Amazonas basin. The authorisation came on Friday, 4 September.

Ibama, the federal environment agency, had already licensed one well in the same block. That well, Morpho, found oil.

The new clearance takes the programme to four wells in total. One is the main well and three are contingent.

All of them sit in block FZA-M-59. It lies offshore from the state of Amapa, north of where the Amazon meets the sea.

Why This Block Matters

Brazil calls the region the Equatorial Margin. It runs along the northern coast and continues into waters off Guyana and Suriname.

Those neighbouring waters have produced some of the largest oil finds of the past decade. Brazilian geologists have long argued the same rocks continue south.

Petrobras drilled Morpho to test that idea. Finding oil turned a geological argument into a commercial question.

Three more wells are how you answer it. One discovery tells you the rock works, not how much is there.

A semi-submersible drilling rig. Rigs of this class work the deep water off Brazil’s northern coast. (Photo: “ENSCO 8506 Offshore Semi-Submersible Oil Drilling Rig (47504222982)” by Tony Webster from Minneapolis, Minnesota, United States, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.)

What the Licence Does and Does Not Do

The authorisation is not a blanket permit. Each well still needs its own technical sign-off from Ibama before drilling starts.

Environmental conditions attach to the work. They cover spill response, wildlife protection and the timing of operations.

That structure is deliberate. Ibama spent years refusing to license the first well in the region at all.

The Exploration and Production segment explores, develops, and produces…

The Objection

Environmental groups have opposed drilling off the Amazon delta since the first application. Their argument is about response time, not about geology.

The nearest support base is far from the drilling site. Critics say a serious spill could reach the coast before equipment arrives.

The delta also holds a reef system that was only mapped in the past decade. Its extent is still disputed among scientists.

Petrobras says its response plan meets the regulator’s requirements. Ibama has accepted that plan for the wells it has licensed.

The Politics of Timing

Brazil holds general elections in October. Energy has become part of the campaign.

Estadao reports the president will refer to the northern oil find in his Independence Day address on Monday. The message is aimed partly at Washington.

That framing suits both sides of the argument. Supporters hear investment and jobs, and opponents hear the Amazon.

What It Means for Production

Nothing in this decision adds a barrel to Brazilian output this year. Exploration wells are years away from production.

Brazil’s existing offshore fields in the Santos basin are mature. Output there will decline without new sources.

The Equatorial Margin is the main candidate to replace them. That is why a licence for three wells reads as strategic rather than routine.

How Brazil Licenses a Frontier Well

Ibama assesses each application against a spill model and a response plan. It also weighs the distance to the nearest support base.

The agency refused the first application for the basin outright in 2023. It granted the Morpho licence only after Petrobras revised its emergency plan.

That history is why this authorisation reads as a shift. The regulator is now processing wells rather than debating whether the region can be drilled at all.

What to Watch

The first marker is when the rig actually moves. A licence is not a spud date.

The second is what the contingent wells find. Three dry holes would change the story quickly.

The third is whether Ibama licenses a second block. That would signal the regulator is now treating the region as open rather than exceptional.

More: Brazil news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Ibama approve in the Foz do Amazonas basin?

It authorised Petrobras to drill three more exploratory wells in block FZA-M-59, on 4 September 2026. With the Morpho well already drilled, the programme now covers four wells in that block.

Did Petrobras find oil there?

Yes. The Morpho well in the same block found oil earlier in 2026, which is what prompted the request to drill further.

Why is the region controversial?

The blocks sit near the mouth of the Amazon, and environmental groups argue that spill response capacity in the area is too far away to contain a serious accident.

Sources: Ibama, Petrobras, Agencia Brasil, Estadao, Valor, Reuters, Rio Times.

World.title: Argentina Moves to Sanction 45 Names Over Falklands Oil Work
World.content:
ARGENTINA · POLITICS

Key Facts — What happened Argentina opened a sanctions process against 45 companies and executives working on oil near the Falklands.

— The legal basis A 2011 law penalises unauthorised drilling on the Argentine continental shelf with up to fifteen years in prison.

— Who is named Navitas Petroleum, Rockhopper Exploration, JHI Associates, Noble Corporation and Fugro are among the targets.

— The catch Sanctions are announced against foreign firms that mostly hold no Argentine assets, so the practical bite is limited.

— Who backed it The G6, Argentina’s main business association, publicly supported the sovereignty claim a day later.

— What comes next The government wants Congress to fast-track related bills once they reach the floor.

The list is the longest Argentina has produced. What is new is not the law, which is fifteen years old, but the willingness to use it at scale.

The waterfront at Stanley. Argentina calls the islands the Malvinas and claims sovereignty over them and their waters. (Photo: “Stanley waterfront” by CHK46, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

Argentina has opened a sanctions process against 45 companies and executives. All are accused of taking part in Falklands oil work that Buenos Aires says is unauthorised.

The move was taken on Friday, 4 September, and reported over the weekend. It is the widest list Argentina has produced on the issue.

The targets are spread across eight countries. They include the United Kingdom, Israel, Canada, the United States, Sweden, Kazakhstan, South Africa and Denmark.

For foreign readers, the shorthand matters. Argentina calls the islands the Malvinas and treats the surrounding seabed as its continental shelf.

The Law Behind It

The instrument is Law 26.659, passed in 2011. It penalises exploring or producing hydrocarbons on the Argentine continental shelf without an Argentine permit.

It also reaches those who give direct or indirect support to such work. Penalties run up to fifteen years in prison.

President Javier Milei issued a decree to speed up how the law is applied. That is what made a list of this size possible.

The law is not new and neither is its use. Rockhopper was first sanctioned in 2013, and Navitas in 2022.

The Casa Rosada in Buenos Aires. The sanctions decision was taken at presidential level and published this week. (Photo: “Casa Rosada – Buenos Aires (8556504814)” by Cyro A. Silva from Rio de Janeiro, Brasil, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.)

Who Is on the Falklands Oil List

Navitas Petroleum appears twice, through its development arm and its Atlantic subsidiary. The Israeli company is a partner in the Sea Lion project north of the islands.

Rockhopper Exploration of the United Kingdom is named again. So are subsidiaries of Borders and Southern.

Two Canadian entities appear, JHI Associates and JHI Falkland. The American driller Noble Corporation and the Dutch survey group Fugro complete the better-known names.

The official communication does not split companies from individuals. Reporting the figure as 45 companies would therefore overstate it.

Why the Oil Services Firms Matter More

Three of the largest oilfield service companies in the world stepped back from the project this week. Halliburton, Baker Hughes and SLB all declined the work.

That is the part with real commercial weight. A sanctions listing is a legal problem, but losing the contractors is an operational one.

Argentine reporting says three companies tied to the Vaca Muerta shale patch also declined to operate near the islands. Those firms have Argentine assets to protect.

The Mercado Libre Question

Argentine outlets have asked whether the country’s most valuable company could be caught by the same law. The story concerns Mercado Libre.

The reported link is not commercial and not contractual. It rests on shared institutional shareholders.

Two Israeli fund managers hold stakes in Navitas Petroleum and also own shares in Mercado Libre. Their combined holding in the e-commerce group was worth about US$28 million in March.

Mercado Libre has not been sanctioned and has not been named by the government. No process against it has been opened, and the company has not commented.

The Business Reaction

Argentina’s G6, the umbrella group for the country’s main business chambers, backed the sovereignty claim on Saturday. It said so publicly and without qualification.

That is less obvious than it looks. Several G6 members do business with the same multinationals now on the list.

Sovereignty over the islands is one of the few issues that unites Argentine politics. Business groups rarely break from it.

What the Falklands Oil Listing Actually Changes

Most of the sanctioned firms hold no assets in Argentina. A listing therefore blocks something they were not doing anyway.

The effect is reputational and financial rather than physical. Banks and insurers read sanctions lists even when governments cannot enforce them.

The measure also raises the cost of hiring anyone who wants Argentine work later. That is the lever with the longest reach.

What to Watch

The first marker is Congress. The government wants Falklands bills fast-tracked once they arrive on the floor.

The second is whether any listed firm actually leaves the Falklands oil project. Rockhopper has been sanctioned since 2013 and is still there.

The third is whether the list grows. A process opened against 45 names can be widened more easily than it was started.

More: Argentina news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many names are on Argentina’s Falklands oil sanctions list?

The government opened a process against 45 subjects on 4 September 2026. These are companies and individuals combined, and the official communication does not break out the split.

What law is Argentina using?

Law 26.659, passed in 2011, penalises unauthorised hydrocarbon exploration or production on the Argentine continental shelf, and those who support it, with up to fifteen years in prison.

Is Mercado Libre sanctioned?

No. Reports describe only shared institutional shareholders between Mercado Libre and Navitas Petroleum. Mercado Libre has not been named by the government and no process against it has been opened.

Sources: Infobae, La Nacion, Perfil, El Cronista, Ambito, Realpolitik, Reuters, Rio Times.

World.title: Fachin Takes the Mendonca Case Away From the Moraes Inquiry
World.content:
BRAZIL · POLITICS

Key Facts — What happened Chief Justice Edson Fachin removed the request to investigate Justice Andre Mendonca from the fake news inquiry.

— Where it went The request now sits in a separate petition handled directly by the court presidency rather than by Moraes.

— Why it matters Moraes both requested the investigation and ran the inquiry it was filed in, which critics called a conflict.

— The catch Fachin has not refused the investigation, so the request survives and could still reach the full court.

— Who must speak first The prosecutor general and Mendonca himself must give written positions before the plenary considers anything.

— What comes next The court sits under heavy security through Brazil’s Independence Day on Monday, 7 September.

It is a procedural move, not a verdict. In a court where procedure is the whole fight, it is the first real check on Alexandre de Moraes in months.

The Supreme Federal Court in Brasilia. The dispute between two of its eleven justices is now handled by a third. (Photo: “Supreme Federal Court – Side” by Dasfour2022, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)
