World.title: IFA 2026: Xiaomi wants its smart-home cars on European roads by 2027
World.content:
Xiaomi may still be best known for its smartphones. But at IFA 2026, the Chinese technology company presented plans for a future that no longer fits inside people's pockets.

 

Home appliances and connected devices have become an increasingly important part of its business. Now, Xiaomi is putting greater emphasis on four wheels — and the shift is hard to miss at IFA.

Inside the company's exhibition space in Berlin, one of the first things visitors encounter is a futuristic-looking car carrying the familiar Xiaomi logo, but on a very different scale.

Xiaomi cars are already a familiar sight for consumers in China. Now the company wants to bring them to European roads too.

In that spirit, Xiaomi announced at IFA 2026 that it plans to launch its electric vehicles in Europe in 2027, marking the next stage of its expansion beyond smartphones and consumer electronics.

Xiaomi has also expanded its range of home appliances and connected devices. Euronews

But simply selling cars is not the company's ultimate goal. Like many of the technology companies exhibiting in Berlin, Xiaomi is increasingly focused on connecting different parts of everyday life.

It calls its approach "Human x Car x Home", an ecosystem designed to link personal devices, the car and technology around the home. In practice, the idea is to let you steer your home from behind the wheel of your car.

Euronews took a closer look at Xiaomi's vision at IFA 2026 to see how that ecosystem is supposed to work.

'Human x Car x Home': The vision

Rather than treating the car as a separate product, Xiaomi wants to integrate it into the same connected system that already links devices around the home. The aim is for users to move between different environments while staying connected to the devices they rely on every day.

Euronews At IFA, Xiaomi presented its "Human × Car × Home" ecosystem, connecting cars, smartphones and home devices.

At IFA, Xiaomi demonstrated what that could look like in practice. From inside the car, users could control devices back at home, including opening and closing connected curtains and switching the air conditioning on or off.

This means the car could effectively become another control point for the smart home. Someone leaving work, for example, could adjust the air conditioning before arriving home, while other connected devices could be controlled directly from the vehicle.

Xiaomi says AI and its HyperOS operating system are intended to provide the technological link between these devices. Its longer-term vision goes beyond users manually controlling individual appliances, with AI eventually using contextual information to coordinate devices across the car, smartphone and home.

For Xiaomi, the car is therefore not only a new product category, but another part of a wider connected ecosystem — extending its technology beyond smartphones and the home and onto the road.

Alongside its more concrete plans, Xiaomi has also left room for imagination, exploring what could become possible further down the road.

Xiaomi's Vision Gran Turismo Euronews

Among the concepts presented at IFA is the Xiaomi Vision Gran Turismo. The electric hypercar concept was developed for the Gran Turismo racing game series and explores ideas around design, aerodynamics and digital interaction.

For now, however, this vehicle remains firmly a concept rather than a preview of a production model expected to hit the road any time soon.

Local partners

But despite leaving room for experimentation, Xiaomi also made clear that its European ambitions go beyond concepts. At its IFA press conference on 3 September, the company took concrete steps towards its planned market entry.

During a signing ceremony, the company signed letters of intent with eight German automotive retail groups: Emil Frey Germany, the Ernst Dello Group, Autohaus Dinnebier, Hahn Automobile, the LUEG Mobility Group, Fett & Wirtz, SPT Avior and Penske-Jacobs.

Germany, however, is only intended to be the starting point, with Xiaomi planning similar partnerships in other European markets.

"Europe is a key market for our global strategy," Xiaomi Chief Marketing Officer Xu Fei said during the press conference.

The company is also planning significant investment to support this broader strategy. Between 2026 and 2030, Xiaomi says it intends to invest more than €24 billion globally in research and development, with a focus on areas including AI, operating systems, semiconductors, intelligent vehicles, robotics and smart manufacturing.

World.title: Report of suspected attack on baby dolphin in Ceuta area where migrants are staying
World.content:
A bottlenose dolphin calf was found dead at around midday on Wednesday on Trampolín beach in Ceuta, according to 'El Faro de Ceuta', and in circumstances that the Association for the Defence of Urban Trees, Biodiversity and the Environment (DAUBMA) considers an attack. The organisation has filed a formal complaint with the Guardia Civil and requested that proceedings be opened to clarify what happened.

 

According to the association's account, the animal reached the shore alive, disoriented, possibly because of the fog in the area that morning. Once on land, DAUBMA says, several people dragged it out of the water and hit it on the head with a stick.

The organisation says it has photographs, videos and social media screenshots that also show blood beneath one of the animal’s eyes, as well as some of the people present trying to wipe it away. In its view, this points to a direct attack and to manipulation of the carcass that is incompatible with any attempt to help the animal. All of this material has been made available to the Guardia Civil.

A verified video that circulated widely, with no perpetrators identified

The footage, first shared on social media, was recorded on the part of the beach where people who entered Ceuta during the mass crossing on 30 and 31 July remain camped.

A worker from the cleaning company Ecoservicios, who was in the area, witnessed the scene and warned those present that they should stop what they were doing and call an environmental collection service.

After that warning, according to witnesses, they tried to return the animal to the sea, although it was no longer showing any signs of life. So far there has been no formal identification of those responsible: that is precisely what DAUBMA is seeking with its complaint to the Guardia Civil.

The case has sparked outrage online, and a local resident, Nadia García Gómez, has launched a petition on change.org calling for those responsible to be identified.

García Gómez stresses that she does not belong to any association and argues for a firm response to animal abuse: "This cruel act must be tried and punished", she wrote online, in which she asks the authorities "to do something about it". The petition points out that the bottlenose dolphin is a strictly protected species in the EU and that injuring or killing an individual can constitute a criminal offence.

DAUBMA and CECAM respond to criticism

Responding to those who ask where animal rights associations are when dead wildlife is found in Ceuta, DAUBMA and CECAM say their work focuses on documenting cases and passing them on to institutions, while lamenting the lack of any response.

They explain that more than three months ago they submitted to the Government Delegation a dossier on other cases of dead or affected animals, including dolphins and turtles showing, they say, signs of having fallen victim to drift nets, which are banned in the EU, but have received no reply.

They add that an attempt to file a complaint with Seprona was initially not processed, so they went to the duty court with technical and graphic material; the court, according to their account, ordered the case to be provisionally closed pending a Seprona report that has still not arrived.

Both organisations say they coordinate with emergency services, the Guardia Civil, Semar and collection companies, and call on the authorities to ensure that wildlife protection does not remain mere rhetoric.

World.title: Mediterranean Sea now at spa temperature, daily average 28.54°C on 13 August
World.content:
Surface waters across the Mediterranean Sea reached an average temperature of 28.54ºC on 13 August, the highest recorded since at least 1940, Spain's State Meteorological Agency reported on Sunday.

 

Aemet itself noted on social media that throughout almost the whole of August the sea was breaking daily temperature records, one after another, with barely any respite.

The warning comes just weeks after Mercator Ocean International, which implements the Copernicus marine service, confirmed that July had already been the hottest month ever measured in the Mediterranean. The average that month was 27.07ºC, with a margin of uncertainty of ±0.27ºC, beating the previous maximum, set in July 2025 (26.68ºC), by four tenths of a degree.

Mercator Ocean's comparison series begins in 1993, meaning that both bodies, despite using different methods and reference periods, concur in describing a sea that has entered a thermal regime not seen before.

Daily average sea temperature in the Mediterranean, 2026 Aemet

This pattern has been in place for months

Data from late June were already pointing that way. Aemet (source in Spanish) warned at the time that Mediterranean temperatures had reached levels more typical of the second half of August, when the sea is usually at its warmest.

At the start of the summer, temperatures rose to 2.6ºC above normal, to the point that the sea exceeded the average usually seen in mid-August while it was still June, an anomaly the agency itself described as exceptional.

On a planetary scale, the phenomenon is not confined to the Mediterranean. July 2026 was the month with the highest global ocean surface temperature in the entire record, with an average of 21ºC between 60º north and 60º south.

Across the Mediterranean basin, 27% of the sea experienced its warmest July since 1993 and around 70% of the surface ranked among the four hottest Julys ever measured, ruling out the idea that the record can be explained by just a few exceptional locations.

It is important to stress that the sea-temperature record cannot be singled out as the direct cause of the high temperatures recorded on land, as many different factors come into play in the atmosphere. It can, however, alter conditions along the coast: water releases heat more slowly than the land surface, so a Mediterranean this warm makes it harder for temperatures to fall at night, increases humidity and leads to hotter nights near the shore.

The build-up of energy in the sea also affects ecosystems. Prolonged marine heatwaves subject organisms adapted to specific thermal ranges to considerable stress and can alter species distribution, increase mortality and change the functioning of entire coastal communities.

With the figure recorded on 13 August, the Mediterranean has once again surpassed the record it had set only a few weeks earlier, in a summer which, on land and at sea, keeps breaking its own records.

World.title: EU chief von der Leyen heads to Greenland in show of support for the island
World.content:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is visiting Greenland on Sunday and Monday as the bloc signals its continued support for the island amid US President Donald Trump's repeated calls for the United States to acquire it.

 

As part of the visit, von der Leyen is expected to sign a joint declaration between the EU and the Danish autonomous territory on Monday.

Since his return to the White House in January last year, Trump has claimed the US needs to take control of Greenland for its "national security," arguing that either China or Russia would otherwise seize the island.

Von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa issued a joint statement in January in which they highlighted the importance of "territorial integrity and sovereignty" and said the EU stood "in full solidarity with Denmark and the people of Greenland."

Speaking at the World Economic Forum's annual meeting in Davos this year, von der Leyen said the EU was also working on a "massive European investment surge" in Greenland in a bid to ramp up Arctic security.

The Commission has proposed allocating €530 million to Greenland under its budget for the 2028–2034 period, which it said reflected its "growing geostrategic importance in the Arctic."

The Financial Times reported that von der Leyen is set to announce an additional €200 million in funding for the island during her visit.

Houses are seen near the coast of a sea inlet of Nuuk, Greenland, on Sunday, Jan. 25, 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

In May, Trump's special envoy to Greenland, Jeff Landry, said it was time the US "puts its footprint back" on the territory.

Landry, who is also the governor of Louisiana, made the comments during a trip to the territory, his first since his appointment to the special envoy role in December 2025.

Speaking from Greenland's capital, Nuuk, Landry told Agence France-Presse: "I think that you're seeing the president talk about increasing national security operations and repopulating certain bases in Greenland."

"Everyone that I've talked to in Greenland would love to see the US repopulate those bases," he continued, adding that the territory "needs the US."

In January, the leaders of five political parties in Greenland’s parliament released a joint statement with a clear message to the US.

"We do not want to be Americans, we do not want to be Danes; we want to be Greenlanders," it read.

The US is reported to have had 17 military facilities and more than 10,000 troops on Greenland at the height of the Cold War. It currently operates just one base on the island, the Pituffik Space Base - the US Department of Defense's northernmost installation.

Pituffik is used for missile warning, missile defense and space surveillance missions, according to the US Space Force.

World.title: Bad Bunny keeps breaking records: 7 Emmys for Super Bowl show
World.content:
The Creative Arts Emmy Awards, held in Los Angeles as a curtain-raiser to the main televised ceremony on 14 September, made Bad Bunny one of the standout figures of the night. The Puerto Rican artist has come away with seven awards thanks to his show during the Super Bowl LX halftime break.

 

The production, officially titled "The Apple Music Super Bowl LX Halftime Show Starring Bad Bunny", went into this edition of the Emmys with a remarkable achievement already under its belt. In July it became the music production in this format with the highest number of nominations, nine in total, since the awards were created, beating the record held by Lady Gaga since 2017.

The Television Academy has now recognised the technical ambition and creativity of the Latin show with seven statuettes. Among them are Best Music Direction, for Brazilian Miguel Gandelman, and Best Choreography for Variety Programming, for choreographers Charm La'Donna and Karina Ortiz. The haul also includes awards for technical direction, lighting design, sound mixing and directing for a special programme.

Bad Bunny's presence at this year's Emmys has not been limited to the sporting and musical arena. His work as a presenter has also been recognised, as the episode of "Saturday Night Live" he hosted at the end of 2025 has won the Emmy for Best Make-up in the variety, non-fiction or reality category.

It has been a record-breaking year for Bad Bunny, who has already received the 2026 Grammy and 2026 Latin Grammy, putting Spanish among the most listened-to and awarded music in the world. His winning streak appears to be continuing with these 7 Emmy Awards.

A continental message before millions of viewers

The singer used the biggest television stage in the United States to assert the idea of America as a single, entire continent, rather than a term used exclusively to refer to the United States.

The show ended with a commemorative ball bearing the slogan "Together we're America", accompanied by a parade of flags and the names of all the countries in the region, from Canada to Chile.

This year's nominations were announced by Puerto Rico-born actress Liza Colón-Zayas, known for her role in the series "The Bear", alongside comedian Jeff Hiller. The 2026 Emmy Awards ceremony will take place on Sunday 14 September at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles.

Other winners on the first night of the Creative Arts Emmys

Bad Bunny's triumph was not an isolated case on the opening night of the Creative Arts Emmys. His Super Bowl show became the most decorated programme of the evening, with seven statuettes, ahead of productions such as "The Traitors", which took six, and "The Late Show With Stephen Colbert", with five.

Stephen Colbert's programme, which came to an end in May after an eleven-year run, won the Emmy for Best Picture Editing for Variety Programming for an episode featuring Paul McCartney and Elvis Costello, as well as the award for Best Lighting Design for a Series for another episode with Bruce Springsteen as guest.

The Muppet Show, on Disney+, picked up four awards and prevailed in the category of Best Pre-Recorded Variety Special ahead of Taylor Swift, whose tour farewell "Taylor Swift, The Eras Tour, The Final Show" was also competing in that section. Sabrina Carpenter, involved in the Muppets special as executive producer and performer, thereby won her first Primetime Emmy.

Other notable awards of the day included Best Documentary or Non-Fiction Series, for "Mr. Scorsese", the Apple TV production about filmmaker Martin Scorsese, and Best Sound Mixing for a Non-Fiction Programme, for "Billy Joel, And So It Goes" on HBO Max. The segment "Blink Again", from the series "Sean Combs, The Reckoning" on Netflix, took the prize for Best Picture Editing for a Non-Fiction Programme.

In the music categories, Miguel Gandelman took the prize for Best Music Direction for Bad Bunny's show and became the third person to win that award for a Super Bowl halftime performance, after Adam Blackstone in 2022 and Kendrick Lamar with Tony Russell last year. Tyler Strickland, for his part, won Best Music Composition for a documentary, non-fiction or reality programme for his work on "John Candy, I Like Me". Both thereby secured their first Primetime Emmy.

Director Hamish Hamilton once again claimed the award for Best Direction for a Variety Special, this time for Bad Bunny's show. It is the third time he has done so in the past four years, after winning in 2023 for Rihanna's halftime show, co-directed with Jay-Z, and in 2024 for his work on the Oscars ceremony.

Actress and director Mariska Hargitay picked up two awards as producer and director of "My Mom Jayne, A Film by Mariska Hargitay", a documentary about her mother, actress Jayne Mansfield. Hargitay will also host the 78th edition of the Emmy Awards, which will be broadcast live on NBC next Monday 14 September from the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles, with a simultaneous stream on Peacock.

Of the 49 categories presented on Saturday, this was the tally. Another 53 will be handed out this Sunday, on the second night of the Creative Arts Emmys. Of these, only 19 will be included in the televised broadcast of the main gala on 14 September. Highlights from both Creative Arts ceremonies will air on Saturday 12 September at 20:00 (Pacific Time) on FXX, and will be available on Hulu from the following day.

World.title: Turkey seeks Black Sea shipping deal as attacks threaten grain trade
World.content:
Turkey is racing to restore safe passage for cargo ships in the Black Sea as attacks on shipping disrupt grain exports and push up prices. Russia and Ukraine are major global wheat exporters, but Black Sea trade has been severely disrupted as both sides step up attacks on shipping and port infrastructure.

Advertising

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan announced this week that Turkey was working on a plan to ensure safe passage in the Black Sea for commercial shipping and said he was in touch with both Ukraine and Russia.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan confirmed that he raised the issue with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, on the sidelines of a gathering of regional leaders in Kyrgyzstan.

The Turkish move comes as Ukraine and Russia have ramped up their attacks on shipping and ports in and around the Black Sea. In 2022, Turkey and the United Nations brokered a deal between Ukraine and Russia to ensure safe passage for Ukrainian grain exports through the Black Sea.

The agreement lasted a year.

While Turkey has maintained good ties with both sides, reaching another agreement will be much harder, warned international relations professor Huseyin Bagci of Ankara’s Middle East Technical University.

“The tension is increasing more than ever before,” Bagci said. “It's not enough to have good relations, because the two sides – the Ukrainians and Russians – should sit down and talk about a common solution to this problem. Turkey cannot solve this problem alone.”

What the SDF’s dissolution means for Syria’s Kurds and neighbouring Turkey

Growing attacks

In August Ukraine offered a ceasefire on commercial shipping, but the offer was rejected by Moscow, which said it wanted a broader deal. Ukrainian drones continue to strike Russian shipping, while Russia has continued missile attacks on Ukrainian ports and ships.

This surge in attacks comes as both nations rush to export their grain harvests.

Grain prices have risen sharply, by as much as 30 percent, international grain broker Can Atbasoglu said, even as both sides scramble to find new routes for their exports.

“Russia will do their best to export as much as they can, both from Russian Baltic ports and EU Baltic ports like Latvia and Lithuania; they're also exporting,” Atbasoglu said.

“Ukraine will also export as much as they can from Romania as well and through the Danube ports. But the export pace will be definitely lower. So it will definitely stay bullish for the markets. Prices are definitely going to stay like this or can have a further increase.”

Fears of wheat price surge amid Ukraine-Russia clashes in the Black Sea

Ships staying put

At one of Istanbul's many shipyards, the docks are crowded with ships that once braved the Black Sea. One vessel bears the scars of a drone attack and is under repair. Others undergo routine maintenance as shipowners hesitate to risk new journeys into dangerous waters.

The superintendent of one ship, speaking anonymously, says repairs are nearly finished, but uncertainty clouds the future.

“We wanted to take the ship out to the Black Sea before entering the shipyard, but because of that risk, we didn’t enter the Black Sea and didn’t take on any cargo. We’ve been in the shipyard for 50 days for repairs, but we don’t know what will happen once the repairs are finished,” the superintendent said.

Turkish shipowners warn that many are on the brink of bankruptcy, as idle ships rack up costs of up to 50,000 euros a month in mooring and crew expenses.

Ziya Ustel, CEO of Turkish shipping company VI-ZA STAR, says high freight rates are being offered for Black Sea routes, but the risks are too great.

“They are offering high freight rates, etc,” Ustel said.

Without a diplomatic solution, few shipowners will be prepared to risk their vessels, Ustel warned.

“The main thing is to find out a real solution,” Ustel added. “Otherwise, no one will try anything anymore.”

Turkish diplomacy

Ankara is expected to step up its efforts to find a solution.

Grain brokers say hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough may be one reason prices have so far remained below the record highs seen at the start of the war.

But if Turkish efforts fail and attacks on Black Sea shipping continue, higher grain prices could have a considerable impact, especially on the world’s poorest nations, many of which depend on Russian and Ukrainian grain.

World.title: Saxony-Anhalt: Far-right AfD secures huge lead in key vote
World.content:
Skip next section BSW open to working with AfD on policy issues

09/06/2026 September 6, 2026 BSW open to working with AfD on policy issues

The Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) has signaled that it could cooperate with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) on individual policy issues in Saxony-Anhalt.

"We will always decide on the substance," BSW lead candidate Claudia Wittig told Germany's public broadcaster ARD.

She used the example of energy prices, saying that such issues "can be done together with the AfD," while there may be less common ground in other areas.

Wittig also argued that, given the AfD’s strong result, it would be "completely undemocratic not to involve them in government in some way."

At the same time, she rejected both AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund and incumbent Christian Democratic Union (CDU) Premier Sven Schulze as potential heads of the next state government.

"We want a nonpartisan premier," Wittig said.

She also argued that her leftist populist party could help bridge an increasingly polarized political landscape.

The BSW, founded in 2024 around former Left Party politician Sahra Wagenknecht, advocates for greater social and economic equality but also calls for more restrictive positions on migration and criticizes Germany’s foreign policy.

Current projections put the party at exactly 5.0%, right on the threshold needed to win seats, but a minor shift in numbers could see it miss out on the state parliament.

World.title: Israeli strikes on Lebanon kill several despite truce
World.content:
Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun has appealed to the international community to "take immediate action to stop these violations" of the ceasefire agreement between Israel and Lebanon.

At least four people were killed in Israeli strikes on Lebanon on Sunday, which comes despite a ceasefire between the two countries, according to the Lebanese Health Ministry.

The Lebanese officials also said around 20 other people, including children, were wounded in the strikes.

The office of Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun called the strikes a "dangerous escalation" that targeted "purely civilian administrations and health centers."

"President Aoun held the Israeli side fully responsible for this ongoing escalation, calling on the United States and the international community to take immediate action to stop ​these violations and hold the perpetrators accountable," his aides said in a statement.

In turn, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said the strikes were a response to "a blatant violation" by Hezbollah militants.

"Terrorists from the Hezbollah terrorist organization launched two drones towards IDF soldiers operating in the Security Zone in southern Lebanon," the military said in a statement, adding that there were no reports of Israeli soldiers wounded.

What do we know about the strikes?

Early on Sunday morning, the Israeli military issued an online evacuation alert for Arab Salim, saying it identified a "Hezbollah facility" there.

Lebanon's state-run National News Agency (NNA) said the Israeli military subsequently carried out a strike on the building mentioned in the original evacuation warning.

NNA also reported that "enemy warplanes launched a strike on another house, destroying it." Two women were killed in the strike.

Two women were reportedly killed by Israeli strikes on Arab Salim village Image: Mohammed Zaatari/AP Photo/picture alliance

Another two people were killed in Israeli strikes near the town of Nabatieh al-Fawqa, which lies on the edge of Israel's "security zone" that it occupies in southern Lebanon.

Lebanon's Health Ministry said an Israeli strike "totally destroyed" a disused hospital. The Health Ministry called the incident "another grave violation of international humanitarian law."

The Israeli military said its targets included what it described as a Hezbollah command center inside a building that was previously used as a hospital, as well as a weapons depot.

"The strikes were carried out in response to Hezbollah’s attempted attack yesterday in the Ali Taher Ridge area and to remove threats posed by Hezbollah," it said.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

World.title: US envoys Witkoff, Kushner arrive in Kiyv after Putin talks
World.content:
The two US offcials are meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv, with national security advisors the UK, France, and Germany reportedly also in Ukraine for talks.

US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner made their first official visit to Ukraine on Sunday as part of fresh efforts toward peace with Russia.

As Ukraine's airspace remains closed due to the conflict, the pair arrived in Kyiv by train from Poland, having spent more than three hours in talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow a day earlier.

Putin had declared a three-day ceasefire to ensure the envoys' safety.

Ukraine peace push? Trump envoys hold talks with Kremlin To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Zelenskyy: Ukraine's peace proposals are ready

Ahead of the visit, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on social media that Kyiv is ready for a “constructive” discussion with its US counterparts.

“We are interested in bringing the end of the war closer," he wrote. "Peace is needed. Security guarantees are needed. A just and sustainable postwar peace is needed. Our proposals are prepared.”

Reuters news agency reported that national security advisors from the United Kingdom, France and Germany were also in Kyiv for talks with the US envoys, citing a source familiar with the matter.

Momentum by US President Donald Trump to end the four-and-a-half-year-old conflict has stalled in recent months after talks with Putin at the Kremlin in January failed to produce a result.

Ukraine's Budanov expects war to continue for many months

Despite hopes of a breakthrough with the Russian leader on Saturday, there were no announcements after the meeting.

Putin’s foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov described the Moscow talks as constructive, frank, and useful but didn’t discuss specific outcomes.

Ushakov said the talks also focused on economic issues and potentially large Russia-US projects.

During previous talks, negotiators have struggled to bring both sides together on a range of key issues, including the future of the industrial Donbas region of eastern Ukraine.

The US and Russia have been discussing tie-ins for months to try and end the war Image: Sputnik/Kremlin Pool/AP Photo/picture alliance

For Ukraine, hard security guarantees from its European allies and Washington are crucial to deterring Russia ​from further aggression.

Kyrylo Budanov, Zelenskyy's chief of staff, told the New York Times last weekend that he did not expect the fighting to end before spring 2027.

He also predicted further Russian strategic air strikes on Ukraine this winter.

The war has escalated in recent months, with Putin seeking the complete conquest of Dombas and Russian drones targeting the Ukrainian capital.

Meanwhile, Ukraine has focused its drone attacks on Russia's energy sector. It has also targeted online retailers deep inside Russia to try and bring the war home to the public.

World.title: India news: Rahul Gandhi backs student protests in Maharashtra
World.content:
Published 09/06/2026 Published September 6, 2026 Congress' Rahul Gandhi says Maharashtra student protest reflects 'shattered' trust in system

In recent days, several parts of Maharashtra also witnessed a protest by tribal students — including a hunger strike Image: ANI/IMAGO

India's main opposition leader Rahul Gandhi has voiced support for students protesting in Maharashtra against alleged irregularities in a state-level recruitment examination.

"Thousands of students are on the streets, protesting peacefully — the reason isn't just one exam or recruitment, but a trust that's been shattered by the entire system," Gandhi said in a statement on X as he called on the government to listen to the protesters' demands and act.

"Otherwise, this echo of the students will only grow louder until justice is served," the senior Congress party leader said.

Why are the Maharashtra student demonstrations about?

Gandhi's remarks come as the Maharashtra government initiated a probe into an alleged paper leak of the Maharashtra Public Service Commission's (MPSC) Food and Drug Administration examination for Drug Inspector posts.

The offline exam was held on March 22, following which there were complaints that some candidates had allegedly received the question paper or questions beforehand.

Aspirants said that their complaints were not looked into. The recruitment process was completed and the MPSC published a merit list of 488 candidates.

However, the commission later canceled the recruitment process and in a statement cited a police inquiry which prima facie indicated that a candidate had got hold of the question paper before the exam and benefited from it.

On Saturday, the Maharashtra government also constituted a high-level committee to take full stock of the existing recruitment exam system in the country's second-most populous state.

The committee is tasked with suggesting measures to make the screening process more transparent, secure, reliable and candidate-friendly.

Tribal students' protest

In recent days, several parts of Maharashtra also witnessed a protest by tribal students — including a hunger strike — over poor conditions in student hostels, student safety and recruitment to some 12,500 vacant posts reserved for tribal communities.

The protesters' demands were accepted by the Maharashtra government, leading to the hunger strike being withdrawn.

On Sunday, Rahul Gandhi railed against the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which leads the government in Maharashtra.

"Whether it's the central or state government, every student is tormented by the BJP regime," he alleged.

"Paper leaks, stalled recruitments, the unbearable cost of education, inhumane conditions in hostels, food like poison ...and now, they've seized control of a constitutional body like MPSC and destroyed its credibility," Gandhi, who is the leader of opposition in the lower house of the Indian parliament, said.

Education minister concedes to 'Cockroach' demands, resigns To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The protests in Maharashtra come after a massive Gen Z-led protest demanding an overhaul of India's examination system, rocked the country in July. The demonstrations marked one of the biggest public challenges to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's three-term rule and culminated with the resignation of the then education minister.

World.title: Germany, Kosovo unite against ticks carrying deadly virus
World.content:
Germany has high-security labs while Kosovo has Hyalomma ticks and experience with the deadly Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever. Working together, German and Kosovar scientists are fighting the disease and its vectors.

It can spot its prey from up to 200 meters (about 650 feet) away — but unlike many of its fellow species, it doesn't lurk in the grass waiting for its victim to come closer. Instead it runs after it, chasing animals and humans alike.

The Hyalomma tick, often called "the great hunting tick," was previously found mostly in Africa, Asia, and southern Europe. But climate change means it can now survive further north and it has already been spotted in Germany and various Eastern European countries. Kosovo, in southeastern Europe, has been a hot spot for the tick for some time now.

The Hyalomma tick is also a vector of the highly pathogenic virus for Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, a potentially deadly disease with a high fatality rate. Symptoms of the disease are comparable to those of Ebola fever or the Marburg virus. These are capable of destroying blood and lymphatic vessels, which can lead to internal bleeding and death.

Ticks are spreading To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Kurtesh Sherifi first read about Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever in the newspaper in 2005, when he was completing his studies as a veterinarian in Berlin. The article said that 11 people in his homeland, Kosovo, had contracted the disease and five had died. He was already interested in pathogens that can be transmitted between animals and humans, known as zoonoses, and Crimean-Congo fever intrigued him.

Back home, Sherifi started work with the faculty of agriculture and veterinary medicine at the University of Pristina. But the budget for research was tight. Kosovo, a small country with only about 1.6 million citizens, didn't have a high-security laboratory or the equipment necessary for investigating the Crimean-Congo fever virus.

Seeking German cooperation

Sherifi got in touch with Germany's largest institution for study in this area, the Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine in Hamburg.

One of the researchers was Petra Emmerich, a virologist and expert on what are known as Risk Group 4 viruses — viruses that cause severe, often fatal, diseases and usually have no widely available treatment. The Crimean-Congo virus is in that risk group.

Emmerich also acts as a reservist in the German military, which is especially interested in viruses that could be used as biological weapons. She was sent to Kosovo in 2009, which is when she met Sherifi.

While the much smaller common longhorn beetle (left) waits for a suitable victim to pass by, the Hyalomma tick prefers to go hunting Image: Fabian Sommer/dpa/picture alliance

A lively exchange began between the researchers. In Kosovo, a structure was established to monitor the spread of the Hyalomma tick and the virus. In 2013, the researchers' joint work began to receive funding through the German Biosecurity Program, run by the country's Foreign Ministry and "intended to help partner countries tackle biological threats."

"It's give and take," said Emmerich of the scientific partnership. "We have the diagnostic expertise and the necessary resources but we don't have the patients." Doctors from Germany regularly come to Kosovo with Emmerich where they can exchange information with their counterparts there.

Raising public awareness is another important pillar of the Germany-Kosovo cooperation.

Farmers in Kosovo are particularly susceptible to infection — and not solely due to ticks biting them, but because they often use their bare hands to remove ticks from animals. If infected blood from the animals gets into a small wound on the human hand, the virus can be transmitted to the human.

"This is quite likely how a large proportion of the [infected] population in Kosovo got infected," Sherifi explained.

Patients require intensive care, isolation

He and Emmerich have visited schools to educate students about the dangers of the virus and how to protect against it. For example, certain tick repellents help, as do long pants and sturdy shoes.

Not all Hyalomma ticks carry the virus, and most people who are bitten by a Hyalomma tick do not become ill. However, the larger problem is that there is neither a vaccine nor any specific course of treatment for those who do end up suffering from Crimean-Congo fever.

Farmers in Kosovo are at particular risk from the Hyalomma ticks Image: Idro Seferi

"If you do get sick, it's particularly severe," Emmerich explained. The disease begins with nonspecific, flu-like symptoms including fever, chills, aches and headaches. In severe cases, a patient will begin bleeding from the skin, nose and gums and may also experience gastrointestinal bleeding. The worst causes can result in organ failure.

Patients require intensive care and isolation because they are highly contagious.

Much of the treatment in intensive care focuses on maintaining a patient's vital functions, but they are also given the antiviral drug, ribavirin. But, as Emmerich said, "ribavirin is not all that effective in acutely ill patients." That is something the scientists have seen firsthand with cases in Kosovo.

The best answer is prevention, which is why it's also very important for the researchers to monitor the spread of the Hyalomma ticks and for them to recommend avoiding certain areas where the ticks are prevalent, if possible.

Successful tick tactics

Over the years, the researchers have not only collected thousands of the ticks but they have also conducted so-called seroprevalence studies. These use blood tests to find antibodies from past infections. This allows the scientists to determine whether humans or animals have come in contact with the virus.

Farm animals are particularly suitable for this type of study, Sherifi said, as the virus doesn't affect them. And unlike wild animals and humans, they usually remain in a clearly defined area. That means that if antibodies are detected in the blood of these animals, it's clear the virus is circulating in that area.

In Kosovo, the number of serious infections has dropped drastically in the past decade, amounting to just five cases in total. In the previous decade, there were about 100 cases. Sherifi and Emmerich believe this indicates how successful their work has been.

Of course, that doesn't mean the ticks and the virus won't spread further in Europe, and the researchers both expect this to happen.

Hyalomma ticks with the Crimean-Congo virus have just been detected in France although, so far, no humans have been infected there.

"Over the past 13 years, Hyalomma ticks have spread geographically," said Emmerich. "As a virologist, that's something to think about, and it needs to be closely monitored."

This is why it's important for the German and Kosovar scientists to pass on what they've learned to countries that haven't yet had as much experience monitoring the Hyalomma ticks, such as Macedonia and Albania.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Germany plans anti-drone shield over Leipzig attack — report
World.content:
Several German cities will receive rapidly deployable units capable of defending against drone strikes on critical infrastructure, according to Bild am Sonntag newspaper.

Germany is planning a comprehensive protective shield to prevent attacks like the failed assault on Leipzig airport, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said Sunday.

On August 4, several small drones targeted Leipzig-Halle Airport in eastern Germany, with one hitting a parked plane, while another is thought to have struck an inbound cargo jet.

German intelligence agencies blamed Russia for the incident, which Moscow has denied.

Leipzig-Halle Airport is a major cargo hub used to fly weapons and supplies toward Ukraine Image: Daniel Kessler/imageBROKER/picture alliance

What did Dobrindt say about the shield?

Dobrindt told Bild am Sonntag newspaper that Russia's hybrid attacks are now a "daily" reality, adding: "These attacks will increase, but we can defend ourselves and protect ourselves."

The newspaper cited information from the Interior Ministry showing the government plans to expand the federal police's mobile drone-defense units.

The measures include vehicles and helicopters that can be quickly deployed to protect airspace over key cities like Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin to counter drone attacks.

Bild said the shield would not only intercept drones, but could also defuse drone bombs and other explosive devices.

The newspaper described how a change in the law would allow critical infrastructure operators — including water, power and defense companies — to detect and defend against drone sabotage.

Jammers flood drones with radio noise, so its pilot can no longer steer it Image: Michael Bihlmayer/Bihlmayerfotografie/IMAGO

Russia's Lavrov accuses Merz of wanting war

On Sunday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov claimed the German accusations levelled against Russia were "by ​and ​large, the ​start of ‌a real war."

He reiterated Russia's denial of any involvement with the Leipzig drone attack and criticized German Chancellor Friedrich Merz for wanting to boost the country's military capability in response to hybrid threats.

"All ‌these statements by Merz about making Germany the leading military power in ‌Europe once again — they are ‌being ​put into practice. He is, in effect, declaring war on us," Lavrov told Russian state-run TV channel Vesti.

He also criticized Germany's closure of Russian House cultural center in berlin and the Russian consulate in Bonn.

Putin denies Russian involvement in Leipzig drone attack To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

New tech planned to boost cyber security

Bild also described how a national protective cyber shield would be set up to detect and intercept hacking attacks.

The measure comes amid hundreds of cyberattacks on government departments, infrastructure and companies each day, many of them blamed on Russia, other states and criminal gangs.

The newspaper said the government ⁠also wants to increase the use of AI, biometric facial recognition ⁠and video surveillance, especially at transport hubs, to identify suspected attackers before they carry out attacks.

Over 1,000 drone sightings in 2025

The head of Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), Holger Münch, told Bild in December that more than a thousand suspicious drone flights were recorded over Germany last year.

These incidents mostly targeted military sites, airports, ports and defense firms and were treated as surveillance or harassment, rather than attacks.

Leipzig airport has been targeted by sabotage before. In July 2024, a suspected Russian incendiary parcel caught fire at the airport's DHL hub.

The cargo hub is also utilized by the Ukrainian military and NATO to airlift arms for use in the Ukrainian defense against Russia's invasion.

World.title: How climate change and food insecurity could fuel future conflicts
World.content:
Climate change, conflict, and trade tensions are putting pressure on the global food system. New research suggests the biggest risk is not food shortages, but whether societies can peacefully adapt to change.

The world's food system is under growing stress, and new research is pointing to areas where this could lead to conflict.

Severe droughts and extreme weather are damaging harvests in many regions. A developing El Niño event is even threatening to worsen food shortages for millions of people next year. At the same time, wars and geopolitical tensions are disrupting supply chains that keep food and farm supplies moving.

The war in Ukraine has repeatedly shaken grain markets, while the Iran war's impact on the Strait of Hormuz has driven up fuel and fertilizer prices, increasing costs for farmers everywhere.

Experts have long warned that rising food insecurity could fuel instability. When people can no longer feed their families, they argue over land, water, and other resources — or they move. In fragile countries, these pressures can contribute to social unrest and even armed conflict.

Now, new research has suggested where some of these risks are greatest. The Climate-Driven Agricultural Decline Index (CADI) , developed by Laura Mayoral, Hannes Mueller and colleagues, maps how climate change is reshaping agricultural productivity around the world. "The heaviest losses are in the tropical regions," said Mueller, a researcher at the Institute for Economic Analysis and the Barcelona School of Economics.

Climate change is already reducing food production in many parts of the world. Hundreds of millions of people live in areas where harvests are smaller than 30 years ago. Mueller mentioned Australia, Argentina, Moldova, Nigeria, Romania, the United States, and Sudan as countries where agricultural losses are already being felt.

"Northern Africa is another region we should pay much more attention to. If you look at the map, it just looks terrible. It really looks horrible," he said.

Burundi's vanishing lakes and the fight to bring them back To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

And climate change is only one part of the story. Wars, trade disruptions, export bans, and rising fertilizer costs can magnify food insecurity.

Within the next 25 years, nearly half of the world's people could be living in areas where farms are producing less food.

New winners, losers, and conflicts

These pressures can undermine governments, help causemigration, and make it easier for armed groups to recruit fighters. In societies that are already unstable, such factors can push them toward crisis.

Yet CADI's research points to a surprising reality: Gains in agricultural productivity also appear to increase the risk of violence. Mueller said the key issue is not just scarcity, but change. The climate crisis and other shocks do not simply make some regions poorer. They also create new opportunities, changing the value of land and resources.

In some places, land that had been marginal becomes more productive and more valuable. And that attracts investors and produces competition for ownership and access.

So countries that appear to benefit overall may face new tensions. Sudan, for example, is projected to produce more food as the climate changes. But while some areas could become more productive, others may suffer losses, creating new winners and losers within the country and increasing the risk of conflict.

This looming instability, Mueller said, also applies to areas where the change in productivity hasn't even happened yet. "If we know that your land is going to become more productive, maybe I want to grab it from you today. That is exactly where negotiations break down and where we will have violence," he said.

Even in stable, wealthy regions, the climate crisis is creating future problems. It may seem trivial, but the change in grape-growing options in Europe is affecting local farmers. Major producers of sparkling wine have started to buy up land in mountainous regions.

"It is not productive yet, but they already know where future grape harvests will be," Mueller said. "Big agricultural companies are buying land. This is happening all over the world. Locals are displaced because large producers come in, land prices rise, and you start having fights about something that is still 20 or 30 years in the future."

How climate change is reshaping the world's wine map To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

One of the CADI team's most striking findings is that agricultural change is more likely to lead to conflict in non-democracies. When climate shocks, food insecurity, and competition over resources hit democracies, they tend to have institutions that force competing interests to negotiate rather than fight.

"Democracies may look annoying and cumbersome. Nothing moves as fast as people want. But this is a great thing because it makes people talk to each other," Mueller said. "There is a platform for negotiation. There are institutions that help people negotiate. That process of constantly finding solutions is at the heart of what prevents conflict."

South Asia as a warning sign

"We do not pay enough attention to the threats to the source of our livelihoods," said Abdullah Fahimi of the think tank German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP). "These threats can trigger major crises and displace millions and millions of people. The regions we should watch most closely are South Asia and the Sahel, where climate vulnerability and rapid population growth mean the number of people affected could rise dramatically."

As India counts its population, researchers warn that climate change could make it harder for parts of the country to produce enough food for a growing number of people Image: Diptendu Dutta/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Fahimi said South Asia stands out because it depends on both vulnerable water supplies and global food markets. Food prices have already risen significantly over the past decades. "South Asia, with a population of around 2 billion, is highly dependent on imports," he added. Those imports include wheat, maize, and palm oil from countries including Russia, Ukraine, Canada, and Malaysia.

At the same time, local agriculture is increasingly threatened by heat waves, floods, declining land productivity, and saltwater intrusion from rising sea levels.

As well as the immediate human toll, events such as the devastating floods that struck Nepal in August 2026 offer a glimpse of the long-term challenges that could become more common in the future. "The Himalayas and the Hindu Kush mountain ranges supply most of the water for agriculture and drinking water in the region," Fahimi said. "Because of climate change, the glaciers and snow are melting very fast."

In the short term, meltwater could increase water availability. But later in the century, he warned, the region could face "a huge humanitarian crisis that could affect around 2 billion people."

Farmland was covered in mud after severe flooding along Nepal’s Bhotekoshi River in late August Image: Ambir Tolang/NurPhoto/picture alliance

As food insecurity deepens, the social and political consequences can multiply. "When resource scarcities or the impacts of climate change force people to look for other livelihood opportunities, sometimes they end up being hired by terrorist groups," said Fahimi, who cited examples from Nigeria and Afghanistan.

In other cases, public frustration is directed at governments if they fail to mitigate the effects on people's livelihoods. Their legitimacy is questioned, and this can escalate into violent conflict.

That echoes Mueller's broader conclusion. Climate change, wars, and trade disruptions do not automatically lead to conflict. But climate adaptation cannot just be about growing different crops or using new technologies. People and societies also need to adapt to changes in who has access to land, water and jobs.

The key question is whether societies have institutions that can manage these changes. Where governments, courts, and local institutions can help communities negotiate new realities, shocks may be absorbed. Where those institutions are weak, the pressure on food systems may become a pressure on peace itself.

Edited by: Hannah Cleaver

Graphics: Olof Pock

World.title: Indonesia: Flights canceled as Anak Krakatau volcano erupts
World.content:
The spread of ash after the volcanic eruption of Anak Krakatau has impacted thousands of passengers, as flights were canceled at Jakarta's international airport.

Hundreds of flights were canceled at Jakarta's international airport after Indonesia's Anak Krakatau volcano erupted early Sunday morning, more than 150 kilometers (93 miles) away.

The volcano produced a fountain of lava and loud sounds heard up to 700 kilometers away, Indonesia's geological agency said in a statement.

The cloud of ash was detected up to a height of 6,000 meters (20,000 feet) on the Java side of the volcano and a plume of up to 15,000 meters on the ‌Sumatra side and some parts of Banten province in Java, the ‌meteorological ​agency BMKG posted on its website.

No incidents of casualties were reported, and no evacuation orders were issued.

Danger remains in Indonesia in the wake of volcano eruptions To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The closest township is more than 16 kilometers away, but the authorities warned residents and visitors to stay at least 3 kilometers from the volcano's active crater.

Two new eruptions were recorded on Sunday, the volcanology agency warned.

Indonesia cancels flights

The ash spread across parts of the capital Jakarta and Lampung province on the southern tip of Sumatra island, Indonesia's Center for Volcanology and Geological Hazard Mitigation said.

Authorities have suspended operations at six airports following eruptions from Mount Anak Krakatoa, the ministry said.

"The Husein Sastranegara Airport in Bandung showed indications of being affected. Consequently, we have declared... the airport closed to flights," Dudy Purwagandhi told a press conference Sunday, mentioning the latest airport to be shuttered.

Operations at Soekarno-Hatta International Airport, the country's largest and in the capital, Jakarta, were suspended earlier.

Soekarno-Hatta International Airport posted on ‌Instagram that it had ⁠suspended ⁠flight operations until 9:30 a.m. (0230 GMT) due to volcanic ash.

New volcano eruptions hit Indonesia To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Due to increased activity from the Mount Anak Krakatau eruption, Soekarno-Hatta International Airport has temporarily suspended flight operations from 5:30 a.m. to 9.30 a.m.," the airport said.

The disruption of flight operations has impacted more than 22,000 passengers, the transport ministry said in a statement, adding that 209 flights were affected, particularly to and from Singapore.

Anak Krakatau lies in the middle between Java and Sumatra in Indonesia's vast island chain, which sits on the Pacific "Ring of Fire," where earthquakes and volcanic eruptions are frequent.

Anak Krakatau means "Child of Krakatau." The volcano is the offspring of the famous Krakatau, whose monumental eruption in 1883 triggered a period of global cooling.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko
