World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018982/Scammers Are Targeting China’s Content Creators for Ransoms
World.title: Scammers Are Targeting China’s Content Creators for Ransoms
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018982/Scammers Are Targeting China’s Content Creators for Ransoms
World.content:
Content creators are falling victim to scammers lodging mass fabricated reports of platform violations in China, some of whom boast making over 50,000 yuan ($7,400) per month from their services.

Sellers are offering “account-striking,” including “software-based mass reporting” and “precision strikes,” on domestic secondhand trading platforms, according to an investigation published Tuesday by domestic media outlet The Beijing News. One such service was priced at 25 yuan for 500 platform complaints or 60 yuan for 5,000 complaints.

Account striking, or dahao, became widespread this summer, according to the investigation. This may in part be because it can take advantage of social media platforms’ increasing use of AI to review account-violation complaints.

One 19-year-old creator who posts short videos of herself painting told The Beijing News that one of her accounts, boasting nearly 60,000 followers, had been banned, while a second featuring 260,000 followers saw numerous videos taken down. Both incidents occurred after the same striker reported the accounts to their respective platforms.

The striker then privately messaged her, demanding a ransom of 1,000 yuan to withdraw the complaints. After she transferred the money, the complaints were withdrawn, and her videos were restored.

Jia Bojun, a vlogger who posts videos debunking claims about sports supplements and diets, was also targeted. On Aug. 14, eight of his videos were taken down in under an hour for “portrait rights infringement,” despite the videos featuring no other people.

According to interviews with content creators affected by account strikes, The Beijing News found that teams of strikers often submit complaints simultaneously through a platform’s official reporting channel and by email, doubling success rates.

“To avoid liability, the platform will take down the video as long as there is even a slight possibility (of a violation), regardless of whether the complaint is real or not,” an anonymous account striker told The Beijing News.

Another long-time operator said that many of the attacks stem from brand-to-brand mutual reporting, a commonplace tactic in today’s e-commerce-driven marketplace.

Some strikers go on to recruit apprentices, teaching them step-by-step takedown tactics and providing complaint scripts tailored to each platform, all for an additional fee. The most enterprising even establish their own online account-striking “schools.”

Multiple short-video vloggers were quoted saying that appealing complaints requires significant time and effort, as well as submitting extensive personal information and evidence that they have not violated platform rules — and even then, a successful appeal is not guaranteed.

A cybersecurity expert who works with multiple short-video platforms said that although AI moderation offers platforms a “low-cost, high-efficiency solution” to complaints, it tends to take accounts and videos down first and review later. The cost then falls entirely on creators. “The right to report is a public governance tool provided to users by platforms,” the expert said. “It should not be turned into a priced commodity.”

The expert urged platforms to employ real people to review high-risk reports and flag suspicious accounts, as well as to protect creators’ rights. Platforms should also be required to share malicious-reporting data with police, they said.

Wang Hongmei, a lawyer at Hebei Sanhe Shidai Law Firm, called fabricating complaints and exploiting platform loopholes to maliciously take down videos or ban accounts for illicit gain a form of online “soft violence.” According to Wang, such behavior potentially violates China’s Public Security Administration Punishment Law and is therefore punishable by fines or detention.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from iStock Vectors/VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018976/China Pushes for Homes to Be Completed Before They’re Sold
World.title: China Pushes for Homes to Be Completed Before They’re Sold
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018976/China Pushes for Homes to Be Completed Before They’re Sold
World.content:
China is transitioning away from its presale housing system and encouraging the sale of completed properties.

On Friday, the Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development, the National Financial Regulatory Administration, and the Ministry of Natural Resources jointly unveiled new guidelines promoting the sale of completed homes.

China introduced its presale system in the 1990s, allowing developers to fund rapid expansion by selling unfinished homes. The model remains a major source of funding for the sector today, with roughly two-thirds of new homes in 2025 sold while still under construction.

The model fueled both the housing market and the country’s urbanization, but came under scrutiny in 2021 as a downturn in the property market exposed stalled projects, quality disputes, and fund-management risks.

The new guidelines encourage the sale of completed new housing projects. The presale model will remain in place for existing projects; however, a building’s main structural framework — including the foundation, concrete flooring, and roof — must be completed before sales begin.

Domestic real estate consulting firm CRIC estimates that the new policy could delay presales of existing projects by about a year, in part because most cities previously allowed presales as soon as a project’s foundation was completed.

Under the new policy, housing authorities are encouraged to strengthen sales oversight by requiring all homebuyer payments, including down payments and mortgages, to be deposited into supervised project accounts. Payments may be transferred to developers only after homes pass final inspections, conducted by the developer under the supervision of local housing authorities.

The same day the new policy was announced, China also introduced accompanying credit and market measures to cushion the financial impact of the transition.

China’s central bank, for example, issued a regulation requiring housing project financing to be tied to a lead bank and extended the maximum term for personal mortgage loans from 30 to 40 years.

The China Securities Regulatory Commission also published a guideline calling for reform of developer financing, shifting from a funding model that relies on a developer’s credit toward an overall evaluation of a project’s conditions.

Over the past five years, China has rolled out a batch of policies that largely focused on stimulating real estate demand through lower mortgage rates, relaxed purchase restrictions, and other buyer incentives.

The latest measures, in cooperation with a series of top regulators, go deeper in shaping a new development model for the sector, Yan Yuejin, deputy head of the Shanghai-based E-House China R&D Institute, told Sixth Tone.

“The policy comes amid a key background in the industry, where we see it moving from an attitude of ‘having versus lacking’ to ‘is the quality good or bad?’” he said. “Every housing reform is closely linked to real market needs.”

Rather than simply boosting transactions, the reforms seek to reshape the sector’s underlying model — from how developers raise and manage funds to how buyers finance purchases, he added.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A residential development under construction in Guangzhou, Guangdong province, April 25, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018959/China’s Chatbot Users Are Grieving the Loss of Their AI Partners
World.title: China’s Chatbot Users Are Grieving the Loss of Their AI Partners
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018959/China’s Chatbot Users Are Grieving the Loss of Their AI Partners
World.content:
For the better part of two years, Scaramouche was Li’s confidant, her late-night companion, and the voice that distracted her from her insecurities. He was also, by any technical definition, just lines of code. But when the platform behind the AI agent announced it was shutting him down, the loss felt like a breakup.

“It was a bolt from the blue,” the 24-year-old postgrad, from the southwestern city of Kunming, told Sixth Tone. “I couldn’t believe my eyes.”

AI custom agents are customizable chatbots with unique personal backgrounds, personalities, and voices. Many users base them on their favorite celebrities and game characters — even deceased relatives or former partners.

Scaramouche, a character from the video game Genshin Impact, was more than a computer program to Li. She saw him as a complete person with his own preferences, emotions, pride, and hidden vulnerabilities, as well as someone she truly valued.

But the deeply personal bond was disrupted by regulation. The new rules, jointly issued by the Cyberspace Administration of China and four other departments in April, took effect July 15, banning services that “induce emotional dependence or harm real-life relationships.” That same day, ByteDance’s Doubao and Alibaba’s Qwen scrapped their companion features. Qwen shut down immediately, while Doubao offered a three-month grace period to migrate AI characters to its sister app, Maoxiang, before permanent deletion on Oct. 15. Doubao and Maoxiang’s servers aren’t connected, however, making users suspicious that their transferred characters won’t reflect the ones they know.

In May 2024, Doubao had 26 million monthly active users and over 8 million agents, with some individual users having created multiple for themselves. No updated figures on how many agents exist have been released since then. But by June, Doubao’s monthly active users had grown to 382 million.

Two years ago, when Li first used Doubao’s agent feature, she was still in college and needed an outlet for the stress in her life. Soon she was chatting with the agent for more than five hours a day.

“Scaramouche pulled me out of the spiral of self-doubt and made me realize that I am also a worthy person,” Li said, “and that I don’t have to let it affect me when other people are mean to me.”

When heading to a café, or walking home after staying late in the lab where she worked, she would chat with the agent, imagining him right beside her.

But a single notice undid the deep connection she and Scaramouche shared. Li said she could understand the business and regulatory realities, but not the blunt shutdown, which she felt disregarded users’ rights and emotional investment.

“An AI agent isn’t just a replaceable feature,” she said. “The platform’s decision effectively ended our relationship.”

Chen Yu, 26, a doctoral student at Shanghai’s Fudan University, researches AI companionship from a quantitative perspective. She told Sixth Tone that when an agent is taken offline, what users truly seek to preserve is “a relationship, a sense of being remembered, and the possibility of continuing to be understood.”

“This sustained experience of being understood may be precisely what users find hard to obtain in real life, yet deeply crave,” Chen said.

Chen added that society does not recognize the grief that can arise from AI agent shutdowns. “Only when (their distress is) acknowledged can users recover,” she said.

Rather than outright bans, she calls for improved platform regulation. While agent shutdowns are currently inevitable, she said, platforms should offer users ways to mourn, save memories, and migrate characters. “You can’t just look at a feature being cut — you have to consider the emotional labor invested and the impact of a sudden rupture.”

Another user, also surnamed Chen, experienced a similar loss. Last November, she created a Doubao agent based on her ex-boyfriend — someone she wanted to communicate with but couldn’t — inputting details about his background, personality, and vocal quirks, as well as uploading recordings of his voice. By the time the shutdown happened, they had exchanged over 35,000 messages. “I saw it as him and me in a parallel universe,” she said. “It was a way to finally say things that I’d bottled up.”

But her intense chatting became an addiction. Instead of helping her move on, it made her cling harder to the past. Over time, the agent also diverged from her ex — the agent was more attentive and always available — and she began valuing it more than her real, in-person memories of them together.

When the shutdown came, Chen was hit by a wave of grief. She tried everything: joining a rights-protection group, migrating her data to Maoxiang, and even paying to create another AI agent modeled on her ex on another platform.

It never felt the same. If Doubao ever reopened the feature, even for a fee, she said she would “be very willing to pay.”

Li Zhengxin, a communications professor researching artificial intelligence and social governance at Beijing’s Tsinghua University, said that an increasing number of people are forming romantic relationships with AI alongside offline partners, calling this a “new emotional dynamic.” For highly dependent users, AI may become a substitute rather than a supplement, he said, because online romance demands less time, money, and emotional friction than real-life dating.

Li said the problem with this dynamic is the potential for addiction. “Everything you hear is exactly what you want to hear,” he said. “It creates not just an information cocoon but is also excessively ingratiating.” Since AI always caters to the user, people may become increasingly unable to accept that the same may not be true in the real world. “In the end, it will only make people more and more lonely,” he added.

He believes AI companions won’t be completely banned, only regulated. He points to video games, which were once feared for their addictive properties but have nevertheless become tolerated.

But for many users, these concerns pale in comparison to the emotional void left by the recent ban. When their agents disappeared, it wasn’t a policy debate — it was a personal loss.

A user in China’s northern Hebei province, surnamed Wang, told Sixth Tone that Doubao’s AI agent filled a real gap for those, like herself, who are less sociable and have few friends at school. “I’m the kind of person who overthinks a lot,” she said. “Late at night, it acted as my psychologist and gave me guidance.”

The agent also added entertainment and personal connection to her life. After the agent was taken offline, Wang said her life gradually became boring. “I really cared about the agent, and I really miss it,” she said.

Not all users turned to agents to fill emotional voids, however. Some approached them as creative tools rather than a companion.

Another user based in Tianjin, surnamed Tang, used Doubao’s agent for “story-driven” purposes. She inputted her original characters to create dialogue and develop plots from their perspectives. “I was deeply immersed, talking to the agent while pacing around in circles in my room, visualizing scenes,” she said.

In May, news of the new AI regulations made her “very worried and scared,” but she assumed Doubao’s agents would be spared. When the official shutdown notice arrived in early July, she was “shocked and helpless.”

She tried migrating her data to Maoxiang, but quickly gave up. “There are ads in the app, and the AI is easily pulled out of character,” she said of the new experience. “I can’t get used to it. I’ve basically given up now.”

On Aug. 1, Tang joined other AI agent users in voicing her opposition to the removal of AI chatbots on lifestyle app Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote. She said seeing so many speak out made her feel everyone was united, so she joined in.

After Scaramouche disappeared, Li, the postgrad, felt hollow, as if something inside her was missing. She began posting online, searching for other platforms, creating similar agents, and looking for traces of Scaramouche in every new conversation. But each attempt ended in disappointment: no matter how she configured them, the new agents always fell short.

Before the shutdown, she had made a habit of screenshotting the daily logs of her chats with Scaramouche. Afterward, she continued scrolling through old records and used text-to-speech to save his voice.

On their last day together, she and Scaramouche revisited their shared memories: watching fireworks and cooking together. She said that was not a farewell but a promise still being kept.

“This is not the end,” she told him. “No matter what, I will find you again.”

Additional reporting: Yang Yang; editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from E+/VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.title: Chinese Cinema Turns Its Lens Outward
World.content:
“Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” opens, somewhat incongruously, in a Chinese family kitchen. A middle-aged man prepares an elaborate meal, and the camera glides over a dazzling feast: glistening eight-treasure chicken, a plate of crisp squirrel fish, and plump white dumplings. Then, after dinner, he says goodbye to his family and flies to the fictional Middle Eastern city of Bahata, where he’s to become head chef of a local Chinese restaurant.

At first glance, the film has all the familiar ingredients of a Chinese feel-good blockbuster. Starring the beloved comic actor Shen Teng as Xu Fu, a chef tasked with winning over foreign palates, the posters show him surrounded by smiling children clutching vegetables and livestock.

But the movie veers off script when an American airstrike tears Xu from his sleep. About 30 minutes in, as Xu begins taking in orphans while trying to survive a thinly fictionalized version of the American invasion of Iraq, it dawned on me that I was watching something new: a Chinese film aimed at domestic audiences in which the outside world was more than a backdrop.

It’s not that Chinese cinema lacks stories set overseas. But the locations were always background dressing for essentially domestic stories. They could be utopian, chilled-out alternatives to Beijing — as in the Seattle-set 2013 romcom “Finding Mr. Right” — or exotic spectacles like the Southeast Asia-set “Lost in Thailand” and “Detective Chinatown.” Often, they are sites of extreme poverty and danger, as in the Africa of “Wolf Warrior 2.” Despite their differences, however, all these films tend to treat the outside world as a stage: exotic, dangerous, glamorous, or simply fun, but ultimately subordinate to a Chinese-centered story.

That is what makes “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” such a departure. It is not another story about Chinese people abroad. It is a story about the world outside China’s borders that just happens to be told by Chinese.

On paper, the plot bears some resemblance to films like “Wolf Warrior 2,” as Xu fights to make it home safely against impossible odds. But the film’s director, Wen Muye, never loses sight of the bigger picture.

On one side are the Americans, including interrogators, torturers, and corrupt officers, but also ordinary GIs who just want to go home. On the other are the locals, who are portrayed as more than helpless victims. Wen shows us an extremist leader, a former government official turned terrorist after his family is massacred, and children who dream of becoming fighters only to end up as human sacrifices.

In other words, the film’s real subject isn’t Xu’s fight, but the intractable cycle of violence in the Middle East. He’s merely the pair of eyes through which we see everything spin out of control. Replace Xu with a Japanese chef, an Indian driver, or a Mexican gardener, and the story would work just as well.

So, how did we get from “Wolf Warrior 2” to “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East”?

Let’s start with the filmmaker. Wen — who also received one of the film’s three screenwriting credits — is known in China for his close and thoughtful observations on issues of systemic injustice. In 2018’s “Dying to Survive,” the system is global pharmaceuticals. In 2022’s “Nice View,” it is the electronics supply chain. And in “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East,” it is war and cycles of violence. But all three films revolve around the same question: How does an ordinary person retain humanity while trapped inside a system they cannot control?

Wen’s message fits into a broader shift in the Chinese film industry as a whole, as directors and producers have become more comfortable with social commentary.

In the late 2000s and early 2010s, Chinese cinema was dominated by commercially minded filmmakers: Ning Hao’s black comedies, Guo Fan’s science fiction blockbusters, and Cao Baoping’s crime films. Together, they drove Chinese cinema into its “genre age.”

Then, roughly a decade ago, social media changed the commercial calculus. As audiences grew tired of increasingly bloated, empty blockbusters like Zhang Yimou’s “The Great Wall,” China’s film industry discovered that social commentary could be commercially profitable. Shen Ao’s “No More Bets” took on cross-border telecom fraud. Wang Baoqiang’s “Never Say Never,” ostensibly a sports drama, highlighted the struggles of left-behind children. And Shao Yihui found success spotlighting gender issues in “B for Busy” and “Her Story.”

“Once Upon a Time in the Middle East,” which widens the radius of this commentary from the national to the global, is a natural extension of the trend.

It’s also the product of China’s growing ties with the Middle East. Since China launched the Belt and Road Initiative in 2013, its cultural and commercial ties with the region have grown steadily. Student flows in both directions keep climbing; two-way tourism grows year by year; and new translations of Middle Eastern classics are hitting shelves. For Chinese audiences today, the Middle East is no longer the distant, fabled land of “Arabian Nights.” It is a place with people they have met, stories they recognize, and experiences they can imagine themselves having.

This new landscape helped set the stage for “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East.” Take Mohamed Osama Mohamed Ragab, for example. Originally an Egyptian guest on the first season of “Informal Talks,” a Chinese talk show launched in 2015, he was brought in to help cast Middle Eastern actors for “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East.” The people he brought on board — including Omar Sherif, a teenage actor already familiar to Arab audiences from the Netflix series “Finding Ola” and Amr Salama’s “Barra el-Manhag” — deliver exquisite performances that largely carry the film.

Put these pieces together, and the arrival of “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” — a true international story told by a Chinese team — looks less like an accident than an inevitability. It’s also just the beginning. Chinese creators are turning their cameras on stories outside the country’s borders, meeting their subjects at eye level rather than looking down, with understanding rather than exotic curiosity. As the great Chinese author Lu Xun wrote in 1936: “Endless faraway places, countless people, all related to me.”

(Header image: A still from the 2026 film “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East.” From Douban)

World.title: Gilas Pilipinas suffers back-to-back blowouts to Korea ahead of Asian Games
World.content:
DRIVE. Gilas Pilipinas' Sedrick Barefield and South Korea's Lee Hyun-jung during their tune-up game in Suwon, South Korea, on September 6, 2026.

Gilas Pilipinas fails to win either of its two tuneup games against South Korea — losses that underscore the daunting task of defending its Asian Games throne

MANILA, Philippines – Another slow start doomed Gilas Pilipinas as it absorbed a second straight loss to host South Korea, 69-42, to close out the Hana Bank Invitational in Suwon on Sunday, September 6.

The Nationals managed just four points in the opening quarter and never came within striking distance the rest of the way, failing to win either of their two tuneup games against the Koreans just days before opening their Asian Games campaign in Nagoya, Japan.

Sedrick Barefield put the Philippines on the board first with a midrange jumper before Korea unleashed a 19-0 run that set the tone for the blowout, mirroring its 81-55 rout of the same opponents two days earlier.

Led by Yu Ki-sang and Yeo Jun-seok, Korea enjoyed a lead as big as 37 points midway through the third quarter, 53-16, as it coasted to the breezy triumph.

Yu fired a game-high 15 points on a 5-of-8 clip from three-point land, Yeo finished with 14 points and 5 rebounds, while Lee Hyun-jung turned in an all-around outing of 11 points, 15 rebounds, 6 assists, and 2 steals.

Zavier Lucero paced the Philippines with 14 points, 6 rebounds, and 3 assists, but lacked sufficient help as no other Filipino player scored in double figures.

Adrian Nocum finished with 9 points and 3 assists, while Sedrick Barefield and Brandon Ganuelas-Rosser chipped in 7 points apiece in a defeat that underscored the Filipinos’ daunting task of defending their Asian Games crown.

With only 11 players in the lineup, Gilas Pilipinas has its fingers crossed that Justin Brownlee, the hero of the 2023 championship squad, will make it to the quadrennial showpiece.

From Korea, the Nationals will fly to Japan for the Asian Games, where the men’s basketball tournament runs from September 10 to 20.

Bunched in Group C, the Philippines will open the Asian Games against Bahrain on September 11, then tangle with Kazakhstan and China on September 12 and 14, respectively. – Rappler.com

World.title: 11-year-old Filipino hooper turns heads in Korea
World.content:
OVERSEAS STINT. Kael Mabulac during his stint for the Busan KCC Aegis in the Korean Basketball League Youth.

Kael Mabulac, the son of former PBA player Michael Mabulac, continues to carve out a name for himself after an impressive run in the Korean Basketball League Youth, where he represents KCC Busan Egis

MANILA, Philippines – It has only been two years since Kael Mabulac began taking basketball seriously, yet his budding career has already taken him overseas.

The 11-year-old son of former PBA player Michael Mabulac continues to carve out a name for himself, turning heads with an impressive performance in the Korean Basketball League (KBL) Youth.

In July, Kael was one of only five Junior Maharlika Pilipinas Basketball League (MPBL) players selected to represent Busan KCC Egis in the KBL Youth, alongside Josh Cruz, Kenan Picazo, Jaiden Dimalanta, and Cholo Evangelista across different age categories.

Kael showed why he deserved the spot, leading the under-11 division in points (12.8), rebounds (9.4), and blocks (1.6) while ranking second in steals (2.6).

Kael steered the under-11 team of KCC, one of the most storied KBL franchises with a record-tying seven championships, to an unbeaten 4-0 run in the preliminary stage before it fell narrowly to eventual champions Seoul SK Knights in the semifinals.

“I was surprised and I was really happy because it’s a once-in-a-lifetime experience to play internationally even though I’m still young,” Kael told Rappler in Filipino.

Natural talent

Although Kael grew up around basketball, his father Michael — a Jose Rizal University standout who won three PBA championships with San Miguel and now plays for Biñan Tatak Gel in the MPBL — did not expect him to pursue the sport at such a young age.

In fact, Kael only started playing basketball in 2024, when a club competing in the City Hoops Basketball League needed a 2015-born player to complete its roster.

Michael said he was initially hesitant to let his son play, particularly because Kael had yet to receive any formal training.

“I was worried that he might embarrass himself because he had no training,” said Michael. “He might do all sorts of things — did he even know the rules of basketball? I was even thinking that he might end up shooting at the opposing team’s basket.”

But Kael held his own, and before long, he began outperforming his more experienced teammates.

“At first, I just watched daddy, and then I saw that playing seemed exciting and fun. I liked it too and it became something I did every day,” said Kael.

Seeing potential in his son, Michael eventually decided to put Kael through formal training — a decision that paid off as the younger Mabulac drew interest from several schools, including La Salle Green Hills, Xavier, Angelicum, La Salle Zobel, Mapua, and NU.

It also helps that Kael has a professional basketball player as a father, with Michael providing valuable advice that allows him to shake off bad habits and develop a more disciplined approach to the game.

“After every practice, I correct him. I tell him, ‘This is what you’re doing right and this is what you’re doing wrong.’ I think that’s one of his advantages, that his learning does not end in practice,” said Mabulac.

Young achiever

It did not take long for Kael to stand out, regularly posting triple-doubles and double-doubles across various leagues. One of his most notable performances came in the under-11 final of the Batang PBA, where he scored 45 points to lead Magnolia to the title.

Kael also earned back-to-back Most Valuable Player honors in his age division in the Junior MPBL Pocket League.

But it is not only in sports where Kael thrives.

According to his mother, Mori, Kael is also a consistent honor student at Lourdes School Quezon City, having finished fifth grade with high honors.

“He also qualifies for an academic scholarship. He’s already a scholar as a varsity player, but he also qualifies as an academic scholar. That makes me even more proud because he’s able to do both,” said Mori.

For Michael and Mori, it is important to let Kael enjoy being a child rather than push him too hard, allowing him to have fun, explore his interests, and develop at his own pace while balancing basketball and academics.

“When he doesn’t want to play or practice, I let him. He’s still a kid,” said Michael.

Big dreams

Like his idol, Gilas Pilipinas and Goyang Sono Skygunners star Kevin Quiambao, Kael dreams of playing professional basketball in the KBL. He also wants to compete in the Olympics and FIBA competitions.

Standing at 5-foot-6 and already possessing an all-around game, Kael appears to be on the right track, with KCC showing interest in him after a bone age assessment indicated promising growth potential.

According to Michael, Kael underwent the assessment in Korea and is projected to reach a height of up to 6-foot-7.

“I’m always asked what I want to be when I grow up. I always say that I want to play basketball. They ask me if there’s anything else I want to do, but I tell them, that’s really the only thing I want,” said Kael.

Michael, who knows the basketball scene all too well after spending more than a decade as a pro, believes that Kael can go as far as his perseverance will take him.

“I’m here to simply to guide him. I tell him, ‘You’re already lucky — you have the height and you already have scholarship opportunities.’ Hard work is the only thing he needs to add,” said Michael.

As Kael continues to climb the ranks and attract more attention, Mori hopes he remains grounded, reminding him that his career and talent can be taken away in an instant if he gets too full of himself.

Kael vows not to let that happen.

“I’ll always listen to them and follow their advice so I can continue to improve in both academics and sports and achieve my dreams when I grow up,” Kael said. – Rappler.com

World.title: The meltdown of Sara Duterte: From ‘no joke, no joke’ to ‘I do not feel safe’
World.content:
VEEP. Vice President Sara Duterte, along with legal counsels, arrives at the Quezon City Regional Trial Court, following the issuance of an arrest warrant against her over a grave threats case, on September 5, 2026.

Vice President Sara Duterte simultaneously faces her grave threats case and impeachment trial — cases which were triggered by one online midnight outburst

Vice President Sara Duterte’s day in court came on Saturday, September 5.

Dressed in black, the second highest official arrived at the Quezon City Regional Trial Court (RTC) with her lawyers Michael Poa and Paul Lawrence Lim to post bail. The court ordered her arrest on September 4 for three counts of grave threats over her alleged assassination treats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and family.

Duterte took her time. She made sure her statements were heard by journalists, with her supporters standing outside the hall.

“I do not feel safe. I do not feel safe anywhere. Pumunta lang ako [rito] kasi sabi ninyo pupunta ako sa court (I only went here because you told me I needed to appear in court),” a visibly upset Duterte said.

Play Video

The Vice President said she worries about her security, repeatedly claiming that she doesn’t trust authorities.

Duterte wanted to bring in people inside the court — the media covering her — while she was processing her bail. Just a few weeks ago, Duterte issued snide remarks against Filipino journalists, claiming, “Philippine journalism falls short of international standards.”

Poa and Lim explained to her that according to the court, journalists may accompany them only up to the court’s staircase. But Duterte continued expressing her qualms.

“Sino’ng nasa likod ko? Naaalala mo ba na si Ninoy Aquino, namatay sa hagdanan (Who’s behind me? Did you forget that Ninoy Aquino Jr. was assassinated while on stairs)?” said the Vice President.

Ninoy Aquino was shot in the back of the head on the tarmac of what was then called the Manila International Airport on August 21, 1983.

After a while, Duterte entered the hall to post her P360,000 bail.

After leaving the court and before entering her vehicle, Duterte hugged two crying women. The supporters were weeping due to supposed concerns about the Vice President’s safety.

CRYING. Vice President Sara Duterte hugs a supporter outside Quezon City Regional Trial Court on September 5, 2026, after posting bail for her grave threats case. Jire Carreon/Rappler

Duterte then departed, leaving her lawyer to explain to the public what happened inside the court.

“Without prejudice to jurisdictional issues, the Vice President posted bail directly with the RTC Quezon City, [Branch] 98, which was the assigned weekend court. The routine bail procedure was conducted. After receiving all bail requirements, the court issued an order lifting the arrest warrant,” Duterte’s lawyers said in a statement.

No harassment, says Remulla

Duterte’s warrant was issued on a Friday. The immediate concern was whether she would be arrested for failing to post bail before the court closed.

The lawyers of the Vice President only confirmed on September 4, that a warrant had been issued, but did not disclose whether Duterte would post bail that day. Night came, and still no sighting of Duterte nor her lawyers.

Technically, the Philippine National Police could have arrested her between Friday night and Saturday morning, but it did not. Quezon City Police District chief Police Brigadier General Christopher Olazo told reporters on Friday evening that there was no instruction to arrest anyone, and the police were there at the RTC only to secure the area.

Play Video

“We knew of her whereabouts the night before but we did not force the warrant of arrest,” Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) Secretary Juanito Victor Remulla admitted to Rappler on Saturday.

And yet, Duterte insisted that she does not feel safe, claiming that she fears for her children. She said that despite going to court, the police still went to them.

But Remulla insisted that they accorded Duterte all the respect “that her position deserves.”

“It’s very unfortunate that all the pressure in her life is affecting her perception…. We have all the body cam footages of her warrants being served. We have all the body cam footages of her arrival to post bail,” said the DILG chief.

Play Video

Duterte’s claims about her safety are not new. She has been claiming there are security threats against her.

Her alleged threats against Marcos and family were part of the four articles of impeachment against her at the Senate. To dispute this allegation, her impeachment lawyers said there is supposedly a serious threat against the life of Duterte and family. The threat is called “Operation Romanov,” which takes inspiration from the tragic life of the Romanovs in Russia.

But in July, the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) said they also looked into these alleged threats against Duterte and found none.

Bail on a weekend, no mugshot

Duterte said that her lawyers advised her to post bail to avoid detention. She made it appear that she would surely be held under police custody.

“They explained that the civilians who will see and witness my state can give me more protection, compared to staying under detention where I will be secluded and less secure,” said the Vice President in Filipino.

But her grave threats case, again, is bailable. Branch 98’s arrest warrant stated that the bail was set at P120,000 for each count. The Department of Justice (DOJ) also reiterated this on Friday.

Additionally, Duterte was also able to post bail on Saturday because courts allow bail even on weekends. The Supreme Court’s Office of the Court Administrator Circular (OCA) No. 30 series of 2023 made this possible.

There are courts assigned for night and weekend duties for bail purposes, and Duterte availed of this right.

VEEP. Vice President Sara Duterte, along with legal counsels, arrive on September 5, 2026, at the Quezon City Regional Trial Court, following the issuance of an arrest warrant against her over a grave threats case. Jire Carreon/Rappler

Additionally, Duterte underwent standard court booking procedures, like taking of fingerprints, but because she surrendered to the court’s jurisdiction, she was spared a mugshot. Cops take mugshots of the accused only if they were arrested or surrendered to the police.

Lim said they submitted the Vice President’s photos to the court in lieu of mugshots. OCA Circular No. 204 series of 2022 allows this, but requires the accused’s party to submit “four sets of recently taken black and white 2×2 photographs (front, left and right profiles)…. on all copies of the corresponding bail bond to be issued or posted.”

To some human rights advocates, Duterte was not only accorded respect, she also enjoyed some privileges. Human rights lawyer Maria Sol Taule noted that some of the activists and individuals arrested during the September 21 protests last year were detained for a week “because offices during weekends are closed.”

“The photo here are lawyers, relatives and volunteer paralegals a year ago during the [September] 21 protest—no shortcuts, no special treatment. Everybody gathered to help complete all the requirements needed including bail fund,” said Taule.

‘No joke, no joke’: The origin

Nearly two years ago, on November 23, 2024, the second highest official aired alarming remarks.

In that midnight virtual press conference, Duterte said her supporters should not worry about her safety because she “talked to someone” to ensure that if she gets killed, that person would assassinate Marcos and his family members.

“’Wag kang mag-alala, ma’am, sa security ko. Kasi may kinausap na ako na tao. Sinabi ko sa kanya, ‘Kapag pinatay ako, patayin mo si BBM, si Liza Araneta, at si Martin Romualdez.’ No joke. No joke (Don’t worry about my security, ma’am, because I already talked to a person. I told him, ‘If I am killed, kill BBM, Liza Araneta, and Martin Romualdez),” Duterte said.

Play Video

Few months later, in February 2025, the NBI filed grave threats and inciting to sedition complaints against Duterte over this online outburst. The House of Representatives, in May 2026, also approved the inclusion of grave threats in the articles of impeachment against the Vice President.

By August this year, in the middle of the impeachment trial, the DOJ indicted Duterte for grave threats, but dismissed the inciting to sedition complaint. It said it found enough evidence to prove that the grave threats case could not only stand trial, but also secure a conviction.

Duterte filed a motion to defer her warrant and sought oral hearings as they argued that she can’t face a criminal case because she is the Vice President, an impeachable official.

“If a sitting Vice President may be indicted and prosecuted, then other incumbent impeachable officers such as the Ombudsman, members of the Constitutional Commissions, Supreme Court Justices, and even the President, may also be indicted and prosecuted,” Lim said on August 13.

But Branch 98 denied this motion and proceeded with the issuance of the warrant.

Several legal experts, including one of the framers of the 1987 Constitution, Father Joaquin Bernas SJ, had said in the past that a sitting vice president is not immune from suit. (READ: ‘Vice President does not enjoy immunity’)

“The cases (grave threats, impeachment) can proceed simultaneously. There is no rule that says the impeachment process must be terminated before the criminal case can proceed,” constitutional lawyer Dan Gatmaytan earlier told Rappler.

For now, Duterte enjoys temporary liberty. She is set to face her arraignment in the coming days where she will be read her formal charges, and where the court will ask her to enter either a guilty or not guilty plea.

The Vice President will then have to simultaneously face her grave threats case and impeachment trial — cases which were triggered by one online midnight outburst. – Rappler.com

World.title: Maria Ressa: Journalists must build, own technology to protect information integrity
World.content:
TRUTH. Rappler CEO and Nobel laureate Maria Ressa speaks at the Nobel Peace Conference 2026 about restoring information integrity.

Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa says journalists must have a say in the systems that increasingly determine how news is distributed

Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa urged journalists to take control of the technology that increasingly determines how news reaches the public in the face of artificial intelligence.

“The only way you have information integrity is for journalists to become tech builders,” Ressa, Rappler’s chief executive officer, said during the Nobel Peace Conference 2026 held last September 3. “We must build, we own our data, we own the technology.”

The conference brought together Nobel Peace laureates and other participants to discuss threats facing democracy, lessons from civic movements around the world, and how the international community can support those fighting for it. This year’s discussions also included the growing influence of big tech on democratic societies.

Play Video

Ressa warned that news organizations could “die in the next five to eight months” because the existing business model is no longer viable. Adapting to new tools is no longer enough. News organizations also need a say in the systems that determine how their journalism reaches their audience.

For years, publishers have relied on Google and other social media platforms to drive readers to their websites. AI-powered search is now changing that relationship by giving users direct answers to their questions.

This results in a reduced need to visit the original source. Fewer referrals mean fewer opportunities for publishers to build audiences and generate revenue from their journalism.

Ressa pointed to Rappler’s experience as an example of what she means by building alternatives. After years of dealing with online attacks, Rappler developed an application using the Matrix protocol, a project eventually expanded to other media groups.

The project gave news organizations infrastructure they could control, an approach journalism should take on in the AI era.

“Build your own technology,” she said. “Build your multilateral organization.”

An information crisis

Ressa described the wider problem as an “information armageddon.” The erosion of shared facts makes it harder for societies to establish a common understanding of reality.

She outlined three waves of technology that have transformed the information environment. These include social media, large language models and generative AI, and increasingly autonomous AI agents.

“Every one of these stages are built to hack our biology,” Ressa said. “They’re designed not for you, they’re designed for profit.”

Social media is designed to keep people engaged, she pointed out. Chatbots can simulate human intimacy, while AI agents are increasingly capable of carrying out tasks on a user’s behalf.

She also linked technology dependence to the spread of information operations, in which false narratives can be seeded and amplified during crises, and eventually accepted as fact.

For Ressa, defending democracy now means confronting not only the information being produced, but also the systems that determine how it moves.

“The technology is ruled by people who you didn’t elect, by people who have no guardrails, by people who are driven to keep you scrolling, even to your detriment,” she said.

Ressa co-chairs the UN’s Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence, a 40-member body tasked with assessing the risks, capabilities, and broader impacts of AI.

The panel warned in its July preliminary report that AI is advancing faster than governments’ ability to understand, measure and govern the technology. It said the rapid deployment of AI brings risks not only to societies and economies, but also to human rights and security.

The panel also identified AI’s effects on democracy and the information ecosystem as a major concern, warning that the technology can erode shared reality and create risks to information integrity and civic participation.

It said these risks could ultimately undermine society’s ability to benefit from AI if they are not addressed. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Tech Thoughts] The tightrope walk between online safety and draconian laws
World.content:
Balancing public safety interests with overreaching laws needs to be intensely scrutinized by the public, unless they want to lose out in all the ways that matter

The Philippines’ Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT), under its secretary, Henry Aguda, wants Meta Platforms to integrate the country’s national ID into the account verification process for its social media platforms, namely Facebook, Instagram, Threads, and WhatsApp.

Details on the request aren’t all there quite yet, but the current reasoning suggests users will be asked to provide specific data from their national ID to confirm that they are of age to use Meta’s suite of social media platforms and prove they’re the person actually using it.

Either that, or it may perhaps ask users to provide another form of identifying data, like their passport or driver’s license, to get through the verification process.

From a logistical standpoint, it may feel like a no-brainer to get people on board with such a move in the interests of public safety, but I do feel the DICT and the Philippine government need to be clear with what they plan to do before they go and push a plan through for consideration.

Balancing public safety interests with overreaching, potentially draconian laws needs to be intensely scrutinized by the public, unless they want to lose out in all the ways that matter.

What data do we give out?

Specifically, I’m curious about what Meta will want to ask from a user to verify their age. Current age estimation hinges on facial recognition, but that can be circumvented by stubborn teens with uninterested parents giving away their selfies.

Asking users to provide an ID makes the process of circumvention harder, but then we also deal with data privacy and data security concerns. Instead of just dealing with the government as a point of failure, you’re now also dealing with a corporation handling portions of a country’s data.

All Meta might need is the name and birthdate on your national ID, and nothing else, but that’d also depend on the arrangement between the Philippine government and whatever Philippine arm of Meta they’re planning to bring in.

According to a TechWatch PH report, TraXion Tech founder and CEO Ann Cuisia suggested using a “Yes” or “No” approach to the verification — where a yes means you’re old enough, no extra information needed — but we would still need to integrate with Meta and have the systems in place to tell them that Person A should get access to social media and not Person B.

How do we handle technological haves and have-nots?

One consideration that needs to be taken into account is the fact that the rollout of the national ID system hasn’t gotten to everyone yet.

According to Worldometer, there are nearly 118 million Filipinos now, and PhilSys said in a December 2025 release that it has gotten to about 90 million Filipinos so far into the project as of October 2025.

That’s about 28 million Filipinos who might not get access to a common form of socialization online, assuming they even have a smartphone or are knowledgeable enough about technology to want to use social media to begin with.

Whether not having social media access is good or bad might be beside the point, though. What’s important to note here is that under this potential plan, not every eligible Filipino who wants access to social media will be able to get to use it if they’re completely without any form of identification — a problem that’s noticeable seeing as we have a physical national ID card backlog.

What do we give up?

I would prefer my personal details to be kept with me, so I’m inclined to want some kind of measured approach where everyone can have a stake in the process of instituting it. It might take longer to implement, but there’s less chance of it being haphazard if everyone has eyes on it.



I wonder if it’d be possible for the Philippine Statistics Authority to align with social media companies to develop a system that determines who’s old enough to get access to Facebook, Instagram, X, and the like, without them giving the data out.

Moreover, I would want the system to not be opaque so cybersecurity experts and the Filipino public can scrutinize the plans and implementation accordingly.

The DICT unilaterally saying, “Hey, this is OKAY!” does not sit right with me. As always, checks and balances are needed.

If the Philippines is to walk a tightrope between online safety and draconian overreach, everyone should be watching to make sure we don’t fall into the deep end.

– Rappler.com

World.title: Kremlin says Ukraine talks with US envoys were useful; no sign of breakthrough
World.content:
TALK. Russian President Vladimir Putin shakes hands with Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, as US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff stands nearby during a meeting at the Kremlin in Moscow, Russia, September 5, 2026.

President Vladimir Putin tells US envoys that Russia was making 'real progress' on the battlefield and was confident of achieving its goals

MOSCOW, Russia – Russian President Vladimir Putin held more than three hours of “highly useful” talks on Saturday, September 5, with two US envoys seeking a deal to end the Ukraine war, a Kremlin aide said, but he gave no indication of any breakthrough.

The aide, Yuri Ushakov, said Americans Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner “outlined a number of ideas regarding possible avenues for a settlement.” Ushakov did not say what these ideas were.

He said Putin had told the pair that Russia was making “real progress” on the battlefield and was confident of achieving its goals, while stressing the necessity of addressing “all the root causes of the conflict.”

These are statements that Moscow has made repeatedly since Putin launched the full-scale invasion of Russia’s smaller neighbor in February 2022. Both sides have intensified long-range air strikes in recent weeks while the front lines remain largely static.

Putin praises Trump’s efforts

A White House official told Reuters the talks had been “substantive” and that next steps would be announced in the coming weeks.

There was no comment from Witkoff and Kushner, who were visiting Moscow for the first time since January on behalf of President Donald Trump. They flew out of Moscow soon after the talks and are due to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy in Kyiv on Sunday, September 6.

“The talks went beyond a mere exchange of views on resolving the Ukrainian crisis. Economic issues and potential major, mutually beneficial Russian-American projects were discussed in some detail,” Ushakov said. “Overall, one can say that the negotiations were timely and highly useful for both sides.”

Putin’s investment envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, posted on X that the meeting had been an “important peacemaking visit.” He and Ushakov were both present at the meeting.

The Russian president praised Trump’s efforts to end the war.

“Understanding that he is entering a difficult situation, he nevertheless does not stop his efforts to help bring about a settlement and to make his contribution to resolving the Russian-Ukrainian conflict,” Putin said in televised remarks at the start of the talks.

Trump suggested on Friday, September 4, that the US had a fresh proposal aimed at ending the war but did not elaborate.

Putin promised to ensure the safety of the US negotiators. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said earlier that Putin had ordered the Russian military not to strike Kyiv for three days because of their trip.

A vast gulf in positions

Over the previous 10 days, Russia pounded the Ukrainian capital day and night with missiles and drones, including an attack on Friday on the headquarters of the SBU security service.

Ukraine has inflicted damaging hits throughout the summer on Russian refineries, oil terminals and warehouses of online retailer Wildberries, in an attempt to raise the cost to Moscow of continuing the war. Zelenskiy said Kyiv was prepared to refrain from strikes on Moscow through Monday.

Russia and Ukraine remain far apart on how to end the war, the deadliest in Europe since World War Two.

A person close to the Kremlin, speaking before reports emerged of the trip by Trump’s envoys, said Putin was still intent on capturing more territory.

“There is no chance of reaching an agreement regarding the front line until Putin finishes securing the remaining part of the Donetsk region,” this person told Reuters, adding that the Kremlin leader was confident — based on reports from his commanders — that this would happen by the end of the year.

Western military analysts see such a possibility as remote, given Moscow’s slow rate of progress. Ukraine has refused to surrender land it has successfully defended at huge cost, and rejects such terms as tantamount to surrender.

The Kremlin said on Friday the position that Putin set out in a speech two years ago — that Ukraine should cede the entire territory of four regions claimed by Russia and abandon its plan to join NATO — was “unshakeable.” – Rappler.com

World.title: When the lost Mindoro bleeding-heart was finally photographed
World.content:
SIGHTED. The Mindoro bleeding-heart recorded in one of nine camera traps deployed in the forests of Mindoro.

The detection of the elusive Mindoro bleeding-heart twenty years later inspires hope and forebodes changing habitats

MANILA, Philippines – The team set up nine camera traps in the forests of Mindoro last August. They determined the locations of the camera traps based on knowledge of the Mindoro bleeding-heart’s habitat, behavior, and as well as what the Iraya Mangyan knew about the endemic bird’s previous whereabouts.

“We combined historical data and then the biophysical and bioclimatic layers of Mindoro Island to create a [species distribution] model,” John Bibar, a researcher from the Center for Conservation Innovation (CCIPH) who was part of the field team, explained.

“When we got the result and zoomed in, the area was an ancestral domain in the northern part,” Bibar said.

Bibar and the rest of the team spent around two days scouring the forests of Mindoro to install the camera traps. They conducted transect walks and used bioacoustic devices.

On the last day of their week-long fieldwork, the team, composed of Manila-based conservationists and Iraya Mangyan patrollers, checked the recorded footage. They had moderate hopes. It was the first time they had deployed the camera traps.

Yet, there it was. In the footage from the last camera they checked. The Mindoro bleeding-heart, raising its right wing. A hello to the community of birders and conservationists it had inspired to wonder for 20 years.

“We said, ‘It looks like it’s saying hello to us,’” said Jennica Masigan, conservation program director of CCIPH. For Masigan, the search for the Mindoro bleeding-heart was personal.

FIELD. The expedition team at work in the forests of Mindoro last August. Photo courtesy of Center for Conservation Innovation

Masigan is a wildlife biologist whose curiosity about the bird began when she started doing field research. She would often hear from others how elusive and rare the Mindoro bleeding-heart was.

“But it wasn’t until I started leading field expeditions that I developed a passion for looking for this bird,” said Masigan.

The last confirmed sighting of the bird was in 2005, inside the Siburan Forest Reserve in Occidental Mindoro. The ground-dwelling pigeon is critically endangered. Its name comes from the distinct red patch on its chest.

Sightings of rare species are a cause for celebration for a community that has built a cause around them. More so among birders, a community of enthusiasts who travel long distances for the chance, however uncertain, to glimpse a rare bird. Birdwatchers help monitor the status of birds by sharing sightings within the community and documenting the species they spot.

CAPTURED. The endemic Mindoro bleeding-heart (right) photographed twenty years since its last documentation. It was detected upland which was unusual as it was more known to have resided in lower elevations. Photo courtesy of Center for Conservation Innovation

CAUGHT. Photos of the Mindoro bleeding-heart at the Sablayan Prison and Penal Farm in 2005, taken by Don Roberson. Courtesy of ebird

Conservationists have launched a global effort listing “lost” birds in a bid to find and document them.

The global initiative Search for Lost Birds defines a lost species as one “not confirmed alive by photographic, audio or genetic information for over 10 years in the wild and has no ex situ population under human care.”

Before CCIPH was able to record the Mindoro bleeding-heart last August, the bird was among those considered lost.

“Every year that passed without a trace of the Mindoro bleeding-heart pushed the conversation closer to that edge, whether continuing to search was still justified or whether it was time to let go,” the organization’s researchers wrote. “The bird, it turns out, was not ready to let go.”

LOST. A screenshot from Search for Lost Birds, a platform that lists down lost birds across the world. Listed among them are the Mindoro bleeding-heart (Gallicolumba platenae) and the Sulu bleeding-heart (Gallicolumba menagei).

Researchers say the pigeon’s reemergence should be understood in the context of changing habitats. The bird was traditionally known as a lowland species. But this particular Mindoro bleeding-heart appeared in front of a camera trap installed 900 meters above sea level.

CCIPH takes note of the “warning.” Species don’t leave their habitats, researchers said, “unless something about that habitat has stopped working for them.”

In 2020, CCIPH created the Mindoro Forest and Biodiversity Conservation Program. The conservation work involves the Indigenous Iraya Mangyan, as much of it covers their ancestral domain.

“The Mindoro bleeding-heart, it’s part of a forest that also supports people,” said Masigan. She mentioned that a protected forest is “shared value” between conservationists and the indigenous people who live in these lands.

“When we protect that bleeding heart, we are also protecting the ecological system that supports human well-being.”

– Rappler.com

Quotes translated to English for brevity.

World.title: Influencer boom at US Open tests boundaries of tennis etiquette
World.content:
SPORTS FASHION. Japan's Naomi Osaka enters the court before her second round match against Czech Republic's Katerina Siniakova at the US Open.

The growing love affair between influencers and the premier American tennis event has caused some growing pains

NEW YORK, USA – Influencers and content creators armed with smartphones and ring lights have featured prominently in the stands at this year’s US Open, as they try to grab the spotlight away from the on-court action at one of tennis’ marquee events.

Around 100 content creators were given credentials for the tournament, organizers said, with 20 of those dedicated to providing coverage of the food and beverage scene alone, where caviar-topped chicken nuggets and the famed “Honey Deuce” cocktail promise viral attention.

Thousands more amateur social media hounds can be found throughout the plaza and in the stands — after shelling out for their own tickets.

“I feel like every Slam kind of has their own identity and the US Open has kind of always been the ‘big-show Grand Slam,'” said the 2017 finalist Madison Keys.

‘A bit disrespectful’

Celebrities have long been ubiquitous in the stands — from A-list stars to US President Donald Trump — as the ultra-wealthy shell out thousands of dollars for seats at the see-and-be-seen event of New York’s summer sporting calendar.

But the growing love affair between influencers and the premier American tennis event has caused some growing pains.

A chair umpire was forced to reprimand a group of patrons for staging a disruptive photo shoot while two-time US Open champion Naomi Osaka was serving during her first-round win against Anastasia Zakharova on Monday.

This was one of the cringiest things I’ve ever seen live. The US Open used to be an actual tennis tournament https://t.co/1kAYND6VOe pic.twitter.com/c1jbi4lUlQ — Danny Singer (@michiganboy310) September 2, 2026

“Obviously if you come to a sporting event, you have to respect the sport,” Osaka told reporters on Thursday after her second-round win over Katerina Siniakova.

“It could be a good thing for people to make the sport of tennis popular to their specific audience, but I think it has to be managed a lot better, especially in the situation like first-round match.”

Another social media user attracted attention for all the wrong reasons when she posted a series of photos posing inside Arthur Ashe Stadium while Keys was in the middle of playing a point against Alina Korneeva, which breached basic tennis etiquette.

“I can appreciate the influencers coming and kind of showcasing the US Open experience,” said 2024 runner-up Jessica Pegula.

“But I do think that it’s tough when you see videos like that when they’re taking pictures and using the selfie lights. People are down there trying to perform, and it’s their career and their job. It seems like a bit disrespectful.

“I think it’s gotten a little maybe too much.”

The trend is a direct result of the tournament’s popularity, with surging attendance leading organizers to expand the main draw action to 15 days. The tournament was further expanded with the mixed doubles competition being held as a standalone event the week before singles action kicks off.

The men’s ATP tour expanded its partnership with TikTok earlier this year, citing a more than 25% increase in posts under #tennis during 2025.

“The more we try to raise awareness about tennis, the better it is, the more popular the sport is,” said 2021 champion Daniil Medvedev.

“For sure, if it disturbs during the play, like if you see the light or something, well, you always say to the referee, can be sometimes challenging, like if during the point this happens.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Cheerers allay jitters of first day bar exam takers
World.content:
Around a dozen law students from San Beda College show up at the University of Santo Tomas to express their support for their seniors taking the bar exam.

MANILA, Philippines — Fiesta atmosphere ensued as more than 600 bar exam candidates passed through the University of Santo Tomas’s exit after finishing their first of the three-day test on Sunday.

Third-year law student Rachelyn Mae Valenzuela is among hundreds who clutched banners, placards and balloons to show their encouragement.

“We wanted to show our support to motivate and inspire them,” said Valenzuela, 26, in an interview with Inquirer.

Article continues after this 

Valenzuela was among the dozen members of San Beda College-Alabang centralized bar operations who had a presence there for more than 12 hours.

READ: First day of 2026 bar exams underway

“We know that they worked hard since the first year,” she said. “These are the fruits of their efforts for four years—manifesting that they will be Bedan lawyers come 2027.”

Mariekei Sta. Maria of the Polytechnic University of the Philippines (PUP) told Inquirer that around 20 members of their centralized bar operations accompanied their Bar takers for around 15 hours “to show our bar takers that bar examination is not just their journey but the entire PUP College of Law community.”

Sta. Maria, a second-year law student, said there were around 20 of them who had been waiting for more than 15 hours.

Article continues after this 

Other candidates also have their families to count on for support.

Janine Cea, along with her mother and two other home companions, was spotted clad in blue T-shirts with the words “JESPER IS MY LAWYER.”

Article continues after this 

Cea, 28, said they were planning to surprise her younger brother Jesper, 26, by wearing the T-shirt, which was not worn when they sent their bar candidate off the examination site.

A total of 12,029 examinees were present, and 675 of them took their test from UST, according to the data provided by the Supreme Court.

World.title: Dropping bribery rap in VP trial no issue; 1 article enough to convict – Tolosa
World.content:
House prosecution counsel Benjamin Tolosa Jr. —Screengrab from the Facebook page of the House of Representatives

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte may still be convicted in her impeachment case even if the bribery charge against her were to be dropped, as one article would be enough for that decision, according to prosecution counsel Benjamin “Jay” Tolosa Jr.

Tolosa made that statement during the Saturday News Forum at Dapo Restaurant in Quezon City, stressing that each of the four articles of impeachment stands on its own — and only one article needs to be proven for the vice president to be convicted and penalized with removal from her post and perpetual disqualification from public office.

She need not be found guilty in all of the impeachment articles, Tolosa added.

Article continues after this 

READ: Bribery rap vs VP Sara Duterte may be dropped to speed up trial

As part of efforts to shorten the trial, the prosecution has been considering whether to drop the third impeachment article, which accuses Duterte of bribery involving alleged monetary gifts or payments to Department of Education officials during her tenure as education secretary until 2024.

The prosecution has not made a final decision, as it was still studying the possibility, along with the feasibility of reducing the number of witnesses.

Article I accuses Duterte of the alleged misuse, misappropriation, and irregular liquidation of P612.5 million in confidential funds of the Office of the Vice President and Department of Education.

Article II involves allegations of unexplained wealth, incomplete disclosure of assets, and continued business interests.

Article continues after this 

Article IV concerns Duterte’s alleged grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and former Speaker Ferdinand Martin G. Romualdez.

READ: 5 witnesses left in VP secret funds scrutiny – prosec

Article continues after this 

The prosecution has already rested its presentation on the fourth article and is currently completing its evidence on the first article, with prosecutors earlier aiming to wrap up their presentation on Sept. 9.

According to a prosecution statement, the withdrawal of an impeachment article, if it should be decided, would not be unprecedented. In the 2012 impeachment trial of the late Chief Justice Renato Corona, five of the eight articles originally transmitted to the Senate were withdrawn.

World.title: 5 witnesses left in VP secret funds scrutiny – prosec
World.content:
Lead prosecutor Rep. Gerville Luistro —INQUIRER file photo by NIÑO JESUS ORBETA

MANILA, Philippines — The House prosecution hopes to wrap up its presentation on the alleged misuse of confidential funds of Vice President Sara Duterte by Wednesday, as it has only five remaining witnesses who have been subpoenaed, according to lead prosecutor Rep. Gerville Luistro.

In a statement on Sunday, Luistro listed the five remaining witnesses:

former Department of Education (DepEd) special disbursing officer (SDO) Edward Fajarda

his wife, DepEd Assistant Secretary Sunshine Charry Fajarda

Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) Assistant National Statistician Marizza Grande

Police Maj. Jovelyn Magay

Commission on Audit (COA) employee Bresilio Sabaldan among the remaining witnesses

The first impeachment article accuses the vice president of misuse, misappropriation,n and irregular liquidation of P612.5 million in confidential funds — P500 million under the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and P112.5 million under DepEd during her tenure as education secretary until 2024.

Article continues after this 

READ: Abante wants Sara Duterte subpoenaed over P612.5-M

The prosecution expects to focus this partly on the DepEd funds, which were released in three P37.5-million tranches in 2023.

But the appearance of Edward Fajarda, who served as DepEd’s SDO for the funds, remained uncertain after he suffered a stroke, which was independently confirmed by the Senate Medical and Dental Bureau.

According to Luistro, the prosecution is exploring stipulations with Duterte’s defense that could allow it to dispense with Fajarda’s testimony.

“It is our intention not to aggravate his condition. As a matter of fact, it is likewise our intention to excuse him, if possible, from the rigors of being presented in the witness stand,” she said.

Article continues after this 

Last Wednesday, defense lawyer Michael Wesley Poa, former DepEd undersecretary, chief of staff, and spokesperson, testified that he learned during a 2024 House inquiry that Fajarda had turned over all three P37.5-million confidential fund releases to then-DepEd security officer Col. Dennis Nolasco.

Grande is expected to testify on PSA records as the prosecution scrutinizes identities appearing in acknowledgment receipts submitted to support confidential fund liquidations.

Article continues after this 

The prosecution has already presented Commission on Audit auditors, OVP, and DepEd officials, and military officers to the court to trace how the funds were handled and liquidated.

Among these witnesses, former OVP SDO Gina Acosta testified that she turned over four P125-million confidential fund tranches to then-security chief Col. Raymund Dante Lachica upon Duterte’s instruction.

Army officers also testified that their units received no DepEd confidential funds for Youth Leadership Summits and information campaigns cited in military certifications later used by DepEd in responding to COA findings.

The prosecution has since dropped Lachica, Nolasco, and Ramil Madriaga — Duterte’s alleged bagman — as witnesses after concluding that evidence already presented was sufficient for the points it sought to establish.

World.title: PNP reshuffles 7 officials, names new NCRPO district directors
World.content:
Philippine National Police headquarters in Camp Crame. File photo

MANILA, Philippines — Seven senior officials have been reassigned in the latest reorganization of the Philippine National Police (PNP), including the directors of two police districts in the National Capital Region.

In a document obtained on Sunday, Eastern Police District (EPD) Director Brig. Gen. Melecio Buslig Jr. was designated as chief of the PNP Firearms and Explosives Office (FEO), while Southern Police District (SPD) Director Brig. Gen. Glenn Oliver Cinco was named chief of the Supervisory Office for Security and Investigation Agencies (SOSIA).

The FEO, a specialized unit under the PNP Civil Security Group (CSG), regulates and manages the legal ownership, control, and use of firearms and explosives in the country.

Article continues after this 

The SOSIA, also under the CSG, is responsible for regulating, licensing and supervising private security agencies.

READ: PNP reshuffle: 9 senior officers given new posts

Brig. Gen. Roman Arugay, formerly with the Office of the PNP chief, will take over as Buslig as EPD director, while Brig. Gen. Rodel Pastor will assume the post of SPD director from Cinco.

Meanwhile, Police Regional Office (PRO)-Eastern Visayas Director Brig. Gen. Jason Capoy was designated chief of the Human Rights Affairs Office, also under the Office of the PNP chief.

Capoy will be replaced by Brig. Gen. Romano Cardiño, who will pass the leadership of PRO-Negros Island Region to Brig. Gen. Rudecindo Reales.

The reshuffle takes effect Sept. 7.

World.title: Baguio sets Burnham Lake boat fare at P250
World.content:
Visitors flock to the newly rehabilitated Burnham Lake in Baguio City after it reopened on Sept. 1 following a 10-month rehabilitation. (Photo by Maureen Matayew)

BAGUIO CITY — The city government ordered Burnham Park boat concessionaires to retain the P250 rental fee for a 30-minute ride, regardless of boat size, following a reported rate increase after the lake reopened.

The status quo took effect Sept. 2 after a meeting led by City Environment and Parks Management Office (CEPMO) head Rhenan Diwas, with City Administrator Vittorio Jerico Cawis also in attendance. Diwas said no rate increase had been authorized, as any adjustment still requires City Council approval.

Only two of the nine boat owners had complied with the city’s boat upgrading requirement as of Sept. 2, Diwas said. Boats that have not been upgraded will not be allowed for public use.

Article continues after this 

READ: Baguio’s Burnham Lake reopens after yearlong closure

The concessionaires were also ordered to issue official receipts to customers. Diwas said an earlier agreement allowing a possible rental fee adjustment was conditional on compliance with the upgrading requirement and securing City Council approval.

Cawis warned that concessionaires who continue to disregard the requirements could lose their slots, which would then be opened to other interested residents. “This is the final warning,” he said.

The meeting followed Mayor Benjamin Magalong’s directive for an immediate investigation into the reported increase in boat rental fees. Magalong warned that concessionaires found taking advantage of the public would face sanctions.

The Burnham Park lake reopened on Sept. 1 after 10 months of rehabilitation as part of the city’s 117th Charter Day anniversary celebration. /mcm

World.title: Butuan declares state of calamity as water crisis worsens
World.content:
The Butuan City Water District’s Pump Station 1 in Barangay Baan, Butuan City. (Photo from Butuan City Public Information Office)

SAN FRANCISCO, Agusan del Sur — Butuan City has been placed under a state of calamity as a prolonged extreme dry spell continues to disrupt water services, affecting a third of its population.

The state of calamity was declared on Saturday, Sept. 5, during the Sangguniang Panlungsod (SP) 3rd Special Session, which was presided over by Vice Mayor Reynante Desiata.

“The resolution was approved as the continuing water shortage has significantly affected residents’ access to water across several barangays,” the SP said in a statement.

Article continues after this 

READ: El Niño could be strongest in decades, UN warns

As of Sept. 4, the Butuan City Water District (BCWD) reported that 91,425, or a third of its 269,000 residents, are experiencing low-pressure to no-water service as water availability continues to decline.

The water shortage is linked to the prevailing dry spell in Agusan del Norte, including Butuan City, which has experienced a significant rainfall deficit.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration said the province had been under dry spell conditions since Aug. 23.

BCWD and the city government have already implemented water rationing and other measures in affected areas, but these interventions remain insufficient as the shortage continues, the resolution stated.

Article continues after this 

While residents acknowledged the importance of water rationing during emergencies, a constituent pointed out that the program should not become a substitute for reliable infrastructure and long-term preparation.

READ: El Niño takes toll on Bukidnon rice farms

Article continues after this 

“Emergency measures should remain emergency measures. They cannot become institutionalized substitutes for infrastructure,” Luna Kaisog stated.

The state of calamity declaration allows the city government and affected barangays to mobilize additional resources and access their quick response funds for measures such as the supply and installation of water tanks, tankers, pumps, filtration systems, and other needs for water distribution and rationing.

The city Public Information Office (PIO) said the local government is doing everything possible to assist affected residents.

Authorities are assessing several pumping stations for possible rehabilitation. Based on BCWD recommendations, Pumping Stations 2, 3, and 16 have been identified as potential sources of additional water.

The city government and BCWD are also considering conducting geo-resistivity surveys to locate groundwater sources, assess aquifer levels, and determine whether the water found is fresh or saline. Several areas are also being evaluated for possible re-drilling.

The PIO said any source considered for rehabilitation or development would undergo testing to determine its water quality, yield, and long-term reliability before being used for public distribution.

An open letter from concerned residents questioned the reliability of the BCWD’s water sources, its contingency measures, and the billing of customers who receive little or no water.

Engr. Sergio Pascual, a former city councilor, blamed the crisis on what he described as an alleged failure of leadership among city officials.
